use: Use for a patient with gestational hypertension or preeclampsia, antepartum or postpartum.
body:
Hypertensive disorder of pregnancy note

_yo G_ P_ at _w_d with _.

BP values: _, _, _ at _ and _

Severe features checklist:

- [ ] SBP 160 or higher or DBP 110 or higher, confirmed within 15 minutes
- [ ] Platelets under 100,000
- [ ] AST or ALT twice upper limit of normal or more
- [ ] Severe persistent RUQ or epigastric pain
- [ ] Creatinine over 1.1 or doubled
- [ ] Pulmonary edema
- [ ] New headache unresponsive to medication
- [ ] Visual disturbances

Labs: CBC _, CMP _, UPCR _

Assessment:
_gestational hypertension / preeclampsia _with / without severe features.

Plan:

- START magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 min, then 2 g/hr IV, _ indicated
- CONT magnesium sulfate 24 hr postpartum
- DECR. magnesium sulfate rate if renal impairment
- Severe-range BP persisting 15 min: treat within 30 to 60 min with one of the following
- START labetalol 20 mg IV, then 40 mg IV after 10 min, then 80 mg IV after 10 min. Avoid in asthma, heart failure, or bradycardia
- START hydralazine 5 to 10 mg IV over 2 min, repeat 10 mg IV after 20 min
- START nifedipine immediate release 10 mg PO, then 20 mg PO after 20 min, then 20 mg PO after 20 min
- START maintenance nifedipine ER 30 mg PO daily, or labetalol 200 mg PO BID _
- Labs every _ hr
- Antenatal testing from dx: twice weekly without severe features, daily with severe features
- Delivery timing, gHTN or preeclampsia without severe features: 37w0d, or at dx if later
- Delivery timing, severe-range BP or severe features, stable: 34w0d, or at dx if later
- Delivery timing, unstable, HELLP, or before viability: soon after maternal stabilization
- START betamethasone 12 mg IM q24h x 2 doses if <34w0d, consider expectant care
- Postpartum BP check within 72 hr if severe, otherwise within 7 to 10 days

use: Use for a neonatal circumcision by Gomco or Plastibell in the residency note format; delete the device paragraph not used.
body:
Neonatal Circumcision Procedure Note

Preoperative diagnosis: Parents desire neonatal circumcision
Postoperative diagnosis: Same
Procedure: Neonatal circumcision, _Gomco / Plastibell, _ cm
Operator: _, supervised by attending Dr. _
Preprocedure counseling: The risks, benefits, and alternatives of the procedure were discussed with the parent or guardian, who consented.

Description: A timeout was performed. The infant was placed supine and restrained. Penile anatomy was normal without hypospadias or chordee _. Oral sucrose 24% was given for analgesia. _ mL of 1% lidocaine without epinephrine, max 0.3 mL/kg, was injected as a _ dorsal penile nerve block or ring block. The field was prepped with _ and draped in sterile fashion.

Gomco: The foreskin was clamped and a dorsal slit made. Adhesions were released bluntly to the coronal margin. The _ cm Gomco clamp was placed with the dorsal slit fully included and the foreskin symmetric on all sides. The clamp was tightened and left in place for _ minutes, the foreskin was excised with a scalpel, and the clamp was removed. Hemostasis was confirmed. Petrolatum gauze dressing applied.

Plastibell: The foreskin was clamped and a dorsal slit made. Adhesions were released bluntly to the coronal margin. The _ cm Plastibell was placed over the glans with the dorsal slit fully included, and the string was tied securely in the groove. The skin blanched beneath the string. The foreskin was trimmed with scissors about 3 mm distal to the string. The bell was not too tight on the glans and did not obstruct the urethra.

EBL: under _ mL
Complications: _

Care instructions given: petroleum jelly with each diaper change, return for bleeding, no wet diaper in 12 hours, fever, or spreading redness _.

The attending physician, Dr. _, was present throughout the entire procedure.

use: Use as after-visit instructions at the new OB or early prenatal visits.
body:
Your first trimester

Your first visits check your health and your baby's due date. Visits are about every 4 weeks.

Tests at the first visit:

- Blood tests for blood type, blood count, immunity to rubella, HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis
- Urine test
- Pap test if you are due
- Ultrasound to confirm your due date, if needed

Genetic screening is your choice. A blood test can screen for Down syndrome and other conditions after 10 weeks. Your choice: _

Take a prenatal vitamin with folic acid every day.

Low-dose aspirin: _

Bring your questions about medicines, food, travel, and exercise to every visit.

Your next visit: _

Call the clinic if you have:

- Bleeding or cramping
- Vomiting so much you cannot keep fluids down
- Burning when you pee
- Fever

Go to the ER if you have:

- Heavy bleeding
- Bad pain on one side of your belly
- Shoulder pain
- Fainting

use: Use as after-visit instructions at second trimester prenatal visits.
body:
Your second trimester

Visits are every 4 weeks. Most people feel their best in this trimester.

Anatomy ultrasound at 18 to 22 weeks:

- Checks your baby's brain, heart, spine, kidneys, and limbs
- Checks where your placenta is
- Your appointment: _

Sugar test at 24 to 28 weeks:

- You drink a sweet drink and have blood drawn 1 hour later.
- A high result does not mean you have diabetes. It means you need a longer test.

You should start to feel your baby move between 18 and 22 weeks.

Start thinking about childbirth classes, feeding plans, choosing a doctor for your baby, and leave from work.

Your next visit: _

Call the clinic if you have:

- Bleeding or leaking fluid
- Cramping or tightening that comes regularly
- A bad headache or vision changes
- Burning when you pee or fever

use: Use as after-visit instructions at third trimester prenatal visits.
body:
Your third trimester

Visits are every 2 weeks from 28 weeks, then every week from 36 weeks.

At 28 weeks:

- Blood count and repeat tests as needed
- Rh shot if your blood type is Rh negative: _
- Tdap shot to protect your baby from whooping cough

At 36 to 37 weeks:

- Group B strep swab. About 1 in 4 people carry this germ. It is not an STI. If positive, you get antibiotics in labor to protect your baby.
- We check your baby's position.

We will talk about your birth plan, pain control, and what happens if you go past your due date.

Count your baby's kicks every day.

Your next visit: _

Go to the hospital if:

- You have contractions 5 minutes apart for 1 hour
- Your water breaks
- You have bleeding like a period
- Your baby moves less than usual
- You have a bad headache, vision changes, or pain under your right ribs

Call Labor and Delivery with questions: _

use: Use as after-visit instructions about prenatal vitamins and folic acid.
body:
Prenatal vitamins

Folic acid is the most important part. Take 400 to 800 mcg every day. It helps prevent birth defects of the brain and spine. Your dose: _

Iron helps your blood. Iodine, vitamin D, calcium, and DHA are also helpful.

If your vitamin makes you sick:

- Take it at night, or with food.
- Ask us about a vitamin with less iron.
- Gummy vitamins are easier to take, but most have no iron. You may need iron separately.
- A vitamin you can keep down is better than one you cannot.

Store-brand vitamins work as well as expensive ones.

Do not take extra vitamin A. Do not take 2 prenatal vitamins to get more of something.

Bring all your supplements and herbal products to your next visit.

Call the clinic if you cannot keep any vitamin down, or cost is a problem.

use: Use as after-visit instructions about food safety and infection prevention.
body:
Food safety in pregnancy

Some germs in food can harm your baby. Listeria is rare but serious.

Avoid:

- Deli meat and hot dogs unless heated until steaming
- Unpasteurized milk, cheese, and juice
- Raw or undercooked meat, eggs, and seafood
- Refrigerated smoked fish unless cooked in a dish
- Raw sprouts

Safe:

- Pasteurized cheese, like cottage, cream, string, feta, and mozzarella. Queso fresco and similar fresh cheeses are safe only if heated until steaming.
- Meat, eggs, and fish cooked all the way through

Other tips:

- Wash fruits and vegetables well.
- Wash hands and cutting boards after touching raw meat.
- Have someone else change the cat litter. If you must, wear gloves and wash your hands.
- Wear gloves when gardening.

Call the clinic if you have fever, muscle aches, or diarrhea after eating a risky food.

use: Use as after-visit instructions about fish and mercury.
body:
Fish in pregnancy

Fish is good for you and your baby's brain and eyes. Eat 2 to 3 servings a week, about 8 to 12 ounces total. Some fish have mercury, which can harm your baby.

Best choices:

- Salmon, sardines, trout, tilapia, cod, catfish, and pollock
- Canned light tuna, shrimp, crab, and scallops

Once a week at most:

- Albacore or white tuna, halibut, grouper, and Chilean sea bass

Do not eat:

- Shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico, marlin, orange roughy, and bigeye tuna

Cook fish until it flakes apart. Avoid raw fish, including sushi made with raw fish.

If you catch your own fish, check your state's advice for those waters.

Call the clinic with questions about a fish not on this list.

use: Use as answers to common "is it safe" questions in pregnancy.
body:
Is it safe in pregnancy?

Caffeine: yes, less than 200 mg a day. That is about one 12-ounce cup of coffee. Tea, soda, and chocolate count too.

Hair dye: yes. Very little gets through your scalp. If you are worried, wait until after 13 weeks.

Baths: warm baths are fine. Avoid hot tubs and saunas, especially in the first 3 months.

Sex: yes, in a normal pregnancy. It does not cause miscarriage or early labor. We will tell you if you need to avoid it.

Exercise: yes. It does not cause miscarriage. Aim for 150 minutes a week.

Eating for two: no. You do not need extra calories in the first 3 months. Add about 340 calories a day in the middle 3 months. Add about 450 a day in the last 3 months.

Medicines: acetaminophen is the best choice for pain. Do not take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin unless we tell you to. Ask us before taking any new medicine or herbal product.

Call the clinic with any other questions.

use: Use as after-visit instructions about vaccines in pregnancy.
body:
Vaccines in pregnancy

Vaccines in pregnancy protect you, and they pass protection to your baby.

Recommended:

- Tdap, for whooping cough, at 27 to 36 weeks in every pregnancy. Your baby is born with protection.
- Flu shot, in any trimester during flu season. Use the shot, not the nose spray.
- RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season, or an RSV shot for your baby after birth. Your baby needs one or the other, not both. Your plan: _
- COVID-19 vaccine: _

Wait until after birth:

- MMR and chickenpox vaccines are not given in pregnancy. If you are not immune, you can get them before you leave the hospital. They are safe while breastfeeding.

People who will hold your baby should be up to date on Tdap and flu shots.

Call the clinic if you are traveling, or there is an outbreak where you live.

use: Use as after-visit instructions about alcohol in pregnancy.
body:
Alcohol in pregnancy

No amount of alcohol is known to be safe in pregnancy. The safest choice is not to drink.

Heavy drinking and binge drinking can cause lifelong problems for your baby. These problems can be prevented.

Drinking before you knew you were pregnant is very common. Tell us how much so we know what to watch for.

If you drink every day, do not stop suddenly on your own. Stopping suddenly can be dangerous. We can help you stop safely.

Call the clinic if you need help cutting back or stopping.

After stopping, go to the ER if you shake, sweat, see things that are not there, or have a seizure.

desc: Smoking, vaping, and cannabis in pregnancy
use: Use as after-visit instructions about tobacco, vaping, and cannabis in pregnancy.
body:
Smoking, vaping, and cannabis in pregnancy

Quitting helps at any point in pregnancy. The sooner the better.

Smoking and vaping:

- Lower the blood flow to your baby
- Raise the risk of a small baby, early birth, stillbirth, and SIDS

Vaping is not safe. Nicotine itself is harmful.

Cannabis:

- Crosses to your baby in any form, smoked, vaped, or eaten
- Is linked to small babies and learning problems later
- Is not a safe treatment for nausea. We have better options.

After birth, keep your home and car smoke-free. Smoke on clothes and hair also harms babies.

Help to quit: _. Free help: call 1-800-QUIT-NOW.

Call the clinic if you want help quitting.

use: Use as after-visit instructions about exercise in pregnancy.
body:
Exercise in pregnancy

Exercise is safe and healthy for most pregnancies. Aim for 150 minutes a week, like 30 minutes on 5 days.

Exercise helps:

- Back pain, swelling, and constipation
- Sleep, mood, and energy
- Lower the risk of gestational diabetes and high blood pressure

Good choices:

- Walking
- Swimming and water exercise
- Prenatal yoga
- Stationary bike
- Light weights. Do not hold your breath.
- Kegels, 3 sets of 10 every day

Avoid:

- Lying flat on your back for a long time after 13 weeks
- Contact sports and activities where you could fall
- Scuba diving
- Hot yoga or exercise in high heat

You should be able to talk while you exercise. If you cannot, slow down.

Stop exercising. Call the clinic if you have:

- Bleeding or leaking fluid
- Dizziness or chest pain
- Bad shortness of breath
- Regular contractions
- Less movement from your baby
- Calf pain or swelling

- Sleep, mood, and energy
- Lower the risk of gestational diabetes and high blood pressure

Good choices:

- Walking
- Swimming and water exercise
- Prenatal yoga
- Stationary bike
- Light weights. Do not hold your breath.
- Kegels, 3 sets of 10 every day

Avoid:

- Lying flat on your back for a long time after 13 weeks
- Contact sports and activities where you could fall
- Scuba diving
- Hot yoga or exercise in high heat

You should be able to talk while you exercise. If you cannot, slow down.

Stop exercising. Call the clinic if you have:

- Bleeding or leaking fluid
- Dizziness or chest pain
- Bad shortness of breath
- Regular contractions
- Less movement from your baby
- Calf pain or swelling

use: Use as after-visit instructions for heartburn, aches, hemorrhoids, sleep, and swelling in pregnancy.
body:
Common discomforts of pregnancy

These are common and not dangerous. Here is what helps.

Heartburn:

- Eat small meals. Do not eat 3 hours before lying down.
- Raise the head of your bed.
- Sodium alginate tablets or capsules can help. Take them after meals and at bedtime.
- Calcium carbonate chews, like Tums, are safe. With 500 mg chews, take no more than 5 a day.
- Take calcium chews at least 2 hours apart from iron or your prenatal vitamin.

Sharp pain low on one side:

- This is often stretching of the ligaments that hold the uterus.
- Move slowly when you stand or roll over. Use warmth.

Constipation and hemorrhoids:

- Drink water, eat fiber, and move every day.
- Put your feet on a stool when you sit on the toilet. Do not strain.
- Witch hazel pads and warm sitz baths help.

Back pain:

- Wear flat shoes. Use a pillow between your knees at night.
- A belly support belt helps some people.

Sleep and leg cramps:

- Sleep on either side after 20 weeks. If you wake up on your back, just turn over.
- Stretch your calves for leg cramps.

Swelling in the feet:

- Put your feet up. Wear compression socks.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Sudden swelling of the face or hands
- One calf that is swollen, painful, or warm
- Belly pain that does not go away, or comes with bleeding, fever, or regular tightening
- Burning when you pee
- Itching of your palms or soles, worse at night, with no rash

use: Use as after-visit instructions about depression and anxiety in pregnancy.
body:
Mood in pregnancy

Depression and anxiety are common in pregnancy. They are not your fault, and they can be treated.

Tell us if you have:

- Low mood most days
- Lost interest in things you enjoy
- Worry that will not stop, or scary thoughts that pop into your head
- Trouble sleeping, even when you have the chance to sleep
- Any thoughts of hurting yourself

Treatment helps you and your baby. Untreated depression raises the risk of early birth and depression after birth.

What helps:

- Counseling, alone or with medicine
- Several medicines are safe in pregnancy. If you stopped a medicine when you got pregnant, tell us.
- Sleep, sunlight, exercise, and time with people who support you

Your plan: _

Call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline any time: 1-833-TLC-MAMA, which is 1-833-852-6262.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988. Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

use: Use as after-visit instructions about preeclampsia, blood pressure, and aspirin.
body:
Preeclampsia warning signs

Preeclampsia is high blood pressure in pregnancy that can affect your organs and your baby. It usually starts after 20 weeks. It can also start in the first weeks after birth. Finding it early helps.

Low-dose aspirin can lower your risk. Your plan: _

Your blood pressure today: _
Next blood pressure check: _

Go to Labor and Delivery or the ER right away if you have:

- A headache that will not go away with acetaminophen
- Vision changes, like spots or flashing lights
- Pain under your right ribs or high in your belly
- Sudden swelling of your face or hands
- Trouble breathing
- Blood pressure of 160 over 110 or higher

Call the clinic the same day if your blood pressure is 140 over 90 or higher.

After your baby is born, these signs still matter. Do not wait for your postpartum visit.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for fetal movement counting.
body:
Kick counts

After 28 weeks, count your baby's movements every day. You learn what is normal for your baby.

How to count:

- Pick a time when your baby is usually active, like after a meal.
- Lie on your side or sit with your feet up.
- Count kicks, rolls, and jabs. Hiccups do not count.
- Most babies move 10 times in less than 2 hours, often much faster.

If you feel fewer than 10 movements in 2 hours, go to Labor and Delivery now.

Also go now if your baby moves much less than usual, even if you counted 10.

Do not wait until the next day. Do not try to make your baby move with cold drinks or sugar first.

Labor and Delivery phone: _

Call the clinic with questions about counting.

use: Use as after-visit instructions about when to go to L&D.
body:
Signs of labor: when to go in

True labor:

- Contractions get longer, stronger, and closer together.
- They do not stop when you rest or change position.
- Pain often starts in the back and moves to the front.

False labor:

- Contractions are uneven and do not get stronger.
- They often stop with rest, water, or a change in position.

When to go to the hospital:

- First baby: contractions 5 minutes apart, lasting 1 minute each, for 1 hour.
- Second or later baby: go sooner, when contractions are 6 to 8 minutes apart.

Go in right away if:

- Your water breaks, as a gush or a steady trickle
- You have bright red bleeding, more than spotting
- Your baby moves less than usual
- You have bad belly pain that does not stop
- You have a bad headache, vision changes, or sudden swelling

Early labor is often more comfortable at home. Try a warm shower, walking, rest, fluids, and a light snack.

Call Labor and Delivery with questions: _

use: Use as after-visit instructions about preterm labor warning signs before 37 weeks.
body:
Signs of early labor

Labor before 37 weeks is early, or preterm. Getting care fast can help your baby.

Go to Labor and Delivery right away if you have any of these before 37 weeks:

- Tightening or contractions every 10 minutes or more often. That is 6 or more in 1 hour.
- Cramps like a period
- Low, dull backache that comes and goes
- Pressure in your pelvis, like the baby is pushing down
- Leaking fluid from your vagina
- Bleeding or spotting
- Discharge that changes and becomes watery, mucus-like, or bloody

Do not wait to see if it goes away.

Labor and Delivery phone: _

Call the clinic if you are not sure what you are feeling.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for bleeding or cramping in early pregnancy.
body:
Bleeding in early pregnancy

Light spotting in early pregnancy is common and often normal. Sometimes it is a sign of miscarriage or a pregnancy outside the uterus, called an ectopic pregnancy.

Your plan:

- Blood test or ultrasound on _
- Use pads, not tampons, so you can see how much you bleed.
- Rest as you feel you need. Activity does not cause miscarriage.

Call the clinic if:

- Bleeding gets heavier or does not stop
- Cramping gets worse
- You pass tissue

Go to the ER right away if you have:

- Bleeding that soaks more than 2 pads an hour for 2 hours
- Bad pain, especially on one side of your belly
- Pain in your shoulder tip
- Dizziness or fainting
- Fever

If your blood type is Rh negative, you may need a shot. Tell any ER you visit.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
body:
Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

Nausea is very common in early pregnancy. It usually gets better by 14 to 16 weeks.

What helps:

- Eat small snacks every 1 to 2 hours. Do not let your stomach get empty.
- Keep crackers by your bed. Eat a few before you get up.
- Eat foods that sound good, even if they are plain.
- Sip fluids between meals, not with meals.
- Try ginger tea, ginger candy, or ginger capsules.
- Avoid smells that bother you.
- Take your prenatal vitamin at night, or switch to one without iron.

Acupressure you can try:

- Find the spot 3 finger widths above your wrist crease, on the palm side, between the 2 tendons.
- Press firmly with your thumb in small circles for 2 to 3 minutes. Then do the other wrist.
- Repeat a few times a day, or wear an acupressure wristband on this spot.
- It may help some people. Keep using the other steps too.

Medicine:

- Vitamin B6, 25 mg by mouth 3 times a day
- You can add doxylamine, 12.5 mg by mouth at bedtime. It can make you sleepy.
- Other medicine: _

If you also have heartburn:

- Heartburn can make nausea worse. Treating it may help both.
- Do not lie down for 3 hours after you eat.
- Try sodium alginate tablets or capsules. It should be the only ingredient listed under Supplement Facts.
- Take _ mg after meals and at bedtime, or as the label says.
- Calcium carbonate chews also help. With 500 mg chews, take no more than 5 a day.
- Do not use baking soda for heartburn.
- Take calcium chews at least 2 hours apart from your prenatal vitamin or iron.

Call the clinic if you cannot keep any food down for 1 day, or you are losing weight.

Go to the ER if you:

- Cannot keep fluids down
- Have not peed in 8 hours
- Vomit blood
- Feel faint

use: Use as after-visit instructions for gestational diabetes.
body:
Gestational diabetes

Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that starts in pregnancy. With good care, most people have healthy babies.

Check your blood sugar:

- When you wake up, before eating. Goal: below 95.
- 1 hour after each meal. Goal: below 140.
- Or 2 hours after each meal. Goal: below 120.
- Write down every number and bring your log to every visit.

Food:

- Eat 3 small meals and 2 to 3 snacks a day.
- Eat protein with every meal and snack.
- Limit bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, and sweets. Choose whole grains.
- Do not drink juice, soda, or sweet tea.

Walk for 10 to 15 minutes after meals. It lowers your blood sugar.

Medicine: _

You may need extra ultrasounds and baby heart rate checks later in pregnancy.

After birth, you need a sugar test at 4 to 12 weeks. Your risk of type 2 diabetes stays higher for life, so get checked every 1 to 3 years.

Call the clinic if:

- Your numbers are above goal 2 or more times in a week
- Your sugar is below 70

use: Use as after-visit instructions when an induction is scheduled.
body:
Induction of labor

An induction means starting labor with medicine or other methods.

Your induction: _ at _
Reason: _

What to expect:

- Medicine or a small balloon may be used to soften and open your cervix.
- If you had a C-section before, we use the balloon, not the softening medicine.
- Then a medicine through your IV may be used to start contractions.
- Induction can take 12 to 24 hours or longer, especially with a first baby. Plan for it to take time.
- Your baby's heart rate will be watched.

If this is your first baby and your pregnancy is healthy:

- You can choose induction at 39 weeks, or wait for labor to start.
- With induction, fewer people had a C-section: about 19 in 100, compared with 22 in 100.
- Fewer had high blood pressure in pregnancy: about 9 in 100, compared with 14 in 100.
- Babies did just as well, and fewer needed help breathing.
- You will likely spend longer on Labor and Delivery, about 20 hours instead of 14.

Before you come:

- Eat a normal meal before you arrive, unless we tell you not to.
- Call Labor and Delivery before you leave home. Sometimes the unit is busy and your time may change.
- Bring your hospital bag.

Call Labor and Delivery or go in before your induction time if:

- Your water breaks
- You have bleeding
- Your baby moves less
- You have regular contractions

Labor and Delivery phone: _

use: Use as after-visit instructions about labor pain relief options.
body:
Pain relief in labor

There is no right way to manage labor pain. You can change your mind at any time.

Without medicine:

- Warm shower or tub
- Walking, rocking, a birthing ball, or changing positions
- Slow breathing
- Firm pressure on your lower back
- Heat on your back and cool cloths on your face

With medicine:

- Nitrous oxide, or laughing gas. You hold the mask. It takes the edge off and wears off in minutes.
- IV pain medicine. It takes the edge off but can make you and your baby sleepy.
- Epidural. This is the strongest pain relief. A thin tube in your lower back numbs the pain. You stay awake.

Epidural facts:

- It does not raise your chance of a C-section.
- Pushing may take longer.
- You will have an IV and a monitor on your belly.

Your preferences: _

Call the clinic with questions about your birth plan.

use: Use as after-visit instructions when referring to maternal-fetal medicine.
body:
High-risk pregnancy referral

We are referring you to Maternal-Fetal Medicine, or MFM. MFM doctors are experts in pregnancies that need extra care. A referral means you get expert help. It does not mean something is wrong.

Reason for referral: _

What MFM may do:

- Detailed ultrasounds of your baby
- Extra checks of your baby's growth
- Advice on medicines, delivery timing, and how you deliver

Most people still deliver with their usual doctor.

Questions to ask MFM:

- What is the concern?
- How will it be watched?
- Does it change when or how I deliver?

Your MFM appointment: _

Call the clinic if you do not hear about your appointment within 1 week.

use: Use as after-visit instructions about VBAC and repeat cesarean.
body:
Birth after a C-section

Many people who had 1 C-section can safely try a vaginal birth. This is called VBAC.

About 60 to 80 out of 100 people who try VBAC succeed.

Things that affect your chances:

- The reason for your last C-section
- The type of cut on your uterus
- Whether you have had a vaginal birth before
- Your health in this pregnancy
- Whether the hospital can do an emergency C-section any time

Risks of VBAC: a small chance that the scar on your uterus opens in labor, less than 1 in 100. This can be serious, which is why labor is watched closely.

Risks of repeat C-section: surgery risks, a longer recovery, and more risk with each future pregnancy.

Your plan: _

Call the clinic if you want to talk more about your options.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for constipation in pregnancy.
body:
Constipation in pregnancy

Constipation is common in pregnancy. Hormones slow your bowels, and iron pills can make it worse.

What helps:

- Drink 8 to 10 cups of water a day.
- Warm soups and broth count as fluid. Soups with beans, lentils, or vegetables add fiber too.
- A warm drink with breakfast can help you go.
- Eat fruits, vegetables, beans, and whole grains.
- Kiwis and prunes help. Try 2 green kiwis or about 10 prunes a day.
- Add psyllium fiber, 1 tablespoon a day in water. Start slowly.
- Walk every day.
- Go when you feel the urge. Put your feet on a stool.

Medicine that is safe in pregnancy:

- Polyethylene glycol, 17 grams in 8 ounces of liquid, once a day.
- For a few days only, if needed: senna or bisacodyl at bedtime.

Do not use mineral oil, castor oil, or enemas unless we tell you to.

If you take iron, ask us about taking it every other day.

Call the clinic if you have no stool in 4 days with medicine, or blood in your stool.

Go to Labor and Delivery if you have belly pain that comes and goes regularly, bleeding, or leaking fluid.

- Kiwis and prunes help. Try 2 green kiwis or about 10 prunes a day.
- Add psyllium fiber, 1 tablespoon a day in water. Start slowly.
- Walk every day.
- Go when you feel the urge. Put your feet on a stool.

Medicine that is safe in pregnancy:

- Polyethylene glycol, 17 grams in 8 ounces of liquid, once a day.
- For a few days only, if needed: senna or bisacodyl at bedtime.

Do not use mineral oil, castor oil, or enemas unless we tell you to.

If you take iron, ask us about taking it every other day.

Call the clinic if you have no stool in 4 days with medicine, or blood in your stool.

Go to Labor and Delivery if you have belly pain that comes and goes regularly, bleeding, or leaking fluid.

desc: Getting ready for pregnancy, for dads
use: Use as instructions for a male partner when a couple is planning a pregnancy.
body:
Getting ready for pregnancy, for dads

Your health matters before your partner gets pregnant. Sperm take about 2 to 3 months to grow. Changes you make now can help.

Smoking, alcohol, and drugs:

- Quit smoking, vaping, and chewing tobacco. Smoking lowers sperm quality.
- Keep your home and car smoke-free. Secondhand smoke is harmful in pregnancy.
- Stop using marijuana. Regular use can lower sperm count.
- Stop other drugs, like cocaine, meth, or pain pills not prescribed to you.
- Cut back on alcohol. Heavy drinking can harm sperm.

Steroids and testosterone:

- Anabolic steroids and testosterone shots, gels, or pills can stop sperm production.
- Sperm can take months to come back after stopping. Sometimes it takes up to 2 years.
- If you take testosterone, tell us. There may be other options while you try for a baby.

Keep sperm cool:

- Heat can lower your sperm count. Limit hot tubs and long hot baths.
- Do not rest a laptop on your lap for long periods.
- If you work in the heat, take cooling breaks in the shade or air conditioning.

A healthy body:

- Aim for a healthy weight. Obesity can lower sperm quality.
- Eat vegetables, fruit, whole grains, fish, and chicken.
- Limit processed meat and sugary drinks.
- Stay active. Exercise with your partner if you can.
- Get enough sleep.

Medicines and work:

- Bring all your medicines and supplements to your visit. Some can affect sperm.
- Do not stop a prescription medicine on your own. Talk with us first.
- If you work with lead, pesticides, solvents, or radiation, ask your employer how to stay safe.
- If you work with chemicals, change clothes and wash up before going home.

Infections and vaccines:

- Get tested for STIs if you or your partner could be at risk. This includes HIV.
- If you have an STI, you both need treatment before trying for a baby.
- Get a flu shot every year.
- Get a Tdap shot at least 2 weeks before the baby is born.
- Stay up to date on your other vaccines.

Family history:

- Tell us about birth defects or genetic diseases in your family.
- If your partner carries a gene for an inherited disease, you may be tested too.

Support your partner:

- Help your partner remember to take folic acid every day.
- Go to prenatal visits together when you can.
- Make healthy changes together. A supportive partner can lower stress for both of you.

Your mood matters:

- Stress can affect sperm. Exercise, sleep, and talking with people you trust can help.
- Partners can get depression too. About 1 in 10 dads have depression during pregnancy or after birth.
- Tell us if you feel down, worried, or angry most days.

Your plan: _

Call the clinic if you have questions about a medicine. Call if you want help to quit smoking, drinking, or drugs.

Call or text 988 if you have thoughts of hurting yourself. Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

desc: Your relationship during pregnancy and after birth
use: Use as instructions for a couple about their relationship during pregnancy and after birth.
body:
Your relationship during pregnancy and after birth

Pregnancy and a new baby change a relationship. Ups and downs are normal for both partners. Talking and teamwork help.

Common changes:

- Mood swings are common in early pregnancy, for both partners.
- Late pregnancy can bring poor sleep and aches.
- After birth, you will both be tired. It takes time to adjust.
- Many couples have less time alone together for a while.

Talk with each other:

- Check in with each other for a few minutes each day.
- Listen first. Then share how you feel.
- Talk about money, chores, and baby care before the baby comes.
- Agree on who you will call when you need help.

Share the load:

- Split chores, meals, and errands. Make a plan you both agree on.
- Take turns getting up with the baby at night when you can.
- If the baby is breastfed, the partner can bring the baby to feed, change diapers, and burp the baby.
- Sleep when the baby sleeps. Protect each other's sleep.
- Take time off from work after the birth if you can. Time off helps the whole family.

Sex and closeness:

- Sex is safe during pregnancy unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
- As the belly grows, you may need new positions. Talk about what feels good.
- After birth, many doctors suggest waiting about 6 weeks. Ask when it is safe for you.
- Low interest in sex for months after birth is normal. Hugs and time together still matter.
- A water-based lubricant can help if sex is dry or uncomfortable.
- You can get pregnant soon after birth. Plan your birth control before the baby comes.

The partner's role:

- Come to prenatal visits when you can.
- Take a childbirth class together.
- Talk ahead of time about how to help in labor.
- Back rubs, timing contractions, and calm words can help during labor.
- Put in a rear-facing car seat before the due date.
- Get a flu shot and a Tdap shot before the baby comes.

Mood after birth:

- Sadness and tears in the first week or two after birth are common. This is called the baby blues.
- Sadness or worry that lasts longer may be depression or anxiety. It can be treated.
- Partners can get depression too. About 1 in 10 dads have depression during pregnancy or after birth.
- Often the partner notices the signs first. Help each other get care.

Money and stress:

- A baby brings new costs. Make a simple budget together.
- Ask us about programs that can help if money is tight.
- Stress is easier to handle when you face it as a team.

Help from family and friends:

- Say yes when people offer meals, chores, or rides.
- Tell visitors what help you need.
- Ask for help early. Do not wait for a crisis.

Safety at home:

- Arguments happen in every relationship. Hitting, threats, and forced sex are never OK.
- Abuse can start or get worse during pregnancy.
- Controlling your money, phone, friends, or birth control is also abuse.
- You deserve to be safe. You can talk to us in private.
- National Domestic Violence Hotline: call 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788. It is open 24 hours a day.

Call the clinic if either of you feels down, worried, or overwhelmed most days.

Call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline any time: 1-833-852-6262.

Call or text 988 if you have thoughts of hurting yourself or the baby. Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

use: Use as instructions for a patient who is planning to become pregnant.
body:
Getting ready for pregnancy

The months before pregnancy are a good time to get healthy. Some problems can be prevented before you get pregnant.

Folic acid:

- Take 400 to 800 mcg of folic acid every day.
- Start at least 1 month before you try to get pregnant.
- Most prenatal vitamins have enough folic acid.
- Some people need a higher dose, like after a pregnancy with a brain or spine defect.
- If you need a higher dose, take it as a separate pill. Do not take extra prenatal vitamins.

Your folic acid dose: _

Medicines and health problems:

- Bring all your medicines, vitamins, and herbal products to your visit.
- Do not stop a prescription medicine on your own. Talk with us first.
- Some medicines can cause birth defects. We may switch them before you try.
- Keep using birth control until we have made any medicine changes.
- Get diabetes, blood pressure, thyroid problems, seizures, and depression under good control first.
- If you have diabetes, the A1c goal before pregnancy is usually under 6.5%.

Vaccines:

- Get your vaccines up to date before pregnancy. Some cannot be given during pregnancy.
- After an MMR or chickenpox shot, wait 1 month before you try to get pregnant.
- The chickenpox vaccine takes 2 shots. Start about 2 months before you plan to try.
- Get a flu shot every year. Ask us about a COVID shot.

Healthy habits:

- Aim for a healthy weight. Being underweight or overweight can cause problems in pregnancy.
- Try to get 150 minutes of activity a week. A 30-minute walk 5 days a week counts.
- Eat fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein.
- Eat fish low in mercury. Do not eat shark, swordfish, marlin, orange roughy, or bigeye tuna.
- Also avoid tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico.

Tobacco, alcohol, and drugs:

- Quit smoking and vaping now. Ask us for help.
- Stop drinking alcohol when you start trying. No amount of alcohol is safe in pregnancy.
- Stop using marijuana, even where it is legal.
- Stop street drugs and pills not prescribed to you. We can help, without judging you.
- Your partner should quit smoking and drugs too.

Tests to ask about:

- STI tests, including HIV and syphilis. If you have an STI, you and your partner both need treatment before trying.
- Blood tests to see if you are protected against rubella and chickenpox.
- Carrier screening. This blood test checks for genes for diseases like cystic fibrosis.

Other steps:

- See a dentist. Dental care is safe before and during pregnancy.
- If you work with lead, mercury, pesticides, solvents, or radiation, ask your employer how to stay safe.
- Wait at least 6 months after a birth before getting pregnant again.
- Getting pregnant less than 18 months after a birth has more risks. Ask us about spacing.

Your safety:

- We ask everyone about safety at home.
- If a partner hurts, threatens, or controls you, you are not alone.
- National Domestic Violence Hotline: call 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.

Your plan: _

Call the clinic when you get a positive pregnancy test.

Call the clinic if you are not pregnant after 12 months of trying. If you are over 35, call after 6 months.

Call or text 988 if you have thoughts of hurting yourself. Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

use: Use as instructions for a parent worried about low milk supply.
body:
Making more milk

Your body makes milk to match how much milk leaves the breast. The more often milk is removed, the more you make.

Is my supply low?

- Your baby's weight gain is the best sign.
- Many parents worry about supply but make enough milk.

What to do:

- Feed or remove milk at least 8 times every 24 hours, including at night.
- Gently squeeze your breast while your baby feeds or while you pump. This helps more milk come out.
- If your baby gets a bottle, pump or hand express at that time too.
- Make sure your pump flange fits. Pumping should not hurt.

Herbs and medicines:

- No tea or herb is proven to make more milk.
- Fenugreek can cause diarrhea. It can cause allergic reactions in people allergic to peanuts, chickpeas, or ragweed.
- A prescription medicine is sometimes used. It only helps if milk is removed often. Ask us first.

Your plan:

- Feeds or pumping: _ times a day
- Extra milk for baby: _ ounces after _ feeds
- Next weight check: _

Call your baby's doctor if your baby:

- Has fewer wet diapers
- Is very sleepy and hard to wake for feeds
- Looks more yellow

Call the clinic if you feel sad, hopeless, or very worried about feeding.

use: Use as instructions for a plugged duct, mastitis, or breast inflammation while breastfeeding.
body:
Breast inflammation and mastitis

Mastitis is swelling and inflammation in the breast. It can cause a red, sore area, fever, and chills. Most cases get better without antibiotics.

What to do:

- Keep feeding your baby as usual. Your milk is safe for your baby.
- Do not pump extra or try to empty the breast. Extra pumping makes more milk and more swelling.
- Put ice or a cold pack on the sore area, as often as every hour.
- Take ibuprofen 800 mg (four 200 mg tablets) every 8 hours.
- You may also take acetaminophen 1,000 mg (two 500 mg tablets) every 8 hours.
- Wear a supportive bra that fits well.
- Use only very light strokes on the skin. Do not rub or massage deeply.

Do not:

- Use heat, castor oil, or Epsom salt soaks
- Use electric toothbrushes or vibrating devices on the breast
- Use a nipple shield to treat this
- Pick or pop a white dot on the nipple

If you get antibiotics:

- Keep breastfeeding while you take them.
- Take every dose until they are gone.
- Antibiotic: _ for _ days

Call the clinic if:

- Fever of 100.4 F or higher lasts more than 24 hours
- The red area spreads or gets worse
- You are not better 48 hours after starting antibiotics
- You feel a hard lump that stays or grows
- It keeps coming back in the same spot

Go to the ER if you feel very sick, faint, or confused, or cannot keep fluids down.

use: Use as instructions for pumping, milk storage, paced bottle feeding, and pumping at work.
body:
Pumping and storing breast milk

Pumping lets your baby get your milk when you are apart.

Pumping tips:

- When you are away from your baby, pump about as often as your baby feeds.
- Use a flange that fits. Pumping should not hurt.
- Gently squeeze your breast while you pump to get more milk.
- Wash your hands before pumping. Clean pump parts after each use.

How long fresh milk keeps:

- Room temperature (77 F or cooler): up to 4 hours
- Fridge (40 F or colder): up to 4 days
- Freezer (0 F or colder): best within 6 months, up to 12 months is OK
- Cooler bag with frozen ice packs: up to 24 hours

Storing milk:

- Label each container with the date you pumped.
- Freeze small amounts, 2 to 4 ounces.
- Do not store milk in the fridge or freezer door.

Thawing and warming:

- Use the oldest milk first.
- Thaw in the fridge overnight, or in warm water.
- Never thaw or heat milk in a microwave.
- Milk does not need to be warmed. Swirl it to mix the fat back in.
- Use thawed milk within 24 hours if kept in the fridge.
- Use warmed or room temperature milk within 2 hours.
- Never refreeze thawed milk.
- Throw out milk left in the bottle 2 hours after the feed ends.

Paced bottle feeding:

This lets your baby feed at a pace like the breast.

- Hold your baby upright. Support the head and neck.
- Use a slow flow nipple.
- Hold the bottle flat, so the nipple is only half full.
- Every so often, lower the bottle so your baby can rest. Raise it when your baby sucks again.
- A feed should take 15 to 30 minutes.
- Stop when your baby turns away or falls asleep. Do not make your baby finish.
- Never prop a bottle.

Pumping at work:

- Most workers have the right to pump at work for 1 year after birth.
- Your employer must give you break time and a private place that is not a bathroom.
- If you keep working while you pump, that time must be paid.
- Employers with fewer than 50 workers may not have to, if it is too hard for them.
- Questions: Department of Labor, 1-866-487-9243.
- Most health plans must cover a breast pump. Call your plan to ask how.

Call the clinic if pumping hurts, your nipples crack or bleed, or your breast gets red and painful.

use: Use as instructions about medicines, alcohol, cannabis, and tobacco while breastfeeding.
body:
Medicines and breastfeeding

Most medicines are safe while breastfeeding. A few should be avoided.

What to do:

- Tell every doctor and pharmacist that you breastfeed.
- Check with us before you start a new medicine, herb, or supplement.
- Your medicines we checked today: _

Where to look:

- LactMed, a free government website: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/
- MotherToBaby: call 866-626-6847 or text 855-999-3525. It is free.
- LactRx is a free phone app from MotherToBaby.

Alcohol:

- Not drinking is the safest choice.
- Up to 1 drink a day is not known to harm your baby.
- Wait at least 2 hours after 1 drink before you breastfeed.
- 1 drink is 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of liquor.
- Pumping and throwing out milk does not clear alcohol faster.
- If you drink a lot, have a sober adult care for your baby.

Marijuana and CBD:

- Do not use marijuana or CBD while breastfeeding. This includes edibles and oils.
- THC is stored in body fat. Your baby can be exposed even after you stop.
- If you cannot stop, use much less and talk with us.
- Never smoke around your baby.

Tobacco and vaping:

- Smoking and vaping can harm your baby. We can help you quit.

Call your baby's doctor if your baby is very sleepy, feeds poorly, or seems unwell after you start a medicine.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for thyroid disease before, during, and after pregnancy.
body:
Thyroid medicine and pregnancy

Pregnancy raises your need for thyroid hormone. Keeping your levels right helps you and your baby.

If you take levothyroxine:

- As soon as a pregnancy test is positive, take 2 extra pills each week.
- An easy way: take a double dose on 2 days each week, like Monday and Thursday.
- Then call the clinic the same day.
- Take it 4 hours apart from your prenatal vitamin, iron, or calcium.
- We will check a blood test every 4 weeks until about 20 weeks.
- We will check again near 30 weeks.
- After the baby comes, go back to your old dose. We will test you at 6 weeks.

If you take methimazole or PTU:

- Take a pregnancy test right away if your period is late or very light.
- Call the clinic within 1 day of a positive test. Your medicine may need to change.
- Stop the medicine and call right away for fever or sore throat.
- Stop PTU and call right away for yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or belly pain.

For everyone:

- Take a prenatal vitamin with 150 mcg of iodine every day.
- Do not take kelp or extra iodine pills.
- Stop biotin (hair, skin, nail vitamins) 2 days before thyroid blood tests.

After the baby comes:

- Your thyroid can swing high, then low, in the first year.
- Call the clinic if you feel shaky, have a racing heart, or cannot sleep.
- Call the clinic if you feel very tired, cold, sad, or have low milk supply.

Your dose: _ mcg. Next blood test: _.

Go to the ER if you have a fast heartbeat with fever, confusion, or vomiting.

Call 911 if you have chest pain or trouble breathing.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
body:
Itching in pregnancy (cholestasis)

Cholestasis of pregnancy is a liver problem that causes itching. It usually starts late in pregnancy. It goes away after the baby is born.

Signs:

- Itching that can be strong
- Itching that is worst on the palms of your hands and soles of your feet
- Itching that is worse at night
- No rash, but scratching can leave marks

Why it matters:

Cholestasis is not usually harmful to you. It raises the chance of early birth and stillbirth for the baby. Checking on your baby and planning the birth lower these risks.

Tests:

- A blood test checks your bile acids and liver. Your bile acid level: _
- If you still itch and the test is normal, we may repeat it.

Medicine:

- Ursodiol helps the itching. It starts to work in 1 to 2 weeks.
- Your dose: _
- Some people get mild nausea or dizziness from it.
- Allergy pills and menthol or calamine creams help only a little.

Your baby:

- Baby heart rate checks start _. How often: _
- Most people with cholestasis give birth between 36 and 39 weeks. Your plan: _
- If birth is planned before 37 weeks, a steroid shot helps the baby's lungs.

After birth:

- The itching usually goes away after birth.
- Cholestasis often comes back in a later pregnancy. Tell your doctor early next time.

Call the clinic if:

- The itching gets worse or keeps you from sleeping
- You still itch 4 weeks after birth

Go to Labor and Delivery right away if:

- Your baby is moving less than usual
- Your skin or eyes turn yellow, or your pee turns dark
- You have pain under your right ribs
- You have a headache that will not go away, or vision changes

desc: Caring for a tear or stitches after birth
use: Use as after-visit instructions for perineal tear or episiotomy care, including after wound breakdown or infection.
body:
Caring for a tear or stitches after birth

Many people tear or need stitches during birth. Most heal well in a few weeks. The stitches melt on their own.

Keep the area clean:

- Spray warm water on the area each time you pee or poop. Use a squirt bottle.
- Pat dry with a clean towel or baby wipe. Do not rub with toilet paper.
- Change your pad every 2 to 4 hours.
- Wash your hands before and after you change your pad.
- Shower every day. Wash gently. Do not wash inside your vagina.
- Wear cotton underwear.

Ease pain and swelling:

- First day: use an ice pack or cold pad on the area.
- After the first day: sit in 2 to 3 inches of warm water for 10 to 20 minutes.
- Do this 1 to 2 times a day. A sitz bath tub fits on the toilet.
- Clean the bathtub before each bath.
- Ibuprofen helps this kind of pain the most. Acetaminophen also helps.
- Your pain medicine: _

Keep stools soft:

- Drink plenty of water.
- Eat 2 green kiwis or about 10 prunes a day.
- Your stool softener: _
- Do not strain when you poop.

Wait 6 weeks before using tampons or having sex.

If your wound got infected or opened:

- Take your antibiotic: _
- Keep using the squirt bottle and warm water soaks.
- An open wound heals from the inside out. It can take several weeks or more.
- Your wound check: _

Call the clinic if you have:

- Pain that gets worse
- Bad-smelling discharge
- A wound that seems to open
- Redness or swelling that is getting worse
- Fever of 100.4 F or higher
- No bowel movement for 4 or more days
- A blood clot larger than a walnut

Go to the ER or call 911 if you have:

- Very bad pain, much worse than the wound looks
- Skin that turns dark, blistered, or crackles when pressed
- Fever with chills, a racing heart, confusion, or feeling very sick

use: Use as after-visit or discharge instructions for parents of a baby observed or treated for neonatal opioid withdrawal.
body:
Opioid withdrawal in your newborn

Your baby was exposed to opioids before birth. After birth, some babies have withdrawal. This is called NOWS.

Signs of withdrawal:

- Crying a lot, or a high-pitched cry
- Shaking or trembling
- Trouble feeding or sucking too much
- Trouble sleeping
- Sneezing or a stuffy nose
- Loose stools, vomiting, or sweating
- Stiff arms and legs

When it happens:

- Signs often start 1 to 3 days after birth. Some start later, up to 1 week.
- Your baby stayed in the hospital _ days to watch for signs.

What you can do:

- Hold your baby skin-to-skin on your bare chest.
- Swaddle your baby snugly in a thin blanket, with room for the hips to move.
- Keep the room quiet and the lights low.
- Gently rock your baby.
- Feed when your baby shows hunger signs. Try small, frequent feeds.
- Do care tasks together, like a diaper change and a feed, so your baby can rest.
- Ask family to help so you can rest too.

Breastfeeding:

- Breast milk helps babies with withdrawal.
- Breastfeeding is safe if you take methadone or buprenorphine as prescribed.
- Do not breastfeed while using opioids that are not prescribed to you. Talk to us first.
- Your plan: _

Medicine:

- Some babies need medicine for withdrawal. We lower the dose slowly.
- Your baby's medicine: _

Safe sleep:

- Always put your baby to sleep on their back.
- Use a firm, flat crib with no blankets, pillows, or toys.
- Your baby should sleep in their own crib, not in your bed.
- Never use weighted swaddles or blankets.

After you go home:

- Your baby may need extra comfort for weeks or months.
- Keep all checkups. Next visit: _
- Early intervention referral: _

Call the clinic right away if your baby has a temperature of 100.4 F or higher.

Call the clinic if your baby:

- Has signs of withdrawal that are getting worse
- Cannot be calmed for a long time
- Is not feeding well or has fewer wet diapers
- Has vomiting or diarrhea that will not stop
- Is not gaining weight

Go to the ER if your baby is very hard to wake or very floppy.

Call 911 if your baby has a seizure, stops breathing, or turns blue.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a pregnant patient with genital herpes.
body:
Herpes and your pregnancy

Many people with genital herpes have healthy babies. The main risk is passing herpes to the baby during birth. Medicine and a birth plan lower this risk.

Medicine at 36 weeks:

- Start daily herpes medicine at 36 weeks. Take it until your baby is born.
- Your medicine: _
- It lowers the chance of sores at birth.
- It lowers the chance you will need a C-section.

If you get an outbreak:

- Signs are tingling, burning, or pain, then blisters or sores.
- Start your outbreak medicine within 1 day of the first sign.
- Do not have sex with a partner who does not have herpes while you have signs.

When labor starts:

- Tell the Labor and Delivery team you have herpes.
- Tell them if you have any tingling, burning, or sores.
- If you have sores or tingling near your vagina, a C-section protects your baby.
- Sores only on your back, thigh, or buttock do not need a C-section.

New herpes late in pregnancy:

- A first outbreak late in pregnancy has the highest risk for the baby.
- Tell us right away about new sores, even if you never had herpes.

After birth:

- You can breastfeed unless you have a sore on your breast.

Call the clinic if:

- You have a new sore or blister
- Sores are not healed after 10 days of medicine
- You run out of medicine

Go to Labor and Delivery right away if:

- Labor starts and you have sores or tingling
- Your water breaks and you have sores or tingling

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a pregnant patient being treated for syphilis.
body:
Syphilis treatment in pregnancy

Syphilis can pass to your baby during pregnancy. It can cause early birth, stillbirth, or serious illness in the baby. Penicillin shots cure it and protect your baby.

Your treatment:

- Number of shots: _
- Shot dates: _
- Shots are 1 week apart. Do not miss a shot.
- If you go more than 9 days between shots, you must start over.
- Penicillin is the only medicine that protects the baby.
- If you are allergic to penicillin, we can still give it after a special allergy process.

After a shot:

- Within 24 hours, you may get fever, chills, headache, or muscle aches.
- This is a reaction to the treatment, not an allergy.
- Acetaminophen can ease the fever and aches.

Your partner:

- Your partner needs testing and treatment too.
- You can get syphilis again if your partner is not treated.
- The health department may contact you to help with this.

Follow-up:

- You will have more blood tests in pregnancy and at birth.
- Your baby will have a blood test and exam after birth.

Call the clinic if:

- You miss a shot
- You have a new sore or rash

Go to Labor and Delivery right away if after a shot you have:

- Contractions or tightening
- Your baby moving less than usual
- Fever that will not go away

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a pregnant patient with HIV.
body:
HIV and your pregnancy

HIV medicine protects your baby. If your viral load stays very low, the chance of passing HIV is 1 in 100 or less.

Your medicine:

- Take your HIV medicine every day, at the same time.
- Your medicine: _
- Do not stop or skip doses, even if you feel well.
- If side effects bother you, call us before you stop.

Blood tests:

- We check your viral load often in pregnancy.
- We check again at 34 to 36 weeks to plan your birth.
- Your last viral load: _

Your birth plan:

- If your viral load is low, you can plan a vaginal birth.
- If your viral load is high, a C-section at 38 weeks protects your baby.
- You may get HIV medicine by IV before birth.
- Your plan: _

Your baby:

- Your baby starts HIV medicine within 6 hours of birth.
- Your baby will have blood tests for HIV in the first months.
- Do not leave the hospital without your baby's medicine.

Feeding your baby:

- Formula or donor milk has no risk of passing HIV.
- Breastfeeding with an undetectable viral load has a very low risk, under 1 in 100.
- If you want to breastfeed, we will make a plan together.
- Never chew food before giving it to your baby.

Call the clinic if:

- You miss doses or run out of medicine
- You cannot keep medicine down because of vomiting

Go to Labor and Delivery right away if:

- Your water breaks
- You have contractions before your planned birth

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a pregnant patient with hepatitis B.
body:
Hepatitis B and your pregnancy

Hepatitis B is a liver infection. It can pass to your baby at birth. Shots for your baby right after birth prevent most infections.

Your tests:

- We check how much virus is in your blood.
- Your viral load: _
- A liver doctor will also see you.

Medicine:

- If your viral load is high, you take tenofovir starting at 28 to 32 weeks.
- Take 1 pill every day.
- Your plan: _

Your baby:

- Your baby gets 2 shots within 12 hours of birth.
- One is hepatitis B vaccine. One is hepatitis B immune globulin.
- More vaccine doses are at 1 month and 6 months.
- A blood test at 9 to 12 months checks that your baby is protected.

Feeding:

- Breastfeeding is safe, even if you take tenofovir.

Your family:

- People in your home and sex partners should be tested.
- They should get the vaccine if they are not protected.

After birth:

- If you stop tenofovir, we check your liver every 1 to 3 months for 6 months.
- Do not stop tenofovir unless your doctor tells you.

Call the clinic if:

- You run out of medicine
- You feel very tired or lose your appetite

Go to the ER if:

- Your skin or eyes turn yellow
- Your pee turns dark
- You have strong pain under your right ribs

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a pregnant patient with a short cervix on ultrasound.
body:
Short cervix

The cervix is the opening of the womb. A short cervix raises the chance of early birth. Treatment can lower this risk.

Your cervix length: _

Your treatment:

- Progesterone placed in the vagina every night lowers the chance of early birth.
- Use it every night until 36 weeks and 6 days.
- Your medicine: _
- Some progesterone capsules contain peanut oil. Tell us if you have a peanut allergy.
- Some people need a stitch in the cervix. Your plan: _

What does not help:

- Bed rest does not help and may raise the risk of early birth.
- You can keep doing your normal activities.

Go to Labor and Delivery right away if you have any of these before 37 weeks:

- Tightening or contractions every 10 minutes or more often
- Cramps like a period
- Low, dull backache
- Pressure in your pelvis, like the baby is pushing down
- Leaking fluid from your vagina
- Bleeding or spotting
- Discharge that becomes watery, mucus-like, or bloody

Labor and Delivery phone: _

Call the clinic if:

- You run out of progesterone
- You are not sure what you are feeling

Go to Labor and Delivery right away if you have any of these before 37 weeks:

- Tightening or contractions every 10 minutes or more often
- Cramps like a period
- Low, dull backache
- Pressure in your pelvis, like the baby is pushing down
- Leaking fluid from your vagina
- Bleeding or spotting
- Discharge that becomes watery, mucus-like, or bloody

Labor and Delivery phone: ***

Call the clinic if:

- You run out of progesterone
- You are not sure what you are feeling

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a pregnancy of unknown location or ectopic pregnancy, including methotrexate treatment.
body:
Pregnancy of unknown location and ectopic pregnancy

Your pregnancy test is positive, but the ultrasound does not show where the pregnancy is yet. This may be a very early pregnancy, a miscarriage, or a pregnancy outside the uterus.

A pregnancy outside the uterus is called an ectopic pregnancy. It usually grows in a fallopian tube. It can burst and cause dangerous bleeding.

Your plan:

- Blood test for the pregnancy hormone on _
- Ultrasound on _
- We repeat these tests until we know where the pregnancy is, or the hormone is gone.

If you get methotrexate:

- Methotrexate is a shot that stops an ectopic pregnancy from growing.
- You will need blood tests on day 4 and day 7, then each week.
- Some people need a second shot.
- It can take up to 8 weeks for the hormone to go away.
- Belly pain 2 to 3 days after the shot is common.
- Nausea, stomach upset, and spotting can happen.

While you are being treated:

- Stop prenatal vitamins and folic acid until we tell you to restart.
- Do not take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin.
- Do not drink alcohol.
- No sex and no hard exercise.
- Stay out of the sun. Methotrexate can cause a sun rash.
- Wait to get pregnant until you have had at least 1 period after the hormone is gone. Some doctors advise 3 months.
- Methotrexate does not seem to hurt your chances of getting pregnant later.

Your next blood test: _

Call the clinic if:

- You have more bleeding than a normal period
- You have pain that is getting worse
- You miss a blood test

Go to the ER right away if you have:

- Bad belly or pelvic pain, especially on one side
- Pain in your shoulder tip
- Dizziness or fainting
- Heavy bleeding

If your blood type is Rh negative, tell any ER you visit.

use: Use as after-visit instructions when the baby is breech late in pregnancy.
body:
Breech baby

Your baby is breech. This means the bottom or feet are down instead of the head. About 3 in 100 babies are breech at the end of pregnancy.

Turning the baby (ECV):

- ECV means a doctor uses their hands on your belly to turn the baby head down.
- It is done in the hospital near your due date, where a C-section can be done if needed.
- The baby's heart rate is checked before and after.
- You may get a shot to relax your uterus first.
- It works about half the time or a little more. It works more often if you have given birth before.
- Most babies who turn stay head down.
- Serious problems are rare, about 1 in 400.
- If your blood type is Rh negative, you get a shot after ECV.

Your ECV date: _

If the baby stays breech:

- Most breech babies are born by planned C-section, usually at 39 weeks or later.
- We check the baby's position with ultrasound that day. Some babies turn on their own.
- Vaginal breech birth is an option in some hospitals with an experienced doctor. Ask us about it.

Things you may hear about:

- Lying with your hips raised or kneeling with your chest down. Studies have not shown these turn the baby.

Call the clinic if:

- You have questions about ECV or your birth plan
- Your baby is moving less than usual

Go to Labor and Delivery right away if:

- Your water breaks or you leak fluid
- You have regular contractions
- You have bleeding

use: Use as after-visit instructions for iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy, with iron-rich foods and how to take iron pills.
body:
Low iron in pregnancy

Your blood test shows anemia from low iron. Your body needs extra iron in pregnancy to make blood for you and your baby. Low iron can make you tired, dizzy, or short of breath.

Your iron pill:

- Your dose: _
- Keep taking your prenatal vitamin too.
- Take iron on an empty stomach if you can. A small snack is OK if it upsets your stomach.
- Take it with orange juice or another vitamin C food. This helps you absorb it.
- Wait at least 2 hours after milk, calcium pills, or antacids before you take iron.
- Do not take it with coffee, tea, or whole grains and bran.
- If you take thyroid medicine, ask us how far apart to take them.

Side effects:

- Black stools are normal with iron.
- Constipation is common. A stool softener can help.
- If iron upsets your stomach, call us. We may change the dose or give iron by IV.

Foods with iron:

- Breakfast cereal with 100 percent of the daily value for iron: 18 mg per serving
- White beans, canned, 1 cup: 8 mg
- Lentils, cooked, 1/2 cup: 3 mg
- Tofu, firm, 1/2 cup: 3 mg
- Spinach, cooked, 1/2 cup: 3 mg
- Kidney beans or chickpeas, 1/2 cup: 2 mg
- Beef, 3 ounces: 2 mg
- Stewed tomatoes, canned, 1/2 cup: 2 mg
- Baked potato with skin, 1 medium: 2 mg
- Cashews, 1 ounce: 2 mg
- Chicken, 3 ounces: 1 mg
- Egg, 1 large: 1 mg
- Raisins, 1/4 cup: 1 mg

Pregnant women need 27 mg of iron a day. Most prenatal vitamins have 27 mg.

Help your body use iron from food:

- Eat a vitamin C food with iron foods. Oranges, strawberries, tomatoes, and potatoes are good choices.
- Adding a little meat, chicken, or fish to beans helps you absorb the plant iron.
- Black tea makes it harder to absorb iron. Drink it between meals.
- Spinach has iron, but your body takes in only a little of it.

Next blood test: _

Keep iron pills away from children. If a child swallows iron, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away.

Call the clinic if:

- You cannot take your iron pills
- You feel more tired, dizzy, or short of breath
- Your stools look tarry or have red streaks
- You have bad stomach cramps or pain

Go to the ER or Labor and Delivery right away if you faint, have chest pain, or have heavy bleeding.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a patient with an early pregnancy loss.
body:
Miscarriage

An early pregnancy loss is a pregnancy that stops growing in the first 12 weeks. It is common. It is not caused by stress, exercise, food, or sex.

Your plan:

- Your choice: _wait for it to pass / medicine to help it pass / a suction procedure
- Your next visit or test is on _.

What to expect:

- Cramps and bleeding with clots can be stronger than a normal period.
- Bleeding often lasts 1 to 2 weeks. It may stop and start a few times.
- Use pads, not tampons, so you can see how much you bleed.

For pain:

- Take ibuprofen, naproxen, or acetaminophen as the package says, with food.
- A hot pack on your belly can help with cramps.

If you use misoprostol:

- Take ibuprofen 1 hour before the misoprostol.
- Cramps often start 2 to 4 hours after the pills and last 3 to 5 hours.
- Nausea, diarrhea, or chills can happen. They should go away within 24 hours.
- No bleeding within 24 hours? Use the second dose if you have one, or call us.

Call the clinic if:

- You still have no bleeding after the medicine
- You feel it is taking too long
- You feel very sad or have trouble coping
- You have questions about another pregnancy

Go to the ER if you have:

- Bleeding that soaks more than 2 maxi pads an hour for 2 hours in a row
- Fever over 101 F, chills, or bad-smelling discharge
- Bad cramps that pain medicine does not help
- Dizziness or feeling like you may pass out

After a miscarriage:

- You can use birth control right away if you want it.
- You can try for another pregnancy as soon as you feel ready.
- If you want to try again, take a prenatal vitamin every day.
- Ask us about support or counseling if you want it.

desc: After a fall or car crash in pregnancy
use: Use as after-visit instructions after minor trauma in pregnancy with reassuring monitoring.
body:
After a fall or car crash in pregnancy

Your exam and monitoring were normal today.

Go to Labor and Delivery or the ER right away if you have:

- Bleeding from your vagina
- Fluid leaking from your vagina
- Cramps or contractions that do not stop
- Belly pain or a belly that feels hard or tender
- Your baby moving less than usual
- Feeling dizzy or faint

Seat belts:

- Always wear both the lap belt and the shoulder belt.
- Put the lap belt low, under your belly and across your hips.
- Put the shoulder belt between your breasts and off to the side of your belly.
- Do not turn off the airbags.

Your safety:

- If someone is hurting you, call us or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233.
- You can also text START to 88788.

Call the clinic if:

- You have pain from other injuries that is not getting better
- You have questions about your pregnancy

use: Use as postpartum instructions after a vaginal delivery.
body:
Recovery after vaginal birth

Bleeding:

- Days 1 to 4: bright red, like a heavy period
- Days 5 to 10: pink or brown, lighter
- After that: yellow or white, light. It can last 4 to 6 weeks.
- Use pads only. Nothing in the vagina until we say it is OK.

Care of your bottom:

- Use a squirt bottle of warm water after each time you pee. Pat dry front to back.
- Use ice packs the first day, then warm sitz baths 2 to 3 times a day.
- Witch hazel pads help swelling and hemorrhoids.

Pain:

- Ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth every 6 hours
- Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours
- Take them on a schedule for the first few days. Both are safe with breastfeeding.

Bowels:

- Drink water, eat fiber, and walk.
- Foods that help: 2 green kiwis or about 10 prunes a day.
- If stools are hard, take polyethylene glycol 17 grams in 8 ounces of drink once a day.
- It is safe with breastfeeding.
- Take it every day while you take opioid pain medicine.
- If you had a 3rd or 4th degree tear, take it every day for _.
- Soft stools make the first bowel movements less painful.

Your postpartum visit: _

Call the clinic if you have:

- Fever of 100.4 F or higher
- Bad-smelling discharge
- Bleeding that turns bright red again after it got lighter
- Trouble peeing
- Red, swollen, or warm leg
- Sad or anxious feelings most of the day

Go to the ER or call 911 if you have:

- Bleeding that soaks 1 pad an hour for 2 hours, or clots bigger than a golf ball
- Chest pain or trouble breathing
- A bad headache, vision changes, or a seizure
- Thoughts of hurting yourself or your baby

use: Use as postpartum instructions after a cesarean delivery.
body:
Recovery after C-section

Incision care:

- You can shower. Let soapy water run over the incision and pat it dry.
- No baths, pools, or hot tubs until it is healed.
- Keep it dry. Tuck a clean cloth under your belly fold if needed.

Activity:

- Walk several times a day. It helps prevent blood clots.
- Do not lift anything heavier than your baby for 6 weeks.
- Do not drive while taking opioid pain medicine. Wait until you can brake hard without pain.
- Hold a pillow on your belly when you cough or laugh.

Pain:

- Ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth every 6 hours
- Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours
- Other pain medicine: _

Bleeding is normal for 4 to 6 weeks. Use pads only.

Bowels:

- Drink water and walk.
- Foods that help: 2 green kiwis or about 10 prunes a day.
- If stools are hard, take polyethylene glycol 17 grams in 8 ounces of drink once a day.
- Take it every day while you take opioid pain medicine.
- It is safe with breastfeeding.

Incision check: _
Postpartum visit: _

Call the clinic if you have:

- Fever of 100.4 F or higher
- Redness spreading from the incision, or pus or drainage
- An incision that opens
- Pain that gets worse, not better
- Red, swollen, or warm leg

Go to the ER or call 911 if you have:

- Bleeding that soaks 1 pad an hour for 2 hours
- Chest pain or trouble breathing
- A bad headache, vision changes, or a seizure
- Thoughts of hurting yourself or your baby

use: Use as postpartum instructions about baby blues, postpartum depression, and psychosis.
body:
Mood after birth

Baby blues:

- Up to 8 in 10 new mothers have tearfulness, mood swings, and worry in the first week.
- This goes away within 2 weeks.

Postpartum depression:

- About 1 in 8 mothers get it. It is a medical illness, not a sign that you are a bad mother.
- Signs: sadness most of the day, or trouble bonding with your baby.
- Other signs: bad anxiety or panic, not sleeping when your baby sleeps, or losing interest in things.
- Feeling numb or not bonded with your baby for more than 2 weeks can be a sign.
- It is treated with counseling, support, and medicine. Many medicines are safe with breastfeeding.
- Do not wait for your 6-week visit. Tell us now.

Postpartum anxiety:

- Constant worry about your baby, checking over and over, and a racing heart.
- This is common and treatable too.

Call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline any time: 1-833-TLC-MAMA, which is 1-833-852-6262.

Call the clinic if signs last more than 2 weeks or are getting worse.

Call 911 or go to the ER right away if you:

- See or hear things that are not there
- Feel very confused or out of control
- Have thoughts of hurting yourself or your baby

You can also call or text 988.

use: Use as postpartum instructions after gestational hypertension or preeclampsia.
body:
Blood pressure after birth

You had high blood pressure in pregnancy. It can stay high, or even start, in the first weeks after birth.

Your medicine: _

Check your blood pressure at home _ times a day. Write it down.

Your blood pressure check: _

Call the clinic the same day if your blood pressure is 150 over 100 or higher.

Go to the ER right away if:

- Your blood pressure is 160 over 110 or higher
- You have a headache that will not go away
- You have vision changes, like spots or flashing lights
- You have pain under your right ribs
- You have chest pain or trouble breathing
- You have a seizure

High blood pressure in pregnancy raises your risk of heart disease later in life. Get your blood pressure checked every year.

use: Use as postpartum instructions about pelvic rest and resuming sex.
body:
Sex after birth

Wait until:

- Your bleeding has stopped
- Any tear or incision has healed
- You feel ready

For many people this is around 6 weeks, but it can be sooner or later.

Until then, put nothing in your vagina. No sex, tampons, menstrual cups, or douching.

When you start again:

- Dryness is common, especially with breastfeeding. Use a water-based lubricant.
- Go slowly. Some discomfort at first is normal.
- Pain that does not get better is not normal. Tell us.

You can get pregnant before your first period comes back, even while breastfeeding. Use birth control.

Your birth control plan: _

Call the clinic if sex is painful after the first few tries.

use: Use as postpartum instructions about returning to exercise.
body:
Exercise after birth

First days:

- Start Kegels when you are comfortable. Squeeze your pelvic floor for 3 to 5 seconds, then relax. Do 10 squeezes, 3 times a day.
- Take short walks.
- Practice deep belly breathing.

Weeks 2 to 6:

- Walk longer and faster as you feel ready.
- Gentle stretching is fine.
- Avoid sit-ups, crunches, planks, heavy lifting, and jumping.
- If you have more pain, bleeding, or pressure in your pelvis, slow down.

After your 6-week visit:

- Return to your usual exercise slowly. Start at half your usual effort.

use: Use as postpartum instructions about contraception after delivery.
body:
Birth control after birth

You can get pregnant as early as 3 weeks after birth, even before your period comes back. Waiting at least 18 months before your next pregnancy is healthiest for most people.

Can start any time, including right after birth:

- IUD
- Implant in the arm
- Shot every 3 months
- Progestin-only pill
- Condoms

Usually started 4 to 6 weeks after birth:

- Pill, patch, or ring with estrogen. Estrogen can raise the risk of blood clots right after birth.

Breastfeeding as birth control works only if all 3 are true:

- Your baby is under 6 months old
- Your period has not come back
- You feed only breast milk, at least every 4 hours in the day and every 6 hours at night

Permanent options: tubal surgery for you, or vasectomy for your partner.

Emergency birth control works best within 5 days after sex.

Your plan: _

Call the clinic to start or change birth control.

use: Use as instructions for getting started with breastfeeding.
body:
Breastfeeding basics

Breastfeeding takes practice. Most problems can be fixed with help.

First days:

- Your first milk is thick and yellow. It comes in small amounts. This is exactly what your baby needs.
- More milk comes in on days 2 to 5.

A good latch:

- Your baby's mouth covers most of the dark area, not just the nipple.
- Both lips turn outward.
- You hear swallowing, not clicking.
- It should not hurt after the first 30 seconds. If it hurts, break the suction with a clean finger and try again.

Feed 8 to 12 times a day. Watch your baby, not the clock. Signs of hunger are rooting (turning to search for the nipple), hands to the mouth, and sucking.

Your baby is getting enough if:

- By day 5, your baby has at least 6 wet diapers and 3 to 4 yellow stools a day
- Your baby is back to birth weight by 2 weeks
- Your baby seems content after feeds

Lactation help: _

Call your baby's doctor if your baby:

- Has fewer wet diapers
- Is very sleepy and hard to wake for feeds
- Looks more yellow

use: Use as instructions for common breastfeeding problems.
body:
Breastfeeding problems

Sore nipples:

- Check the latch first. This is the most common cause.
- Rub a little breast milk on your nipples after feeds and let them air dry.
- If you pump, make sure the flange fits and the suction is not too strong.
- If your nipple turns white or purple with burning pain after feeds, keep it warm and avoid cold.

Engorgement, when breasts are hard and full:

- Feed your baby when hungry. Do not pump to empty the breast.
- Before a feed, press gently around the nipple or hand express a little milk to soften it.
- Use cold packs after feeds to bring down swelling.

Plugged duct or breast swelling:

- Keep feeding as usual. Do not pump extra to empty the breast.
- Use ice and take ibuprofen for pain and swelling.
- Use only light, gentle massage. Deep massage and heat can make it worse.

Low supply worries:

- The more your baby feeds, the more milk you make.
- Most people who worry about supply have enough.

Pumping: most insurance covers a breast pump. Milk keeps 4 days in the fridge and 6 to 12 months in the freezer.

Using formula is not failure. A fed baby is what matters most.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Fever of 100.4 F or higher with a red, painful area on your breast
- Flu-like aches with breast pain
- Burning nipple pain during and after feeds
- Cracked or bleeding nipples that do not heal
