use: Use as after-visit instructions teaching parents of a young child how to use time-out and daily special time.
body:
How to use time-out

Time-out is a short break from your attention after a problem behavior. It is for young children, about ages 2 to 5. It works best when your child gets lots of praise and attention at other times.

When to use time-out:

- Unsafe or hurtful behavior, like hitting, biting, pushing, or throwing things
- Not following a direction after a warning

When not to use time-out:

- For whining. Ignore whining instead.
- When your child is very upset or scared. Stay close and help them calm down.

Pick the spot:

- Choose a safe, boring spot, like a sturdy chair at the end of a hallway.
- Keep it away from toys, TV, windows, and people.
- If you use a room, keep the light on and stay nearby. Never use a closet.

Step by step:

- Give one calm warning. Say it, do not ask it: "If you hit again, you will go to time-out."
- Wait about 5 seconds. If your child stops, praise them.
- If the behavior happens again, say calmly: "You hit. Time-out."
- Walk your child to the spot. Do not lecture, scold, or argue.
- Set a timer for 1 minute for each year of age. A 3-year-old gets 3 minutes.
- Most young children need only 2 to 5 minutes.
- During time-out, do not talk to, look at, or touch your child.
- Ignore yelling, crying, and promises to be good.

If your child gets up:

- Put your child back without talking. Start the timer over.
- You may need to do this many times at first. It gets easier.
- If your child keeps leaving, warn that they will lose a privilege, like bike time today. Then follow through.

Ending time-out:

- Your child should be quiet for the last 5 seconds before getting up.
- Then repeat the direction your child did not follow, like "Pick up the blocks."
- If your child still says no, go back to time-out.
- Praise the next good thing your child does. Start fresh.

Tips:

- Use time-out every time for the same behavior.
- All caregivers should do time-out the same way.
- Never warn of a time-out and then not follow through.
- If two children fight, put both in time-out in separate spots.
- Children 3 and older can learn to take a break and come back when calm.
- For school-age children, taking away a privilege is another choice.

Special time:

Special time is a short play time each day where your child leads. It builds warmth and cooperation.

- Play together for 5 to 15 minutes every day. Start with 5 minutes if that is easier.
- Do it at the same time each day. Put your phone away.
- Let your child pick the toy or game. Follow their lead.
- Choose blocks, crayons, or other toys that build. Skip screens and toys that play on their own.
- Praise what you like: "You are sharing so nicely."
- Describe what your child is doing, and copy their play.
- Avoid questions, commands, and criticism during this time.
- Ignore small misbehavior. If your child does something unsafe, stop play and use time-out.
- Keep special time every day, even on hard days. It is not a reward to earn.

Call the clinic if behavior is not getting better, or if you feel angry or out of control. Call 911 if a child is hurt or in danger.

- Ignore small misbehavior. If your child does something unsafe, stop play and use time-out.
- Keep special time every day, even on hard days. It is not a reward to earn.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for parents at a child behavior visit, with core parenting tools, a behavior chart, and referral.
body:
Helping your child's behavior

Many children have hard behavior at times. The 4 tools below help most children behave better. They work best when every caregiver uses them every day.

Our plan:

- Behaviors to work on first: _
- Referral: _
- Next visit: _

Tool 1, special time:

- Play with your child for 5 to 15 minutes every day. Let your child lead.
- Praise, describe, and copy their play. Skip questions, commands, and criticism.
- Keep special time every day, even on hard days.

Tool 2, praise:

- Catch your child being good. Praise right away.
- Say exactly what you liked: "Thank you for putting your shoes away."
- A smile, a thumbs up, or a high-five also counts.

Tool 3, ignore small stuff:

- Ignore whining, pouting, or interrupting if no one is in danger. Do not look, talk, or touch.
- The behavior often gets worse at first. Stay calm and do not give in.
- As soon as the behavior stops, praise what your child is doing well.
- Never ignore hurting others, unsafe acts, or breaking things. Stop it right away.

Tool 4, clear directions and steady consequences:

- Get close, make eye contact, and use your child's name.
- Give one direction at a time. Say it, do not ask it.
- Say what to do, not what to stop: "Walk, please" instead of "Don't run."
- Use a calm, firm voice. Offer a choice of two when you can.
- If your child does not listen, repeat the direction once and warn of a consequence.
- Follow through every time with time-out or loss of a privilege.
- Give consequences right away. Young children learn best this way.
- Praise your child when they listen.

Behavior chart:

- Pick 1 or 2 behaviors. Say what you want, like "Gets dressed by 7:30."
- Our target behaviors: _
- Choose a reward your child really wants. It does not need to cost money.
- Our rewards: _
- Make a simple chart with pictures. Put it where your child can see it.
- Give a sticker or mark right after the behavior. Say what your child did well.
- Never take away a sticker or reward your child already earned.
- When the behavior becomes a habit, pick a new one or slowly stop the chart.

Parenting programs:

Parent training programs teach these tools step by step, with a coach. They are a top first treatment for behavior problems.

- Programs include Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT), Triple P, and The Incredible Years.
- Most programs take 8 to 16 sessions.
- Our referral: _

Home safety:

- If you have guns at home, store them unloaded and locked.
- Lock up the ammunition in a separate place.

- Parenting a child with hard behavior is stressful. You are not alone.
- When you feel angry, take a break first. Breathe deeply and count to 10.
- Take breaks. Let another adult take over when you need it.
- Tell us if you feel sad, hopeless, or very stressed most days. We can help.
- For help with food, housing, or bills, call 211.
- If you or your child are in crisis, call or text 988 any time.

Call the clinic if:

- Behavior gets worse, or is not better by your next visit
- Your child often hurts others, hurts themselves, or breaks things
- Problems at school or daycare get worse
- You feel you might lose control or hurt your child

Call 988 or go to the ER if your child talks about suicide or hurting someone. Call 911 if anyone is hurt or in danger.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for parents after reduction of a pulled elbow (nursemaid's elbow).
body:
Pulled elbow

Your child has a pulled elbow, also called nursemaid's elbow. A bone in the elbow slipped partly out of place. This often happens when a child is pulled or swung by the hand or arm.

We put the bone back in place today. It does not cause lasting harm.

What to expect:

- Most children use the arm again within 30 minutes.
- Your child does not need a sling.
- It can happen again, most often in young children.

Help prevent it:

- Lift your child under the arms, not by the hands or wrists.
- Do not swing your child by the hands or arms.
- Do not tug or yank your child's hand or arm.

Call the clinic if:

- Your child still does not use the arm normally by the next day
- It happens again

Go to the ER if:

- The elbow or arm swells, bruises, or looks bent
- Your child's hand turns pale, cold, or numb
- Your child had a fall and now will not use the arm

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a child or teen with Osgood-Schlatter disease.
body:
Osgood-Schlatter knee pain

Osgood-Schlatter causes pain and a bump just below the kneecap. It happens during growth spurts in active kids. Running, jumping, and kneeling make it hurt.

It is not dangerous. It does not cause lasting damage. It usually goes away when your child stops growing. The bump may stay.

Sports and activity:

- Your child can keep playing if the pain is mild.
- A dull ache that goes away soon after play is OK.
- If it hurts during play, stop for that day.
- If your child limps or has pain at rest, take a short break from sports.
- Swimming and biking put less strain on the knee.
- A strap just below the kneecap is optional.

Ice and pain medicine:

- Put ice on the knee for 15 to 20 minutes after sports.
- Wrap the ice in a towel. Do not put it right on the skin.
- Ibuprofen can ease pain. It does not make the problem go away faster.
- Ibuprofen dose: _
- Do not use ice or pain medicine before sports. They can hide pain.

Stretches, 1 to 2 times a day after exercise:

- Front of thigh: stand and hold a wall. Pull your heel toward your bottom.
- Back of thigh: sit with the leg straight. Reach toward your toes.
- Hold each stretch 30 seconds. Do it 3 times on each leg.
- Stretch gently. Do not bounce.

Strength exercises, every day for the first 4 weeks:

- Thigh hold, as we showed you: _
- Hold it for 30 seconds, then rest. Do this 10 times.
- Bridges: lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Lift your hips, then lower slowly.
- After 4 weeks, add squats. Later, add lunges. Move up only if pain stays mild.

Back to full sports when your child can jog, sprint, and hop on that leg without pain.

Call the clinic if:

- Pain is worse at night or wakes your child up
- The knee is red, hot, or very swollen
- Your child has a fever with knee pain
- Your child cannot walk on the leg
- Pain is not better in _ weeks

desc: Stomach pain that keeps coming back
use: Use as after-visit instructions for parents of a child with functional abdominal pain or pediatric IBS.
body:
Stomach pain that keeps coming back

Your child has functional belly pain. The pain is real. The nerves in the gut are extra sensitive, and the gut and brain affect each other.

We did not find signs of a serious problem. Many children with this pain get better over months. Some have pain on and off for years.

What helps most:

- Keep your child in school, even on pain days.
- Keep up sports, hobbies, and time with friends.
- Keep regular times for meals and sleep.
- Have your child drink water through the day.
- Stay calm and kind when your child has pain. Do not ask about the pain over and over.
- Do not give treats or extra screen time on pain days.

During a pain spell:

- Help your child rest for a short time, then get back to normal things.
- Try distraction, like drawing, music, a story, a walk, or stretching.
- Practice slow, deep breathing together.
- Try tightening and then relaxing one muscle group at a time, from toes to head.

Treatments that work:

- Gut-directed hypnosis is a guided relaxation program. It has the best proof of helping.
- It can be done with a therapist or with an audio program at home.
- Home programs use short sessions at least 5 days a week for 3 months.
- Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, teaches skills to handle pain.
- Your plan: _

Food:

- Do not cut out whole food groups unless we tell you to.
- Some children feel worse with greasy or spicy foods, caffeine, or fizzy drinks.
- Do not give any medicine or supplement without asking us first.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Has pain that is different, worse, or more often
- Has pain that wakes them up at night
- Is missing school because of pain
- Has new vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation
- Has blood in the poop
- Is losing weight

Go to the ER if your child has sudden, severe belly pain. Also go if your child is not drinking and is peeing much less.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for parents of a child with iron deficiency, with kid-sized iron-rich foods and milk limits.
body:
Iron for kids

Your child's iron is low. Iron helps the blood carry oxygen. It also helps the brain grow. Medicine and food can bring the iron back up.

Iron medicine:

- Give _ of iron by mouth once a day.
- Give it with water or juice. Do not give it with milk.
- Keep it apart from calcium pills.
- Liquid iron can stain teeth. Mix it with water or juice, and brush teeth after.
- Stools may turn dark. This is OK.
- Constipation and upset stomach can happen. Tell us if they are a problem.
- Keep giving it for at least 3 months, even when your child seems fine.

Keep iron away from children:

- Too much iron can kill a young child.
- Store it up high, locked, and in a child-safe bottle.
- If your child swallows extra, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away.

Milk limits:

- No cow's milk before age 1.
- Age 1 to 2: about 16 ounces, or 2 cups, of whole milk a day.
- Age 2 to 5: 16 to 24 ounces, or 2 to 3 cups, a day.
- Never more than 24 ounces a day. Too much milk blocks iron and fills kids up.
- Soy milk is the only plant milk that can replace cow's milk.

Iron-rich foods:

- Iron-fortified cereal: check the label. Some have 18 mg per serving.
- White beans, canned, 1/2 cup: 4 mg
- Lentils, cooked, 1/2 cup: 3 mg
- Tofu, firm, 1/2 cup: 3 mg
- Spinach, cooked, 1/2 cup: 3 mg, but the body takes in only a little
- Kidney beans or chickpeas, 1/2 cup: 2 mg
- Beef, 3 ounces: 2 mg. A toddler serving of 1 ounce has about 0.7 mg.
- Baked potato with skin: 2 mg
- Green peas, 1/2 cup: 1 mg
- Chicken or turkey, 3 ounces: 1 mg
- Hard-boiled egg: 1 mg
- Enriched rice, 1/2 cup: 1 mg
- Bread, 1 slice: 1 mg

How much iron kids need each day:

- Age 1 to 3: 7 mg
- Age 4 to 8: 10 mg
- Age 9 to 13: 8 mg
- Teen boys: 11 mg. Teen girls: 15 mg.

Help the body take in iron:

- Serve a vitamin C food with iron foods. Try oranges, strawberries, tomatoes, or broccoli.
- Add a little meat, chicken, or fish to beans or greens.

Blood test again on _.

Call the clinic if your child cannot take the iron, or seems more tired or pale.

Go to the ER if your child swallowed extra iron, or is very weak, breathing fast, or fainting.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for parents after a simple febrile seizure.
body:
Febrile seizure

Your child had a seizure caused by fever. This is called a febrile seizure. It is scary to watch, but it is not dangerous. It does not cause brain damage or long-term health problems.

Febrile seizures happen in young children between 6 months and 5 years old. They often happen on the first day of a fever. They run in families. Most children outgrow them by school age.

Will it happen again?

- About 1 in 3 children have another one.
- The risk is higher if the first one happened before 18 months of age.
- Most children who have febrile seizures do not get epilepsy.

About fever medicine:

- Fever medicine helps your child feel better.
- It does not prevent febrile seizures.
- You do not need to wake your child to give it.
- Acetaminophen dose: _
- Ibuprofen dose, if 6 months or older: _
- Never give aspirin to a child.

If your child has another seizure:

- Stay calm. Note the time it starts.
- Lay your child on the floor or a bed, away from hard or sharp things.
- Turn your child on the side so spit or vomit can drain out.
- Do not put anything in the mouth. Your child will not swallow the tongue.
- Do not hold your child down.
- Most seizures stop in 1 to 2 minutes.
- Your child may be sleepy afterward. This is normal.

Call 911 if:

- The seizure lasts 5 minutes or longer
- Your child has trouble breathing or turns blue
- Your child does not wake up normally after the seizure

Go to the ER if your child:

- Has a stiff neck
- Is very sleepy, hard to wake, or confused
- Has another seizure in the same day

Call the clinic after any new seizure, even if your child seems fine.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for pelvic organ prolapse, with pelvic floor exercises.
body:
Pelvic organ prolapse

Prolapse means the bladder, womb, or bowel has dropped down into the vagina. It can feel like a bulge or heaviness. Exercises and daily habits can ease symptoms and help keep it from getting worse.

Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels):

- Find the muscles: squeeze as if you are stopping gas or pee.
- Keep your legs and buttocks still. Breathe normally.
- Sit with knees slightly apart, or lie down with knees bent.

Slow squeezes:

- Squeeze as hard as you can and hold for up to 10 seconds.
- At first you may only hold 2 or 3 seconds. That is OK.
- Rest 4 to 5 seconds between squeezes.
- Do 8 to 10 slow squeezes.

Fast squeezes:

- Squeeze quickly, then let go right away.
- Do 10 to 20 fast squeezes.

How often:

- Slow plus fast squeezes make 1 session.
- Do 3 to 5 sessions a day, at least 1 hour apart.
- Do not do them while you are on the toilet.
- Give it time. Strength builds over weeks to months.
- A pelvic floor physical therapist can check that you are doing them right.

The squeeze before you strain:

- Tighten your pelvic floor just before you cough, sneeze, or lift.

Daily habits:

- Avoid heavy lifting, like boxes or full laundry baskets.
- Avoid running, jumping, deep squats, sit-ups, and crunches.
- Safe choices: walking, swimming, water classes, seated cycling, and gentle strength training.
- Put your feet on a footstool when you poop, so your knees are above your hips.
- Do not strain to poop.
- Drink about 50 to 70 ounces of fluid a day.
- Eat 2 or 3 green or gold kiwifruit a day to keep stools soft.
- Choose rye bread instead of white bread.
- If you have a cough that will not go away, tell us.
- If you are overweight, losing weight can help.

If you have a pessary:

- Your pessary is removed and checked every _ months.
- Next check: _

Call the clinic if:

- The bulge gets bigger or more uncomfortable.
- You have vaginal bleeding, a bad-smelling discharge, or pain.
- You have trouble peeing, or feel your bladder does not empty.
- You have trouble pooping.
- Your pessary falls out, hurts, or is hard to remove.

Go to the ER if:

- You cannot pee at all.

- Your pessary falls out, hurts, or is hard to remove.

Go to the ER if:

- You cannot pee at all.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a nosebleed, with home first aid and prevention.
body:
Nosebleeds

Most nosebleeds start in the front of the nose. They look scary but usually stop with firm pressure at home.

To stop a nosebleed:

- Stay calm. Sit up and lean forward a little.
- Do not lie down or tip your head back.
- Gently blow out any clots.
- If age 6 or older, spray oxymetazoline (a decongestant spray) 2 or 3 times in the bleeding side.
- Pinch the soft part of your nose shut with your thumb and finger.
- Hold for 10 to 15 minutes by the clock. Do not let go to check.
- If it is still bleeding, pinch again for 10 more minutes.
- Do not use the spray more than 3 days in a row.

After it stops:

- Do not blow or pick your nose.
- Avoid bending over, straining, or lifting heavy things.
- Keep your head above your heart.

To prevent more nosebleeds:

- Put a thin layer of saline gel or petroleum jelly inside each nostril 3 times a day.
- Use a cotton swab. Include a dose at bedtime.
- Spray saline (salt water) in your nose to keep it moist.
- Run a humidifier in your bedroom.
- Keep children's fingernails short. Help them stop picking.
- If you smoke, quit. Smoke dries the nose.

If you take a blood thinner or aspirin:

- Keep taking it unless we tell you to stop.

If you have nose packing:

- Do not blow your nose or pull on the packing.
- Packing removal: _

Call the clinic if:

- You have nosebleeds often, or from the same side again and again.
- One side of your nose also feels blocked.
- You bruise easily or your gums bleed.
- Someone in your family has many nosebleeds.

Go to the ER if:

- Bleeding does not stop after 30 minutes of pressure.
- Blood runs down your throat even while you pinch.
- The nosebleed came after a head injury.
- You feel dizzy, faint, or very weak.
- You have trouble breathing.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for temporomandibular disorder, with self-care and jaw exercises.
body:
Jaw pain (TMD)

TMD is pain in the jaw joint and the chewing muscles. Stress, clenching, and grinding can make it worse. Most people get better with simple care at home.

What to do:

- Eat soft foods like pasta, eggs, and soup.
- Do not bite food with your front teeth.
- Rest your jaw: teeth apart, tongue resting lightly behind your upper front teeth.
- Hold a warm towel on your jaw for 15 to 20 minutes, twice a day.
- Or use ice wrapped in a towel, no more than 5 minutes at a time.
- Gently rub the sore jaw muscles.
- Support your chin with your hand when you yawn.
- Find ways to relax and manage stress.

Things to avoid:

- Chewing gum or pen tops
- Biting your nails
- Clenching or grinding your teeth
- Opening your mouth very wide

Jaw exercises:

Stop if an exercise hurts.

- Goldfish, partial: put your tongue on the roof of your mouth. Put 1 finger on your jaw joint and 1 on your chin.
- Let your lower jaw drop halfway open, then close. Watch in a mirror so your jaw opens straight.
- Goldfish, full: do the same, but open as wide as you can while your tongue stays up.
- Do each one 6 times. Do the set 6 times a day.
- Chin push: put your hands under your chin. Open a little against your hands and hold 20 seconds.
- Chin tucks: sit tall. Pull your chin straight back to make a double chin. Hold 2 to 3 seconds, repeat 10 times.

Medicine:

- Your pain medicine: _
- Use it for the shortest time that helps.

Call the clinic if:

- Your jaw pain is not better in _ weeks.
- Your jaw locks open or closed.
- You cannot open your mouth enough to eat or drink.
- You have fever, face swelling, or a painful tooth.

Call right away or go to the ER if:

- You are over 50 and your jaw hurts when you chew and eases when you stop.
- Your scalp is tender, or you have a new headache at the side of your head.
- You have double vision or vision loss.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for patients taking warfarin.
body:
Warfarin

Warfarin is a blood thinner. It lowers your risk of blood clots. The INR blood test shows if your dose is right.

Your INR goal is _. Your next INR check is on _.

How to take it:

- Take _ mg by mouth each day, or as written on your dose calendar.
- If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember that same day.
- Do not take 2 doses the next day to make up for it.
- Do not change your dose unless the clinic tells you to.
- If your pills look different, call your pharmacy or the clinic.

Vitamin K foods:

Vitamin K changes how warfarin works. You do not need to stop these foods. Eat about the same amount each week.

- Very high: 1 cup cooked kale, spinach, collard greens, or turnip greens.
- High: 1 cup beet greens, mustard greens, or dandelion greens.
- Medium: 1 cup broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, asparagus, okra, or raw spinach.
- Example: if you eat 1/2 cup cooked greens 3 times a week, keep doing that.
- Nutrition shakes and some multivitamins have vitamin K too.
- Keep cranberry juice, green tea, and fish oil small and steady.
- Call the clinic before a big diet change, or if you are sick and not eating.

Medicines and safety:

- Do not drink large amounts of alcohol.
- Ask the clinic before any new medicine, vitamin, herb, or antibiotic.
- Do not take aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen unless your doctor says it is OK.
- Tell every doctor and dentist that you take warfarin.
- Use a soft toothbrush, waxed floss, and an electric razor.
- Prevent falls with good lights. Remove loose rugs and cords.

Signs of bleeding:

- Bleeding gums or nosebleeds
- Pink, red, or dark brown urine
- Red or black stools
- Large or dark bruises
- Heavy periods or bleeding between periods

Call the clinic if you have any sign of bleeding, a fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or you could be pregnant.

Call 911 or go to the ER if:

- You fall hard or hit your head, even if you feel fine.
- Bleeding does not stop after 15 minutes of pressure.
- You vomit blood or have black, tarry stools.
- You have a sudden bad headache, weakness, or dizziness.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for parents of a baby with a hip finding or risk factors for hip dysplasia.
body:
Hip dysplasia and hip-healthy swaddling

Hip dysplasia means the ball of the hip does not sit firmly in its socket. It is not painful for babies. Found early, most cases are treated well.

What we found:

- Hip exam today: _
- Your baby's risk factors: _

Next steps:

- We check your baby's hips at every checkup until 6 to 9 months.
- Hip ultrasound: _. Ultrasound works best from 6 weeks to about 4 to 6 months.
- After about 4 months, an x-ray may be used instead.
- Hip specialist visit: _

Hip-healthy swaddling:

- Use a thin blanket.
- Wrap the arms and chest snugly, but leave the legs loose.
- Let the legs bend up and out at the hips.
- Never wrap the legs straight and tight together.
- You should fit 2 to 3 fingers between the blanket and your baby's chest.
- Stop swaddling when your baby starts trying to roll. Some babies roll at about 2 months.

Safe sleep:

- Always put your baby to sleep on their back.
- Use a firm, flat crib with no loose blankets.
- Do not let your baby get too hot.
- Never use weighted swaddles or blankets.

Carriers and seats:

- Carriers and seats that let the legs move freely are fine.
- Avoid anything that holds the legs straight and tight together for long periods.

If your baby needs a brace:

- A brace holds the hips in a spread-apart position.
- Follow the specialist's directions for wearing it: _

Call the clinic if:

- One leg looks shorter than the other
- The skin folds on the thighs or bottom look uneven
- One leg does not spread out as far as the other at diaper changes
- You have questions about the brace or swaddling

use: Use as after-visit instructions for patients with adrenal insufficiency on steroid replacement.
body:
Adrenal insufficiency: staying safe

Your body does not make enough cortisol. Cortisol is a hormone you need to live. Your pills replace it, so take them every day.

Your daily medicine:

- Hydrocortisone _ mg when you wake up.
- Hydrocortisone _ mg at _.
- Fludrocortisone _ mg each morning. _

Sick-day rules:

- Fever over 100.4 F: take double your usual hydrocortisone dose.
- Fever over 102.2 F: take triple your usual dose.
- Keep the higher dose until you are well. This is often 2 to 3 days.
- Drink extra fluids with salt, like broth or sports drinks.
- If you throw up within 30 minutes of your pills, take them again.

Give your shot right away if:

- You throw up again, or you cannot keep pills down.
- You have bad diarrhea or a serious injury.
- You feel faint, confused, or very weak.
- You are not sure. An extra emergency dose will not hurt you.

How to give the shot:

- Your kit has hydrocortisone _ mg.
- Push down on the top of the vial to mix the powder and liquid.
- Turn the vial gently until the liquid is clear. Do not shake it.
- Draw the medicine into the syringe.
- Clean the outer middle part of your thigh with an alcohol pad.
- Put the needle straight in and push the medicine in.
- Then call 911, even if you feel better.

Every day:

- Wear a medical ID bracelet or necklace that says adrenal insufficiency.
- Carry your shot kit and extra pills everywhere you go.
- Check the date on your kit so it does not expire.
- Tell every doctor, dentist, or surgeon that you take steroids. You may need extra doses for procedures.

Call the clinic if you often feel tired or dizzy when you stand, or you crave salt. Call 911 or go to the ER if you have vomiting, severe weakness, confusion, or fainting.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for patients with restless legs syndrome.
body:
Restless legs

Restless legs causes an urge to move your legs. It is often worse in the evening and at night.

What helps:

- Walk, stretch, or rub your legs when the feeling starts. Relief often lasts only while you keep moving.
- Keep your mind busy when you sit, with puzzles, games, or reading.
- Cut back on alcohol and caffeine.
- Avoid sleep or allergy pills with diphenhydramine or doxylamine, unless your doctor says they are OK.
- Some medicines for depression, nausea, or mental health can make it worse. Ask us before you stop any medicine.
- If you have sleep apnea, use your CPAP every night.

If you take iron pills:

- Take 1 ferrous sulfate 325 mg pill once a day in the evening.
- Take it on an empty stomach with orange juice or vitamin C 200 mg.
- Do not take it within 2 hours of milk, calcium, antacids, tea, or coffee.
- Take it at least 4 hours apart from thyroid medicine.
- Once a day works as well as twice a day, with less stomach upset.
- Stop iron 2 days before your next iron blood test.
- We will check your iron in about 3 months.

Your RLS medicine:

- Take _ at _.
- It can make you sleepy or dizzy. Do not drive until you know how it affects you.

Call the clinic if your symptoms start earlier in the day or spread to your arms. Also call if they get stronger on your medicine. Call the clinic if iron upsets your stomach or you cannot sleep most nights.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for a teen with scoliosis and their parents.
body:
Scoliosis

Scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine. It most often starts between age 10 and the end of growth. The exact cause is not known.

What to know:

- It is not caused by heavy backpacks or poor posture.
- It is rarely painful.
- Curves mostly grow during growth spurts. That is why we check during the teen years.
- Your child can keep playing sports and being active.

Your child's plan:

- Curve size today: _ degrees.
- Next check and x-ray: _.
- We usually check every 6 to 12 months until growth is done.

If your child has a brace:

- Wear it for the hours we set: _. This is often about 18 hours a day.
- More hours in the brace work better.
- The brace does not straighten the curve. It helps keep it from getting worse.
- Take it off for sports. Put it back on after.
- Check the skin under the brace every day for red or sore spots.

Other treatment:

- Special scoliosis exercises from a physical therapist may help a little.
- Surgery is only for large curves, usually over 45 to 50 degrees.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Has back pain that is bad or does not go away
- Has numbness, weakness, or trouble walking
- Has shoulders, waist, or ribs that look more uneven
- Has brace rubbing that causes sores

use: Use as after-visit instructions for an adult starting treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder.
body:
OCD

OCD causes unwanted thoughts that keep coming back. These are called obsessions. It also causes urges to do things over and over. These are called compulsions. Treatment helps most people.

What to know:

- OCD is a health condition. It is not your fault.
- Rituals ease worry for a short time, but the worry comes back.
- Stress can make symptoms worse.

Therapy:

- The best talk therapy for OCD is called exposure and response prevention, or ERP.
- You face your fears in small steps without doing the ritual.
- Worry may go up at first. With practice, the urges usually get weaker.
- Do the practice your therapist gives you between visits.
- It often takes about 13 to 20 weekly visits.

Medicine:

- Your medicine: _. Your dose: _.
- It can take 8 to 12 weeks to work.
- OCD often needs a higher dose than depression does.
- Side effects can include headache, upset stomach, and trouble sleeping.
- Do not stop it on your own. Talk with us first.
- Most people keep taking it for at least 1 to 2 years after it works.

Family and friends:

- Joining in rituals or giving the same reassurance over and over can keep OCD going.
- Ask your therapist how your family can cut back, step by step.

Every day:

- Keep a regular sleep schedule.
- Be active most days.
- Spend time with people you trust.

Call the clinic if:

- Symptoms take up more of your day, or you cannot keep up at work or school.
- Medicine side effects bother you.

Call or text 988 any time if you have thoughts of hurting yourself. Call 911 if you are in danger now.

use: Use when discharging a patient after a pneumothorax.
body:
Collapsed lung (pneumothorax)

Air leaked out of your lung into your chest. This made part of your lung collapse. Most people heal fully.

What to do:

- Do not smoke. This includes cigarettes and marijuana.
- Smoking makes it much more likely to happen again.
- Ask us for help to quit smoking.
- Get your follow-up chest X-ray on _.
- Do not fly until 1 week after an X-ray shows your lung has healed.
- Never scuba dive again. The only exception is after a special surgery on both lungs.

Will it happen again?

- About 2 to 3 out of 10 people have it again within 1 year.
- If it happens again, you may need surgery to stop it.

Call the clinic if:

- You have questions about your X-ray or follow-up.
- You have mild new chest pain.

Go to the ER or call 911 if:

- You get short of breath.
- Your chest pain gets sudden or bad.

- You get short of breath.
- Your chest pain gets sudden or bad.

use: Use when discharging a patient after alcohol-associated hepatitis.
body:
Alcohol hepatitis

Alcohol has hurt your liver and made it swollen. This can be life-threatening. Stopping alcohol is the most important step.

What to do:

- Do not drink any alcohol.
- Ask us about medicine that helps you stay away from alcohol.
- Join a treatment program or see a counselor.
- Take prednisolone _ mg every day until _.
- Prednisolone raises your risk of infection and stomach bleeding.
- Take your vitamins as prescribed: _.

Eat enough to heal:

- Your body needs extra food right now.
- Your calorie goal is _ calories a day.
- Your protein goal is _ grams a day.
- Each of these has about 7 grams of protein: 1 ounce of meat, fish or chicken.
- Or 1 large egg, or 1/2 cup of cooked beans or lentils.
- Eat less salt.

Call the clinic if:

- Your skin or eyes get more yellow.
- You start drinking again and want help.

Go to the ER or call 911 if:

- You are confused or very sleepy.
- You vomit blood, or see blood in your stool or urine.
- You have a fever over 101 F.
- Your belly swells up fast.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for adults with bronchiectasis, teaching daily airway clearance and what to do in a flare-up.
body:
Bronchiectasis and clearing your lungs

Bronchiectasis means some airways are wide and damaged. Mucus collects there and germs can grow. Clearing the mucus every day helps you feel better.

When to clear your lungs:

- Do it 1 or 2 times a day when you feel well.
- Do it more often when you have a flare-up.
- Keep going for at least 10 minutes.
- Stop when you have 2 clear huffs or coughs, or after 30 minutes.
- If you use an inhaler that opens your airways, use it first.
- Use your other inhalers after you clear your lungs.

The active cycle of breathing:

- Sit up in a comfortable chair. Relax your shoulders.
- Gentle breathing: breathe slowly and quietly with your lower chest for about 30 seconds.
- Deep breaths: take 3 or 4 slow, deep breaths in. Let each one sigh out.
- Gentle breathing again for a short rest.
- Huff: take a normal breath in. Then breathe out hard and long with your mouth open.
- A huff sounds like you are fogging up a mirror.
- Cough only when you hear mucus when you huff. Spit the mucus out.
- If you feel dizzy, stop and go back to gentle breathing.
- Repeat the cycle until your chest feels clear.

Other things that help:

- Your therapist may give you a small device you blow into. It shakes the air and loosens mucus.
- Lying in certain positions lets gravity drain mucus. Your therapist will show you which ones.
- Breathing in a salt-water mist before you start can loosen mucus, if we prescribed it.
- Stay active. Walking and exercise help move mucus.
- Get a flu shot every year. Ask us about pneumonia, COVID-19, and RSV shots.

If you have a flare-up:

A flare-up means you feel worse for 2 days or more. You may cough more, make more or darker mucus, feel more short of breath, or feel more tired.

- Spit mucus into your sample cup before you start antibiotics. Bring it to the lab or clinic.
- Start your standby antibiotic _ if we gave you one. Take it for _ days.
- Do your airway clearance more often.

Call the clinic if:

- You have a flare-up.
- You see streaks of blood in your mucus.
- You are not better 3 days after you start an antibiotic.

Go to the ER or call 911 if:

- You cough up more blood than a few streaks.
- You are very short of breath or have chest pain.
- You have a high fever with shaking chills, or you feel faint or confused.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for patients with symptomatic gallstones waiting for or declining surgery.
body:
Gallstone attacks

Gallstones are hard lumps that form in the gallbladder. A stone can block the gallbladder for a while and cause a painful attack.

What an attack feels like:

- Steady pain in the upper right belly or under the breastbone.
- It often starts after a large meal, in the evening or at night.
- Most attacks ease within 1 to 5 hours.
- After one attack, more are likely. Most people have another within 2 years.

What to do:

- Keep your surgery visit: _. Removing the gallbladder stops the attacks.
- For pain, you may take ibuprofen _ mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed.
- Ask us first if you have kidney disease, stomach ulcers, or bleeding problems. Ibuprofen may not be safe for you.

Eating to help prevent attacks:

- Eat smaller meals. Large, heavy meals can set off attacks.
- Limit fried foods, fast food, and rich desserts.
- Choose healthy fats like olive oil and fish.
- Eat high-fiber foods every day: oatmeal, brown rice, whole wheat bread, beans, fruits, and vegetables.
- Eat a small handful of nuts, about 1 ounce, 5 days a week. Peanuts and peanut butter count.
- Eat fewer sweets, sugary drinks, white bread, and white rice.
- If you need to lose weight, lose it slowly. Crash diets can cause more gallstones.

Call the clinic if:

- You have another attack that goes away.
- You have questions about your surgery.

Go to the ER if:

- Pain lasts more than 5 hours.
- You have a fever or chills.
- Your skin or the whites of your eyes turn yellow.
- Your urine turns dark like tea, or your stools turn pale.
- You keep throwing up.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for gastroparesis, with small particle diet foods, meal habits and medicine safety.
body:
Slow stomach emptying (gastroparesis)

Gastroparesis means your stomach empties too slowly. Food sits in the stomach and can cause nausea, vomiting, fullness, and bloating. Changing how you eat helps most people.

How to eat:

- Eat 5 or 6 small meals a day instead of 2 or 3 large ones.
- Choose soft, well-cooked foods. Mash or blend foods if you need to.
- Chew each bite very well. Cut meat into very small pieces.
- Choose low-fat and low-fiber foods.
- Sit up while you eat and for 1 hour after.
- Do not drink alcohol or fizzy drinks.

Foods that are usually easier:

- White bread, bagels, English muffins, flour tortillas, saltines, pretzels.
- Cream of Wheat, grits, quick oats, Rice Krispies, Cheerios.
- Plain rice, plain pasta, and potatoes or sweet potatoes without the skin.
- Eggs, tofu, chicken or turkey without skin, shrimp, tuna in water, cottage cheese.
- Applesauce, bananas, and canned peaches or pears.
- Cooked carrots and beets, tomato sauce, and tomato juice.
- Plain yogurt, pudding, custard, broth, and creamed soups.

Foods to avoid:

These foods can form a hard ball in the stomach that will not empty.

- Raw apples, berries, oranges, figs, coconut, and persimmons.
- Brussels sprouts, green beans, sauerkraut, and potato skins.
- Beans, peas, and lentils.

On bad days:

- Switch to liquids: broth, clear soups, low-fiber juices, sports drinks, or a liquid meal drink like _.
- Drink plenty of water or drinks with sugar and salts, like sports drinks.

If you have diabetes:

- Keep your blood sugar in your target range. High sugar slows the stomach even more.

Your medicine: _

- If you take metoclopramide, take it 30 minutes before meals and at bedtime.
- Stop it and call us right away if you get movements you cannot control, like lip smacking or twitching.
- We will plan to stop metoclopramide within 12 weeks.

Call the clinic if:

- You keep losing weight.
- You cannot keep down food for 24 hours.

Go to the ER if:

- You cannot keep down any liquids.
- You vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds.
- You have bad belly pain, or you feel dizzy or faint.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for women with recurrent UTIs, covering water, cranberry, vaginal estrogen and preventive medicine.
body:
Preventing bladder infections

You have had several bladder infections. These steps can lower the chance of another one.

Drink more water:

- If you drink less than 6 cups of fluid a day, add about 6 cups of water a day.
- This cuts infections about in half.

Cranberry:

- Cranberry juice or cranberry pills every day can lower infections by about 1 in 4.
- No dose is proven best. Pick one you can take every day.

D-mannose:

- D-mannose powder does not prevent infections. We do not suggest it.

Vaginal estrogen, if you are near or past menopause:

- This is a small, low dose of estrogen placed in the vagina.
- Put 1 insert in your vagina at bedtime every night for 2 weeks.
- Then use it 2 nights a week, like Monday and Thursday.
- Estrogen pills do not prevent bladder infections. The vaginal kind does.

Your prevention medicine: _

- Methenamine: take 1 gram 2 times a day, morning and night. It is not an antibiotic.
- Antibiotic after sex: take 1 dose after sex.
- Daily antibiotic: take 1 low dose every night.

If we gave you a standby antibiotic:

- When symptoms start, leave a urine sample first if we asked you to.
- Then start the antibiotic _ for _ days.

Call the clinic if:

- It burns when you pee, or you need to pee often or urgently.
- Your symptoms are not better 2 days after you start the antibiotic.
- You see blood in your urine.

Go to the ER if:

- You have fever, chills, back or side pain, or vomiting.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for overactive bladder, with bladder training, fluid and caffeine advice and medicine tips.
body:
Sudden urges to pee (overactive bladder)

Overactive bladder causes sudden, strong urges to pee. You may go often, wake at night to pee, or leak. Bladder training helps many people.

Bladder diary:

- For 3 days, write down what you drink, when you pee, and when you leak.
- Bring it to your next visit.

Bladder training:

- Start by peeing every _ hours while awake, even if you do not feel the urge.
- When an urge hits, stop and stand or sit still.
- Squeeze your pelvic muscles quickly 5 to 10 times. Breathe slowly.
- Wait for the urge to fade. Then walk calmly to the bathroom.
- Slowly stretch the time between bathroom trips by 30 to 60 minutes.
- The goal is every 3 to 4 hours without leaking. This often takes 6 to 12 weeks.

Pelvic floor exercises:

- Squeeze the muscles you use to stop pee or hold in gas.
- Hold for 6 to 8 seconds, then relax. Do 8 to 10 in a row.
- Do 3 sets, 3 or 4 days a week. Keep it up for at least 4 months.

Drinks:

- Drink about 6 to 8 cups of fluid a day. Cutting back too much can make urges worse.
- Cut down on coffee, tea, soda, and energy drinks. Less caffeine can calm urges.

Other habits:

- If you are overweight, losing weight can help.

Your medicine: _

- Mirabegron can raise blood pressure. We will check it at your visits.
- It can take 4 to 8 weeks to see the full effect.
- Older bladder pills can cause dry mouth, constipation, and memory problems. Ask us before you start one.

If these steps do not help, we can refer you for nerve stimulation or bladder injections.

Call the clinic if:

- It burns when you pee, or you have a fever.
- You see blood in your urine.
- You feel like your bladder does not empty, or you can only dribble.

Go to the ER if:

- You cannot pee at all and your belly hurts.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for chronic venous insufficiency, varicose veins, or venous ulcers.
body:
Leg vein problems (venous insufficiency)

The valves in your leg veins are weak. Blood pools in your lower legs. This can cause aching, swelling, and skin changes.

Compression stockings:

- Put them on when you get up. Take them off at bedtime.
- Wear them every day.
- Your stocking strength: _ mmHg
- Replace them about every 6 months. Washing makes them lose their squeeze.

What else helps:

- Rest with your legs raised above the level of your heart. Prop them on pillows while lying down.
- Walk every day. Leg muscles pump blood back up when you walk.
- Do calf raises. Rise up on your toes, then lower slowly. Do _ a day.
- Do not stand or sit still for a long time. Move your feet and legs often.
- If you are overweight, losing weight helps.

Horse chestnut seed extract:

- If we suggested it, buy one that says standardized to 50 mg escin.
- Take 1 capsule twice a day, for up to 12 weeks.
- Never eat raw horse chestnut seeds, bark, or leaves. They are poisonous.

If you have a leg sore:

- Keep it covered with the dressing we showed you.
- Wear your wraps or stockings as told. Squeezing helps the sore heal.
- After it heals, keep wearing stockings every day.
- Raise your legs at least 1 hour a day, 6 days a week. This helps keep sores from coming back.

If a vein bleeds:

- Lie down and raise the leg above your heart.
- Press hard on the spot with a clean cloth.
- Call 911 if the bleeding will not stop.
- See us soon after. A vein doctor can treat the vein so it does not bleed again.

Call the clinic if:

- Your legs hurt more or swell more
- You get a new sore or a sore gets bigger
- A sore is not better after 4 weeks
- Your stockings slip or you cannot put them on

Go to the ER or call 911 if:

- One leg suddenly swells and hurts
- You have chest pain or trouble breathing
- Your leg is red, hot, and painful, and you have a fever

use: Use as after-visit instructions for arm or leg lymphedema.
body:
Lymphedema

Lymphedema is swelling from fluid that cannot drain well from an arm or leg. It is often lifelong. Daily care keeps it from getting worse.

Compression:

- Wear your sleeve or stocking during the day. Take it off at night.
- Tell us if it feels too tight or too loose.
- Your garment: _
- On long flights, wear your garment. Keep your arm above heart level when you can.

Move and exercise:

- Use the swollen arm or leg for everyday tasks.
- Aim for 150 minutes a week of walking or other activity, plus strength exercises.
- Lifting weights is safe when you start light and build up slowly with a trainer or therapist.
- Rest the limb above heart level 2 or 3 times a day, for about 45 minutes.
- Do not sit in one position more than 30 minutes. Do not cross your legs.
- If you are overweight, losing weight helps the swelling.

Skin care every day:

- Wash the skin and use lotion to keep it moist.
- Check the skin for cuts, cracks, rashes, or red spots.
- Use an electric razor, not a blade.
- Wear gloves for gardening, cooking, and housework.
- Use sunscreen SPF 30 or higher and bug spray.
- Cut toenails straight across. Do not walk barefoot outside.
- Keep feet clean and dry. Wear cotton socks.

Protect the limb:

- Have blood draws, IVs, and shots in your other arm or another body part.
- Avoid hot tubs, saunas, heating pads, and ice packs on the limb.
- Do not wear tight clothes, tight jewelry, or bands around the limb.
- Carry your purse or bag on the other arm.

If you get a cut:

- Wash it gently with soap and water.
- Put on antibiotic ointment.
- Cover it with a loose, dry bandage.

Call the clinic right away if:

- The limb is red, warm, more swollen, or painful
- You have a fever of 100.4 F or higher
- You have a rash or a cut that will not heal
- The swelling gets worse, or new swelling lasts longer than 1 to 2 weeks
- Rings, watches, or shoes feel tighter

Go to the ER if:

- You have a fever with chills and the limb is red and spreading
- You feel very sick, confused, or dizzy
- You have chest pain or trouble breathing

If you get a cut:

- Wash it gently with soap and water.
- Put on antibiotic ointment.
- Cover it with a loose, dry bandage.

Call the clinic right away if:

- The limb is red, warm, more swollen, or painful
- You have a fever of 100.4 F or higher
- You have a rash or a cut that will not heal
- The swelling gets worse, or new swelling lasts longer than 1 to 2 weeks
- Rings, watches, or shoes feel tighter

Go to the ER if:

- You have a fever with chills and the limb is red and spreading
- You feel very sick, confused, or dizzy
- You have chest pain or trouble breathing

use: Use as after-visit instructions with home stretches for frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis).
body:
Frozen shoulder

Frozen shoulder is a stiff, painful shoulder. The tissue around the joint gets thick and tight. It gets better slowly, often over 1 to 3 years.

The three stages:

- Freezing: pain gets worse and the shoulder gets stiffer. This lasts about 6 weeks to 9 months.
- Frozen: pain may ease, but the shoulder stays stiff. This lasts about 4 to 6 months.
- Thawing: motion slowly comes back. This takes about 6 months to 2 years.

Pain relief:

- Ibuprofen or naproxen eases pain. Take it with food.
- Ask us first if you have kidney disease, stomach ulcers, or take a blood thinner.
- A steroid shot in the shoulder can ease pain for a few weeks. It works best early.
- Your plan: _

Home stretches:

Do these 5 to 6 days a week. Stretch until you feel a gentle pull. Stop before it hurts.

- Pendulum: Lean forward with your good hand on a table. Let the sore arm hang down.
- Gently swing the hanging arm forward and back, then side to side, then in small circles. Do 2 sets of 10.
- Cross-body stretch: Use your good hand to pull the sore arm across your chest. Hold 30 seconds.
- Relax 30 seconds, then repeat. Do 4 times.
- Inward turn: Hold a yardstick behind your back with both hands. Pull it sideways to stretch the sore shoulder.
- Hold 30 seconds, relax 30 seconds. Do 4 times.
- Outward turn: Keep the sore elbow at your side and hold one end of a stick. Push it outward with your good hand.
- Hold 30 seconds, relax 30 seconds. Do 4 times.
- Arm raise: Lie on your back. Use your good arm to lift the sore arm overhead to a gentle stretch.
- Hold 15 seconds, then lower slowly. Do _ times.

Other tips:

- If you have diabetes, keeping your blood sugar in range helps your shoulder recover.

Call the clinic if:

- You are not getting better after 6 to 12 weeks of stretching
- The pain keeps you from sleeping most nights
- You cannot lift your arm after a fall or injury

Go to the ER or call 911 if:

- Your shoulder is red, hot, and swollen, and you have a fever
- Shoulder pain comes with chest pressure, shortness of breath, or sweating

use: Use as after-visit instructions for Morton (interdigital) neuroma.
body:
Morton neuroma

A Morton neuroma is a thick, irritated nerve between two toes. It is most often between the 3rd and 4th toes. It can feel like burning or like a pebble in your shoe.

Shoes:

- Wear shoes with a wide, roomy toe area.
- Choose flat or low heels.
- Avoid tight, narrow, or pointed shoes and high heels.

Metatarsal pad:

- A small pad inside your shoe spreads the bones and takes pressure off the nerve.
- Place it just behind the ball of your foot, not under it.
- Your pad: _

Other things that help:

- Rest your foot when it hurts. Taking your shoe off can ease the pain.
- Use a cold pack on the sore area. Put a thin towel between the pack and your skin.
- Ibuprofen or naproxen eases pain for a short time. Take it with food. Do not use it for months.

Treatments we may offer:

- A steroid shot between the toes can ease pain for at least 3 months.
- If shoes, pads, and shots do not help, a foot specialist can offer other treatments or surgery.
- Surgery helps most people, but leaves the skin between those toes numb for good.

Call the clinic if:

- Your pain is not better after 6 weeks of shoe changes and a pad
- The pain or tingling is constant
- Your foot swells or it hurts to walk even without shoes

Go to the ER if:

- Your foot is red, hot, and swollen and you have a fever

desc: Steroid pills, taking and stopping safely
use: Use as after-visit instructions for patients on or finishing a course of prednisone or another steroid pill.
body:
Steroid pills: taking and stopping them safely

Steroid pills like prednisone calm swelling and an overactive immune system.

How to take your steroid:

- Your dose: _
- Take it with food.
- Take it at the same time each day.
- If you miss a dose and do not know what to do, call us. Do not take a double dose.

Stopping your steroid:

- If you took it for less than 3 to 4 weeks, you can usually stop at the end.
- If you took it for longer, never stop it suddenly. Your body may not make enough of its own steroid.
- Lower your dose only as we tell you. Your plan: _
- While you lower the dose, you may feel tired, achy, sick to your stomach, or moody. This is common.
- Tell us if these feelings are hard to bear. We can slow down the plan.

What to expect while you take it:

- Trouble sleeping.
- Mood changes. You may feel wired, cranky, or down.
- More hunger and weight gain.
- Higher blood sugar and higher blood pressure.

Check your blood sugar if we ask you to:

- Check once a day, before lunch or supper, or 1 to 2 hours after.
- Your goal is _.
- Signs of high sugar are feeling very thirsty, peeing a lot, blurry vision, and feeling weak or tired.

Protect your bones if you take it for 3 months or longer:

- Aim for 1,000 to 1,200 mg of calcium a day, mostly from food.
- 8 ounces of plain low-fat yogurt has about 450 mg.
- 1 cup of milk has about 300 mg.
- 3 ounces of canned sardines has about 330 mg.
- 1 cup of calcium-fortified orange juice has about 350 mg.
- Take vitamin D _ IU each day.
- Do strength exercises and weight-bearing exercise like walking. Do not smoke.

Sick-day rules, if we told you your body may not make enough steroid:

- If you have a fever, need antibiotics, or are sick in bed, take _ mg each day.
- Keep the higher dose until you are well. This is often 2 to 5 days.
- Tell every doctor, dentist, and surgeon that you take or recently took steroids.
- Carry your steroid card with you.

Avoid infections:

- Steroids make it harder to fight germs. They can also hide the signs of infection.
- Wash your hands often and stay away from sick people.
- Call us if you are near someone with chickenpox or measles.
- Do not get any vaccine before you talk with us.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Fever, chills, sore throat, cough, or other signs of infection.
- Blood sugar over _ two times in one day.
- Eye pain, redness, or changes in your vision.
- Feeling very sad, confused, or not like yourself.
- Tiredness, weakness, nausea, or salt cravings while lowering or after stopping your dose.

Call 911 or go to the ER if you have:

- Vomiting and you cannot keep your pills down.
- Severe weakness, fainting, or confusion.
- Black, tarry stools.
- Trouble breathing.

use: Use as after-visit instructions for an adult with otomycosis.
body:
Fungal ear infection

You have a fungal infection in your ear canal. It often causes itching, fullness, and muffled hearing. It can happen after antibiotic ear drops.

Your ear drops:

- Use clotrimazole ear drops in the _ ear.
- Use 1 vial twice a day, about 12 hours apart.
- Use them for 14 days, even if your ear feels better.
- Stop any antibiotic ear drops unless we told you to keep using them.

How to put in the drops:

- Hold the vial in your hand for 1 to 2 minutes to warm it. Cold drops can make you dizzy.
- Lie down with the sore ear facing up.
- Gently pull your outer ear up and back.
- Squeeze in the whole vial.
- Stay lying down for 1 minute.
- Throw the vial away after each use.

Keep your ear dry:

- Put a cotton ball coated with petroleum jelly in your ear when you shower.
- Do not swim until your ear has healed.
- Dry the outside of your ear gently with a towel.
- Do not put cotton swabs or anything else in your ear.

Call the clinic if:

- Your ear is not better after 14 days of drops
- Pain gets worse, or you get a fever
- Fluid drains from your ear
- The infection comes back

Go to the ER if:

- Your face feels weak or droops
- You have very bad ear pain

use: Use as after-visit instructions for chronic suppurative otitis media.
body:
Long-lasting ear drainage

You have a hole in your eardrum that keeps draining. This is a long-lasting middle ear infection. Ear drops and keeping the ear dry help it settle down.

Your ear drops:

- Put _ drops in the _ ear, twice a day, for _ days.
- Hold the bottle in your hand for 1 to 2 minutes first. Cold drops can make you dizzy.
- Lie down with the draining ear facing up.
- Put in the drops, then push on the small flap in front of the ear 4 times.
- Stay lying down for 5 minutes.
- Do not use any other ear drops unless we tell you to.

Keep your ear dry:

- Put a cotton ball coated with petroleum jelly in your ear when you shower.
- Do not swim until an ear doctor says it is OK.
- Do not put cotton swabs or anything else in your ear.
- Wipe drainage from the outer ear with a clean tissue.

Next steps:

- We will check your ear again in _ weeks.
- A hearing test is planned _.
- An ear doctor may fix the hole with surgery.

Call the clinic if:

- Drainage is not better after you finish the drops
- Drainage comes back
- Your hearing gets worse

Go to the ER if:

- You feel dizzy or the room spins
- Your face feels weak or droops
- You have a bad headache, stiff neck, or fever

use: Use to send a benign or atypical nevus biopsy result to the patient.
body:
Your skin biopsy results are back. The _ spot from your _ is not cancer and is not melanoma.

Benign mole: This is a normal, harmless mole. Nothing more needs to be done.

Atypical mole: This mole looked a little unusual under the microscope. This is common. It is not cancer, and it almost never turns into cancer.

The biopsy removed the whole mole.

A small part of the mole may still be in the skin. For this type of mole, we usually watch the area instead of removing more.

Check the scar and call us if you see:

- A new dark or colored spot in or next to the scar
- Color spreading past the edge of the scar
- A spot that grows or changes

People with atypical moles have a slightly higher chance of melanoma somewhere on the skin. Check your skin once a month. Call us about any mole that:

- Is not the same on both sides
- Has a ragged or blurry edge
- Has more than one color
- Is bigger than a pencil eraser
- Changes in size, shape, or color
- Looks different from your other moles

Plan a full skin check with your family doctor once a year. Tell us if anyone in your family has had melanoma.

use: Use at well child visits to give families screen time limits by age.
body:
Screen time for kids

Under 18 months: avoid screens except video chats with family.
18 to 24 months: if you use screens, pick good shows or apps. Watch with your child.
Ages 2 to 5: limit screens to 1 hour a day of good shows. Watch together and talk about what you see.
Ages 6 and up: make a family media plan. Set limits on time and type of media.

Why limits matter:

- Eyes: lots of up-close screen time may raise the risk of nearsightedness (blurry far vision).
- Attention: kids who use screens a lot are more likely to have trouble paying attention later.
- Sleep: screen time can make it hard for kids to sleep at night.
- Speech: a TV that is on, even in the background, means less talking with your baby. That slows how fast your baby learns to talk.
- Weight: kids move less during screen time, and food ads lead to more snacking.
- Mood: heavy social media use is linked to sadness, worry, poor body image, and bullying.

Try instead:

- Play outside every day. Outdoor time helps protect your child's eyes.
- Read books, play games, and talk together.

Keep screens out of bedrooms.
Turn screens off 1 hour before bed.
Do not use screens during meals.

Call us if your child has trouble sleeping, gets very upset when screens end, or seems sad or withdrawn.
epic:
Screen time for kids

Under 18 months: avoid screens except video chats with family.
18 to 24 months: if you use screens, pick good shows or apps. Watch with your child.
Ages 2 to 5: limit screens to 1 hour a day of good shows. Watch together and talk about what you see.
Ages 6 and up: make a family media plan. Set limits on time and type of media.

Why limits matter:

- Eyes: lots of up-close screen time may raise the risk of nearsightedness (blurry far vision).
- Attention: kids who use screens a lot are more likely to have trouble paying attention later.
- Sleep: screen time can make it hard for kids to sleep at night.
- Speech: a TV that is on, even in the background, means less talking with your baby. That slows how fast your baby learns to talk.
- Weight: kids move less during screen time, and food ads lead to more snacking.
- Mood: heavy social media use is linked to sadness, worry, poor body image, and bullying.

Try instead:

- Play outside every day. Outdoor time helps protect your child's eyes.
- Read books, play games, and talk together.

Keep screens out of bedrooms.
Turn screens off 1 hour before bed.
Do not use screens during meals.

Call us if your child has trouble sleeping, gets very upset when screens end, or seems sad or withdrawn.

use: Use for summer anticipatory guidance at child visits.
body:
Summer safety for kids

Wear a helmet for bikes, scooters, skates, and skateboards.
Watch your child closely around any water, including bathtubs, pools, lakes, and splash pads.
Stay within arm's reach of young children in water.
Use sunscreen SPF 30 or higher. Put it on again every 2 hours and after swimming.
Keep babies under 6 months out of direct sun.
Use bug spray with DEET or picaridin to prevent tick and mosquito bites. Do not use it on babies under 2 months.
Check for ticks after time outside.
Give lots of water on hot days.
Never leave a child alone in a car.

Call us if your child has a rash or fever after a tick bite.

Call 911 if your child stops breathing, is pulled from the water, or is hot and confused.

use: Use to give a patient home piriformis stretch instructions.
body:
Piriformis stretch

Lie on your back with both knees bent.
Cross one ankle over the other knee.
Hold the outside of the crossed leg's knee with the opposite hand.
Gently pull that knee toward the opposite shoulder until you feel a stretch in your buttock.
Breathe slowly and hold for 20 to 30 seconds.
Switch sides.
Do this 2 to 3 times on each side, 1 to 2 times a day.

Stop if the stretch causes sharp pain.

Call us if the pain lasts more than 6 weeks or spreads down your leg.

Go to the ER if you have new leg weakness, numbness between your legs, or trouble controlling urine or stool.

use: Use as a handout for general heart-healthy lifestyle changes.
body:
Healthy choices can lower your risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease and memory loss.
They can also help your weight and your mood.
Pick 2 or 3 of these to start before your next visit:

- Eat a breakfast with protein, like eggs, yogurt or nuts
- Eat smaller portions at meals
- Cut back on sugary drinks, sweets, white bread and white rice
- Drink water instead of soda or juice
- Eat vegetables and fruits of different colors every day
- Cook with olive oil or canola oil instead of butter
- Eat fish 2 times a week
- Walk or move your body for 30 minutes, 5 days a week
- If you drink alcohol, drink less. Less is better.
- If you smoke or vape, ask us for help to quit
- Use sunscreen when you are outside

Call us if you have questions or want help making a plan.
Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of stroke like face drooping or weakness on one side.

#Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism _controlled / uncontrolled on _.
TSH _.

- CONT levothyroxine _ mcg PO daily
- Take on an empty stomach 30-60 min before breakfast, or at bedtime 3 hr or more after last meal
- Separate by 4 hr from calcium, iron, antacids, PPIs, sucralfate, bile acid binders, sevelamer
- Stay on one brand or one generic maker; recheck TSH after any switch
- Recheck TSH in 6-8 wk after dose change, annually when stable
- INCR. or DECR. levothyroxine by 12.5-25 mcg/day per TSH
- Goal TSH in reference range; 4-6 acceptable if age >70-80

- Persistent symptoms with normal TSH: look for other causes; no routine T3 combination or desiccated thyroid
- Dose need much higher than expected: check adherence, timing, celiac disease, H. pylori, atrophic gastritis
- Endocrinology referral if TSH or symptoms not improving after 2-3 dose adjustments

- START levothyroxine 1.6 mcg/kg PO daily, full replacement

If age 60 or older or heart disease:

- START levothyroxine 25-50 mcg PO daily; 12.5-25 mcg PO daily if known CAD

If pregnant or planning pregnancy:

- Preconception goal TSH between lower limit of normal and 2.5
- INCR. by 2 extra doses per week at positive pregnancy test, patient to call clinic
- TSH every 4 wk until midgestation, then near 30 wk
- After delivery: DECR. to prepregnancy dose, TSH at 6 wk

- START aluminum hydroxide 160 mg-magnesium carbonate 105 mg chewable 2-4 tabs PO after meals and at bedtime PRN, max 16 tabs/day, alternative antacid

- Taper or abrupt stop both OK; counsel transient rebound sxs, antacid or alginate PRN
- Do not deprescribe if LA grade C or D esophagitis, Barrett's, peptic stricture, esophageal ulcer, EoE, IPF, or high UGIB risk

- STOP PPI if off-therapy reflux testing is normal, unless another indication
- START baclofen 5-20 mg PO TID only with proven reflux, for regurgitation or belching; dizziness, somnolence, constipation
- No prokinetic unless gastroparesis is proven
- GI referral; high-resolution manometry before fundoplication, magnetic sphincter augmentation, or TIF
- Roux-en-Y gastric bypass if obese; sleeve gastrectomy may worsen reflux

If functional heartburn or reflux hypersensitivity:

- Neuromodulator _, or referral for CBT, hypnotherapy, diaphragmatic breathing, relaxation training

If extraesophageal sxs:

- ENT and pulmonary evaluation for non-GERD causes _
- Reflux testing before PPI if no heartburn or regurgitation
- PPI BID trial x 8-12 wk if typical sxs too; objective testing if no response

If long-term PPI:

- Consider Mg at start and periodically, B12 if deficiency symptoms _

body:
#Acute otitis media
Likely AOM given _bulging TM w/ ear pain and fever / bulging TM w/ ear tugging, fussiness after URI / mild bulging TM w/ intense erythema, ear pain <48 hr.
_ side, _mild / moderate / severe, age _.

DDx:
>AOM; most likely given bulging TM _, _
>Otitis media with effusion; considered but unlikely given _, will _
>Otitis externa; considered but unlikely given _, will _

- Dx: moderate-severe TM bulging, new otorrhea not from AOE, or mild bulging plus otalgia <48 hr or intense TM erythema
- No AOM dx without middle ear effusion on pneumatic otoscopy or tympanometry
- Severe: moderate-severe otalgia, otalgia 48 hr or more, or temp 39 C or higher
- Abx at dx if severe, otorrhea, or bilateral AOM at 6-23 mo
- Duration: 10 days if <2 yr, severe symptoms, or otorrhea; nonsevere 7 days age 2 to 5, 5 to 7 days age 6 and older
- START acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO q6h PRN, max 75 mg/kg/day
- START ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO every 6 to 8 hr PRN if 6 mo or older, max 40 mg/kg/day
- Recheck if no improvement in 48 to 72 hr

If nonsevere:

- Observation x 48 to 72 hr with safety-net prescription. Applies to unilateral AOM at age 6 to 23 mo, or any AOM at age 2 yr or older _
- Ensure f/u, START abx if worse or no better in 48 to 72 hr

If no amoxicillin in past 30 days and no conjunctivitis:

- START amoxicillin 80 to 90 mg/kg/day PO divided BID, max 2 g/dose and 4 g/day _

If amoxicillin in past 30 days or conjunctivitis:

- START amoxicillin-clavulanate 90 mg/kg/day of amoxicillin with 6.4 mg/kg/day of clavulanate PO divided BID, max 2 g amoxicillin/dose _
- Use ES suspension or ER tablet. Also for recurrent AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin

If non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy:

- START cefdinir 14 mg/kg/day PO divided daily or BID, max 600 mg/day _
- START cefpodoxime 10 mg/kg/day PO divided BID, max 200 mg/dose, as an alternative
- START cefuroxime 30 mg/kg/day PO divided BID, max 500 mg/dose, as an alternative
- START ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM or IV x 1 dose, max 1 g (label) or 2 g (AAP), if unable to take PO

If anaphylactic penicillin allergy:

- START clindamycin 30 to 40 mg/kg/day PO divided TID, max 600 mg/dose
- START levofloxacin 10 mg/kg/dose PO BID, max 375 mg/dose, if 6 mo to <5 yr, as an alternative
- START levofloxacin 10 mg/kg/dose PO daily, max 750 mg/dose, if 5 yr or older, as an alternative

If no improvement after 48 to 72 hr of abx:

- Recheck TM, change abx if TM still bulging
- START amoxicillin-clavulanate as above if amoxicillin failed
- START ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM or IV daily x 3 days, max 1 g/dose (label) or 2 g/dose (AAP), if amoxicillin-clavulanate or oral cephalosporin failed
- ENT consult if amoxicillin-clavulanate or oral cephalosporin fails

If recurrent AOM:

- Recurrent: 3 or more episodes in 6 mo, or 4 in 12 mo with 1 in the past 6 mo
- ENT referral for tubes if middle ear effusion present at assessment
- No tubes if no effusion in either ear
- No abx ppx for recurrent AOM

If adult:

- START abx at dx, no data support observation in adults
- START amoxicillin 875 mg PO BID or 500 mg PO TID x _ days
- ENT referral if >2 episodes per yr, or effusion persists >6 wk

#Chronic constipation
_ on current regimen, _.

- Fiber 25 g/day women, 38 g/day men; increase slowly over several wk
- Diet: 2 green kiwifruit/day or prunes 100 g/day (about 10) x 4 wk; rye bread in place of white bread
- Mg sulfate-rich mineral water 0.5-1.5 L/day x 2-6 wk; avoid if sodium or magnesium restricted

- START magnesium oxide 500 mg-1.5 g PO daily as alternative osmotic; avoid in renal insufficiency

- START warm tap water enema PR or mineral oil enema 120 mL PR daily PRN, max 1 per 24 hr _
- HOLD fiber supplements until impaction cleared
- Avoid sodium phosphate enemas if >55 yr, CKD, HF, dehydrated, or on diuretic, ACEi, ARB, NSAID

- START polyethylene glycol 105 g PO in 1 L water over 6 hr daily, max 3 days; max 26 g/hr if heart disease
- START maintenance polyethylene glycol 17 g PO daily after cleanout

use: Use for the A&P of established hyperthyroidism on or starting treatment.
body:
#Hyperthyroidism
_Graves disease / toxic nodule / toxic multinodular goiter / subclinical, _ on current regimen.
TSH _, free T4 _, total T3 _. CBC _, LFTs _, HR _, eye findings _.

- START propranolol 10-40 mg PO q8h for symptoms _
- DECR. beta blocker and STOP once thyroid levels normalize
- CBC with differential and hepatic panel before starting methimazole
- Reconsider antithyroid drugs if baseline ANC <1000 or transaminases >5x upper limit of normal
- START methimazole PO daily: 5-10 mg if free T4 1-1.5x ULN, 10-20 mg if 1.5-2x, 30-40 mg if 2-3x _
- Agranulocytosis about 0.3%, dose dependent, 95% within first 100 days
- PTU only for first trimester, thyroid storm, or minor methimazole reaction declining RAI or surgery; severe liver injury risk
- Counseled to stop methimazole and call for fever, sore throat, rash, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, or abdominal pain
- CBC with differential if fever or sore throat; routine CBC monitoring not needed
- Free T4 and total T3 at 2-6 wk after start; TSH can stay suppressed for months
- DECR. methimazole by 30-50% once euthyroid, labs in 4-6 wk, then every 2-3 mo on stable dose
- CONT methimazole 12-18 mo for Graves disease, then stop if TSH and TRAb normal _
- Remission about 20-30% in the US; lower in men, smokers, and large goiter
- Not in remission: RAI or thyroidectomy, or long-term low-dose methimazole by preference _
- Endocrinology referral for radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy: toxic nodule, multinodular goiter, relapse, drug intolerance, or preference _
- Thyroidectomy favored for compressive symptoms, large goiter, cancer concern, or moderate to severe eye disease
- No RAI if active moderate to severe or sight-threatening eye disease
- Smoking cessation and avoid secondhand smoke: lowers eye disease risk _
- Restore euthyroidism promptly if eye disease or eye disease risk factors
- F/u in _ wk

If asthma or COPD, or for once-daily dosing:

- START atenolol 25-100 mg PO daily _

If pregnant:

- Euthyroid on methimazole 5-10 mg/day or less: consider stopping, TSH and free T4 every 1-2 wk
- Needs drug in first trimester: STOP methimazole, START PTU 50-150 mg PO TID; methimazole 5 mg = PTU 100 mg BID _
- After 16 wk: CONT PTU or switch to methimazole; neither clearly preferred _
- TRAb at confirmation of pregnancy; repeat at 18-22 wk if elevated

If subclinical:

- Repeat TSH, free T4, free T3 in 2-4 mo to confirm subclinical disease _
- Subclinical, TSH persistently <0.1: treat if age 65 or older, heart disease, osteoporosis, postmenopausal off estrogen or bisphosphonate, or symptoms _
- Subclinical, TSH 0.1-0.4: consider treatment if age 65 or older or the same risks; otherwise observe _

If mild Graves eye disease of short duration:

- START selenium 100 mcg PO BID x 6 mo

If RAI planned:

- Pregnancy test within 48 hr before RAI
- Avoid pregnancy for 6 mo after RAI
- Free T4, total T3, TSH at 1-2 mo, then every 4-6 wk x 6 mo or until stable on levothyroxine

#Bipolar disorder
Bipolar _I / II, currently _euthymic / depressed / hypomanic / manic / mixed on current regimen, _.
PHQ-9 _, item 9 _. Safety screen _, firearms access _. Sleep _, substance use _, pregnancy potential _.

- CONT _ as maintenance mood stabilizer
- Avoid antidepressant monotherapy; STOP antidepressant if manic or mixed symptoms emerge

- Safety plan reviewed, 988 and COPES 918-744-4800 given

If lithium:

- START lithium carbonate 300 mg PO TID, INCR. by 300 mg every 3 days to target level _

desc: Fever in an infant 8 to 60 days
use: Use for a well-appearing term infant 8 to 60 days old with temperature 38.0 C or higher, not for infants under 8 days.
body:
#Fever in a well-appearing infant, _ days old
Likely _viral illness given + viral panel, normal UA and markers / UTI given + UA, no other source on exam / bacteremia given abnormal procalcitonin or ANC, no focus.
Tmax _ C rectal, GA _ wk, well appearing. UA _, procalcitonin _, ANC _, CRP _, CSF _.

DDx:
>_; most likely given _, _
>UTI; considered but unlikely given _, urine cx _
>Bacteremia or bacterial meningitis; considered but unlikely given _, blood and CSF cx _
>HSV infection; considered but unlikely given _, HSV studies _

Applies to:

- Well-appearing, 37 to <42 wk gestation, 8-60 days old, rectal temp 38.0 C or higher at home in past 24 hr or in clinic
- Excluded: preterm, under 2 wk with perinatal maternal fever or abx, focal bacterial infection, clinical bronchiolitis, immune compromise
- Excluded: vaccines within 48 hr, congenital or chromosomal anomalies, technology dependence, complicated neonatal course
- Ill appearing: full sepsis evaluation and abx per local protocol _ local

Definitions:

- Positive UA: any leukocyte esterase, >5 WBC/hpf centrifuged, or >10 WBC/mm3 uncentrifuged
- Abnormal inflammatory marker: procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL, CRP >20 mg/L, ANC >4,000 with procalcitonin or >5,200 without
- Without procalcitonin: obtain ANC and CRP, temp >38.5 C also counts as abnormal

All ages:

- HSV risk: maternal genital HSV lesions, vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucosal ulcers, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, high ALT
- HSV risk at 8-21 days also: maternal fever from 48 hr before to 48 hr after delivery
- HSV risk also: CSF pleocytosis with negative Gram stain
- HSV workup: CSF and blood HSV PCR, surface swabs of mouth, nasopharynx, conjunctivae and anus, ALT
- START acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h if HSV risk
- Avoid ceftriaxone in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia or on calcium-containing IV fluids, use ceftazidime instead
- Enterovirus PCR on CSF if pleocytosis or during enterovirus season
- STOP abx and d/c when cx negative at 24-36 hr, infant well or improving, HSV PCR negative if sent
- Positive cx: START targeted abx for organism, site, and response
- Return now for ill appearance, poor feeding, color change, breathing trouble, or fewer wet diapers

If age 8-21 days:

- UA by cath or SPA, urine cx if UA positive, blood cx, LP for CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, cx
- Inflammatory markers optional
- START abx and admit to a unit experienced with neonates
- UTI or no focus: START ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV q8h plus ceftazidime 50 mg/kg IV q8h
- Alternative: START ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV q8h plus gentamicin 4 mg/kg IV q24h
- Meningitis: START ampicillin 75 mg/kg IV q6h plus ceftazidime 50 mg/kg IV q8h

If age 22-28 days:

- UA by cath or SPA, or bag or voided UA with cath urine cx if positive. Blood cx and inflammatory markers.
- LP if any inflammatory marker abnormal. LP optional if all normal.
- Admit and START abx if UA positive or CSF abnormal
- Admit if CSF not obtained or uninterpretable
- Home only if UA, markers and CSF normal, family reliable, and recheck in 24 hr. Give parenteral abx first.
- UTI or no focus: START ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV or IM q24h
- Meningitis: START ampicillin 75 mg/kg IV q6h plus ceftazidime 50 mg/kg IV q8h

If age 29-60 days:

- Bag or voided UA, cath urine cx if positive. Blood cx and inflammatory markers.
- All markers normal: no LP needed
- Markers and UA normal: no abx, observe at home, reassess in 24 hr
- UA positive, markers normal: no LP, START oral abx, home, recheck in 12-24 hr
- START cephalexin 50-100 mg/kg/day PO divided QID, or cefixime 8 mg/kg PO daily
- Any marker abnormal: LP optional, hospital or home observation _
- Abnormal markers with normal CSF: parenteral or oral abx. CSF not obtained or uninterpretable: parenteral abx.
- Abnormal markers, no meningitis: START ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV or IM q24h
- CSF abnormal: admit. START ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV once daily or divided q12h, plus vancomycin 20 mg/kg IV q8h.
