>Lymphedema; most likely given _, _
>DVT; considered but unlikely given _, duplex ultrasound
>Cancer recurrence or lymphatic obstruction; considered but unlikely given _, imaging _
>Venous insufficiency, heart, kidney, or liver edema; considered but unlikely given _, _

- Stage 0 subclinical; I pitting, subsides with elevation; II elevation rarely helps, fibrosis later; III elephantiasis, skin changes
- Measure both limbs at set points; 2 cm or more difference is significant; serial measures over time
- Complete decongestive therapy referral: lymphatic drainage, multilayer bandaging, exercise, skin care _ local
- Maintenance compression garment: highest class tolerated, about 20 to 60 mmHg; daytime, off at night
- Elastic garment for stage I; flat-knit garment for stages II and III
- Pneumatic compression pump only with garments, not instead of them
- Exercise: 150 min/wk moderate aerobic plus progressive resistance; supervised resistance training is safe
- Weight loss if overweight; obesity speeds progression
- Skin: daily wash and moisturizer, treat tinea and fissures, nail care, no barefoot walking
- Blood draws, IVs, and shots in the unaffected limb when possible
- No long-term diuretics; marginal benefit and electrolyte risk
- Cellulitis: treat promptly with abx _; red, hot, painful limb or fever needs same-day care
- Surgery referral (lymphovenous bypass, node transfer, liposuction) only after conservative care fails
- F/u in _ mo with repeat measurements

If 2 or more leg cellulitis episodes despite skin care:

- START penicillin VK 250 mg PO BID x 12 mo; protection fades after stopping

body:
#Radiculopathy
Likely _L5 radiculopathy given weak great toe extension / S1 radiculopathy given weak plantar flexion, absent ankle reflex / cervical radiculopathy given positive Spurling.
SLR _, crossed SLR _, Spurling _, strength _, reflexes _, sensation _. Saddle anesthesia _, bladder or bowel change _, gait _.

>Cauda equina syndrome; considered but unlikely given no saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, or fecal incontinence; emergent MRI if present
>Infection, malignancy, or fracture; considered but unlikely given no fever, IVDU, cancer hx, weight loss, or trauma _
>Cervical myelopathy; considered but unlikely given no hand clumsiness, gait change, hyperreflexia, or clonus _

- Red flags absent _
- Lumbar: about 90% start to improve within 6 wk and resolve by 12 wk
- Stay active, limit bed rest
- START naproxen 500 mg PO BID with food x _ days; benefit for sciatica is small and short-term
- No gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines, or opioids for chronic sciatica
- PT: supervised exercise with strengthening, stretching, and directional preference exercises _
- No imaging in the first 6 wk without red flags

- Epidural steroid injection referral if acute severe sciatica; modest short-term relief only
- Spine surgery referral after 6 wk if persistent motor deficit, or severe sciatica with positive SLR and matching MRI
- Surgery gives faster relief; results similar to conservative care at 2 yr
- Emergent MRI and spine surgery for cauda equina, epidural abscess, or severe progressive weakness
- Return now for new weakness, saddle numbness, urinary retention, or fecal incontinence

- Prednisone gives modest function gain, no pain relief, more side effects; not recommended (NICE)

- MRI cervical spine if no improvement after 4 to 6 wk, or progressive deficit
- Epidural steroid or spine surgery referral if no improvement after 4 to 8 wk with matching imaging
- Urgent MRI and neurosurgery if myelopathy: hand clumsiness, urinary urgency, ataxia, hyperreflexia, or clonus

body:
#Systemic glucocorticoid therapy
On prednisone _ mg PO daily x _ wk for _, _tapering / completed course / long-term therapy.
BP _, weight _, glucose _, A1c _, K _. Other steroid routes (inhaled, injected, topical) _.

- Counseled on expected effects: insomnia, mood change, increased appetite, weight gain, higher glucose and BP
- BP and weight each visit
- A1c and K at baseline if long-term
- Physiologic dose is prednisone 4-6 mg/day or hydrocortisone 15-25 mg/day
- Adrenal crisis signs (vomiting, severe weakness, hypotension, confusion): hydrocortisone 100 mg IM now, then ED
- Before planned long-term therapy: live vaccines 4 wk or more before start, non-live vaccines 2 wk or more before
- AM prednisone raises glucose afternoon to evening; fasting glucose underestimates it
- f/u _ wk

If course <3-4 wk:

- STOP prednisone at end of course; no taper or cortisol testing needed, at any dose

If >3-4 wk above physiologic dose:

- Assume HPA-axis suppression; risk higher if >3 mo, dexamethasone or betamethasone, combined routes, obesity, or older age
- Taper only once the underlying disease is controlled
- Switch dexamethasone or betamethasone to prednisone or hydrocortisone once a long-acting steroid is no longer needed
- DECR. prednisone >40 mg/day by 5-10 mg every wk
- DECR. prednisone 20-40 mg/day by 5 mg every wk
- DECR. prednisone 10-20 mg/day by 2.5 mg every 1-4 wk
- DECR. prednisone 5-10 mg/day by 1 mg every 1-4 wk
- At 5 mg/day or less: DECR. by 1 mg every 4 wk while watching for adrenal insufficiency sxs, or check AM cortisol
- No cortisol testing while on supraphysiologic doses
- Withdrawal sxs (malaise, fatigue, nausea, myalgia, poor sleep, mood change), often below 15 mg/day: INCR. to last tolerated dose, then slow the taper
- AM cortisol 8-9 AM, 24 hr or more after last dose: >10 mcg/dL, STOP prednisone
- AM cortisol 5-10 mcg/dL: CONT physiologic dose, repeat in weeks to months
- AM cortisol <5 mcg/dL: CONT physiologic dose, repeat in a few months
- No fludrocortisone for steroid-induced adrenal insufficiency
- Stress dosing until recovery is shown; steroid emergency card
- Minor illness (fever, abx, bed rest): INCR. to prednisone 10 mg/day in 1-2 doses x 2-5 days until well
- No increase for minor illness if already on prednisone 10 mg/day or more
- Vomiting, unable to take PO, or severe illness: hydrocortisone 100 mg IM now, then ED
- Surgery with anesthesia: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg/24 hr infusion or 50 mg IV q6h
- Endocrinology referral if no HPA recovery after 1 yr at physiologic dose, or any adrenal crisis

If no known diabetes:

- A1c before starting if high risk for steroid hyperglycemia
- Fingerstick glucose daily, before or 1-2 hr after lunch or evening meal
- Glucose >216 (12 mmol/L): check QID, before meals and at bedtime
- If >216 twice in 24 hr: START NPH insulin 10 units SQ each AM with prednisone
- INCR. NPH by 10-20% daily to goal _
- DECR. insulin as prednisone tapers, about 20-25% per 5 mg step from 20 mg
- Hyperglycemia persists after steroids stop: A1c or fasting glucose to test for diabetes

If known diabetes:

- Fingerstick glucose QID, before meals and at bedtime
- If on bedtime basal insulin: move dose to AM, INCR. by 10-20% daily by pre-supper glucose
- If on basal-bolus insulin: INCR. prandial insulin by 10-20% daily to goal _
- If not on insulin: START NPH insulin 10 units SQ each AM, INCR. by 10-20% daily
- Dexamethasone or multiple daily doses: basal insulin often needed for fasting glucose
- DECR. insulin in step with each steroid dose reduction

If prednisone 2.5 mg/day or more for >3 mo:

- Calcium 1,000-1,200 mg/day, food first: plain low-fat yogurt 8 oz 450 mg, milk 1 cup 300 mg, canned sardines 3 oz 330 mg
- START vitamin D3 600-800 IU PO daily or more, goal 25-OH vitamin D 30 ng/mL or higher
- Progressive resistance, weight-bearing, and balance exercise; stop smoking; alcohol 2 drinks/day or fewer
- Fracture history, BMD with VFA or spine x-ray within 6 mo of starting
- FRAX if age 40 or more; if prednisone >7.5 mg/day, multiply major fracture risk by 1.15 and hip by 1.2
- Moderate risk: adjusted FRAX major 10-19% or hip >1% to <3%, or T-score -1 to -2.4
- High risk: T-score -2.5 to -3.4, or adjusted FRAX major 20-29% or hip 3% to <4.5%
- Very high risk: prior fragility fracture, T-score -3.5 or lower, or adjusted FRAX major 30% or more or hip 4.5% or more
- Also very high risk: prednisone 30 mg/day or more for >30 days, or 5 g/yr or more cumulative
- Repeat BMD with VFA every 1-2 yr
- Calcium, 25-OH vitamin D, creatinine before starting a bisphosphonate

If age 40 or more and moderate, high, or very high fracture risk:

- START alendronate 5 mg PO daily, 10 mg if postmenopausal and not on estrogen
- Take on waking with 6-8 oz plain water, 30 min before food, drink, or other meds; stay upright 30 min
- If oral bisphosphonate not tolerated: START zoledronic acid 5 mg IV once yearly; avoid if CrCl <35
- If very high risk: refer for teriparatide or abaloparatide, preferred over antiresorptives
- Steroids stopped, no new fracture, T-score above -2.5: STOP bisphosphonate, CONT calcium and vitamin D

If long-term therapy:

- Eye exam for cataract and glaucoma at baseline, then every 6-12 mo
- Early IOP check if personal or family hx of glaucoma, diabetes, high myopia, or connective tissue disease
- K every 6-12 mo

If prednisone 20 mg/day or more x 4 wk or more:

- PJP ppx if also on another immunosuppressant, or has an immunosuppressive condition or connective tissue disease
- START TMP-SMX 400/80 mg (1 SS tab) PO daily, or 800/160 mg (1 DS tab) PO 3x/wk
- CBC, CMP periodically on TMP-SMX

If prednisone 20 mg/day or more x 14 days or more:

- No live vaccines until 1 mo or more after stopping
- Non-live vaccines may give a weaker response

If sulfa allergy and PJP ppx needed:

- START dapsone _ or atovaquone _ PO

If also taking an NSAID:

- START esomeprazole 20 mg PO daily while on both, up to 6 mo

body:
#Elevated ferritin
Likely _MASLD given obesity or metabolic syndrome, normal TSAT / alcohol or inflammation given heavy drinking or high CRP / hemochromatosis given high TSAT, C282Y homozygous.

- Iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation with ferritin; fasting not required
- CBC, CMP, GGT, CRP, ESR, A1c, lipids
- Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody _
- Ferritin <1000 with normal TSAT and otherwise well: lifestyle changes, repeat in 2 to 3 mo

- High TSAT: CBC, retic count, MCV to exclude iron-loading anemia _
- H63D or S65C alone without C282Y: not at increased risk of iron overload
- Suspected overload without C282Y homozygosity: MRI liver iron quantification, or biopsy if fibrosis staging needed

- Phlebotomy: ferritin monthly, then maintain near 50 ng/mL; avoid vitamin C supplements
- C282Y homozygote with ferritin >1000, high ALT, or low platelets: hepatology for fibrosis staging
- Screen first-degree relatives if hemochromatosis confirmed

body:
#Constipation
Likely _functional constipation given hard stools, straining / medication-induced given opioid or anticholinergic / dyssynergic defecation given digitation, paradoxical contraction.
Duration _, onset _. BMs _ per wk, Bristol type _. Straining _, digitation _. Alarm features _. CRC screening _. DRE _.

DDx:
>_; most likely given _, _
>Colorectal cancer; considered but unlikely given no alarm features _, colonoscopy if alarm features or due for screening
>Hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, or diabetes; considered but unlikely given _, TSH, calcium, glucose if features suggest
>Dyssynergic defecation; considered but unlikely given DRE _, anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion if laxatives fail

- Rome IV, 2 or more in >1/4 of BMs: straining, hard stools, incomplete evacuation, blockage, manual maneuvers; or <3 BMs/wk
- Criteria met x 3 mo, onset 6 mo or more before; loose stools rare without laxatives; IBS criteria not met
- Bristol type 1-2 hard, 3-4 normal, 6-7 loose
- Alarm features: blood in stool, anemia, weight loss 10 lb or more, abdominal or rectal mass
- Alarm features: new onset age 50 or older, family history of CRC
- Med review: opioids, anticholinergics, TCAs, antipsychotics, CCBs, diuretics, clonidine, iron, calcium, aluminum, bismuth, 5-HT3 antagonists, NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, antiparkinson drugs
- STOP or DECR. constipating meds if feasible before further testing _
- CBC
- TSH, calcium, glucose only if clinical features suggest a cause _
- No colonoscopy without alarm features unless due for CRC screening, age 45 or older
- DRE: resting tone, squeeze, push effort, perineal descent _
- Dyssynergia on DRE: high resting tone, paradoxical contraction or poor relaxation on push, reduced perineal descent
- A normal DRE does not exclude a defecatory disorder

If alarm features or due for screening:

- Colonoscopy _

If no response to fiber and osmotic laxatives:

- Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion test _
- Defecography if manometry and balloon expulsion are inconclusive _
- Colonic transit study if manometry and balloon expulsion are normal _

If dyssynergia confirmed:

- Pelvic floor PT with biofeedback _

If refractory to medical therapy:

- GI referral with test results _
- Colorectal surgery referral for rectocele or refractory slow transit, after transit testing _

use: Use for the workup of constipation in infants and children.
body:
#Pediatric constipation
Likely functional constipation given _withholding, hard painful stools / soiling, large rectal fecal mass / large stools clogging the toilet.
Age _, onset age _. BMs _ per wk, Bristol type _. Meconium by 48 hr _. Growth _. Abdomen _, spine _, anus _, neuro _.

DDx:
>Functional constipation; most likely given _, no red flags
>Hirschsprung disease; considered but unlikely given meconium within 48 hr, normal growth _, rectal suction biopsy if suspected
>Hypothyroidism or celiac disease; considered but unlikely given normal growth _, TSH or tTG IgA if features
>Spinal cord abnormality; considered but unlikely given normal spine and neuro exam _, MRI spine if abnormal

- Under 4 yr, 1 mo of 2 or more: 2 or fewer BMs/wk; excessive retention; painful or hard BMs; large stools; large rectal mass
- Under 4 yr and toilet trained, may add: 1 or more accidents/wk; stools that clog the toilet
- 4 yr or older, 2 or more weekly x 1 mo: 2 or fewer toilet BMs/wk; 1 or more accidents/wk; retentive posturing
- Also counts at 4 yr or older: painful or hard BMs; large rectal mass; stools that clog the toilet
- Red flags: meconium >48 hr, onset <1 mo, family history of Hirschsprung, failure to thrive, distension, bilious vomiting, fever, ill appearance
- Red flags: explosive stools, gush of stool on DRE, occult blood, narrow ribbon stools, tight empty rectum, abnormal anal position
- Red flags: sacral dimple or hair tuft, midline pigmentation, absent anal wink or cremasteric reflex, low leg tone or reflexes
- Diagnosis by history and exam when no red flags
- No routine labs to screen for hypothyroidism, celiac disease, or hypercalcemia without red flags
- No routine abdominal x-ray; KUB only if impaction suspected and rectal exam refused or unreliable _
- DRE if red flags, uncertain diagnosis, or intractable constipation _
- No barium enema as an initial test, no routine colonic transit study or allergy testing
- Peds GI referral if red flags, or no response to max doses of 2 laxative classes x 3 mo _
- Psychology referral if normal stooling not restored within 3 mo of treatment _

If poor growth or thyroid findings:

- TSH, free T4 _

If celiac features or poor growth:

- Tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA _

If features suggest a metabolic cause:

- Calcium, potassium; glucose _

If pica or lead exposure:

- Blood lead level _

If failure to thrive, respiratory symptoms, or family history of CF:

- Sweat chloride test _

If abnormal spine or lower extremity neuro exam:

- MRI lumbosacral spine _

If Hirschsprung suspected:

- Peds GI and surgery referral for rectal suction biopsy if <12 mo, full-thickness biopsy if older _

If intractable and cow milk protein allergy suspected:

- Cow milk protein-free diet trial x 2-4 wk _

#Reflux symptoms
Likely _GERD given heartburn, regurgitation, no alarm features / extraesophageal reflux given cough, hoarseness, heartburn / functional heartburn given normal EGD, normal pH study.
Heartburn _ x/wk x _ yr, regurgitation _, extraesophageal sxs _. Alarm features _. PPI trial _, response _. BMI _.

DDx:
>GERD; most likely given _, _
>Functional heartburn or reflux hypersensitivity; considered but unlikely given _, wireless pH monitoring off PPI
>Rumination or supragastric belching; considered but unlikely given _, pH-impedance off PPI or manometry
>Cardiac chest pain; considered but unlikely given _, cardiac evaluation before GI testing

- START empiric PPI once daily 30-60 min before breakfast x 8 wk if typical heartburn or regurgitation and no alarm features
- INCR. PPI to BID, or switch PPI once, if partial response
- STOP PPI or step down to on-demand use if sxs resolve
- EGD first if dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, vomiting, or anemia
- EGD first if multiple Barrett's risk factors _
- Barium swallow and manometry are not diagnostic tests for GERD

If no response to 8 wk PPI or sxs recur off PPI:

- EGD with biopsies after HOLD PPI 2-4 wk
- 96-hr wireless pH monitoring off PPI if EGD shows no LA grade B or worse esophagitis or long-segment Barrett's
- AET >6% on 2 or more days: GERD; AET <4% on all days: not GERD, STOP PPI unless another indication
- pH-impedance off PPI instead if prominent belching, suspected rumination, or pulmonary sxs

If proven GERD with sxs despite BID PPI:

- pH-impedance monitoring on BID PPI
- High-resolution manometry before antireflux surgery or endoscopic therapy, to exclude achalasia and absent contractility
- GI referral

If extraesophageal sxs: cough, hoarseness, throat clearing, asthma:

- Evaluate non-GERD causes: ENT laryngoscopy, pulmonology _
- No heartburn or regurgitation: reflux testing off PPI before any PPI trial
- With heartburn or regurgitation: PPI BID trial x 8-12 wk
- No response after 12 wk: objective reflux testing; do not cycle through other PPIs
- Laryngoscopy findings alone do not diagnose reflux

If chest pain:

- Cardiac evaluation first; then EGD and/or reflux monitoring if cardiac workup negative

If predominant epigastric pain or dyspepsia:

- Age 60 or older: EGD
- Age <60: H. pylori stool antigen or urea breath test, treat if positive

- Laryngoscopy findings alone do not diagnose reflux

- Cardiac evaluation first; then EGD and/or reflux monitoring if cardiac workup negative

If predominant epigastric pain or dyspepsia:

- Age 60 or older: EGD

use: Use for the workup of an abnormal or discordant TSH and free T4.
body:
#Abnormal thyroid function tests
Likely _subclinical hypothyroidism given high TSH, normal FT4 / subclinical hyperthyroidism given low TSH, normal FT4 / hypothyroidism given high TSH, low FT4.
TSH _, free T4 _, total T3 _. Meds _, biotin _, acute illness _, pregnancy _, pituitary disease _.

DDx:
>Primary thyroid disease; most likely given _, _
>Nonthyroidal illness; considered but unlikely given _, repeat after recovery
>Drug effect; considered but unlikely given _, _
>Assay interference; considered but unlikely given _, biotin or heterophile antibodies, repeat in another assay

- High TSH, low free T4: primary hypothyroidism
- High TSH, normal free T4: repeat TSH, free T4, and TPO Ab in 2-3 mo
- Low TSH, high free T4 or total T3: thyrotoxicosis; TRAb or radioiodine uptake for cause, scan if nodular
- Low TSH, normal free T4 and total T3: repeat in 2-4 mo; exclude glucocorticoids, dopamine, acute illness
- Low or normal TSH with low free T4: suspect central hypothyroidism; TSH may be mildly high but <10
- Normal or high TSH with high free T4 and T3: exclude assay interference first
- Then TSH-secreting adenoma vs thyroid hormone resistance: pituitary MRI, alpha subunit, family history, THRB testing
- Biotin: falsely low TSH and high free T4; stop biotin, repeat in 2 days or more
- Heparin: spuriously high free T4
- Estrogen and pregnancy raise TBG and total T4 without true hyperthyroidism
- Amiodarone: high T4 with normal TSH possible; hypo- or hyperthyroidism in some
- Lithium, checkpoint inhibitors, interferon, tyrosine kinase inhibitors: hypo- or hyperthyroidism
- T3 only for suspected thyrotoxicosis; never to diagnose hypothyroidism; total T3 preferred over free T3
- Hospitalized: test only with real suspicion of thyroid disease; low T3 alone suggests nonthyroidal illness
- TSH can rise transiently during recovery from illness; recheck after recovery
- Screening asymptomatic nonpregnant adults: insufficient evidence of benefit

If suspected central hypothyroidism:

- Repeat TSH and free T4 to confirm
- AM cortisol before levothyroxine; replace glucocorticoid first if adrenal insufficiency not excluded
- Pituitary MRI and other pituitary hormones _
- Treat to free T4 above median of normal range; TSH not useful
- Endocrinology referral

If discordant results persist after interference excluded:

- Endocrinology referral

body:

- Orthostatic BP lying and standing _

body:
#Short stature
Likely _familial short stature given short parents / constitutional delay given delayed bone age / pathologic cause given velocity <5 cm/yr.
Height _ cm (_ SD), velocity _ cm/yr, midparental height _ cm, bone age _, BMI _.

DDx:
>Familial or idiopathic short stature; most likely given _, normal velocity and bone age
>Constitutional delay of growth and puberty; considered but unlikely given bone age _, _
>Hypothyroidism, celiac disease, or GH deficiency; considered but unlikely given velocity _, labs _
>Turner syndrome; considered but unlikely given _, karyotype _

- Plot serial heights: WHO chart if <2 yr, CDC chart if 2 yr or older
- Normal velocity: 8 cm/yr at 2-3 yr, 7 cm/yr at 3-5 yr, 5-6 cm/yr from 5 yr to puberty
- Midparental height: (father + mother + 13 cm) / 2 for boys, (father + mother - 13 cm) / 2 for girls

- IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 with peds endocrinology if GH deficiency suspected

- Also refer: projected height >10 cm below midparental, SGA without catch-up by 2 yr, no cause found
- Also refer: no puberty by 13 yr in girls or 14 yr in boys
- Recheck height in _ mo

use: Use for the workup of puberty signs before age 8 in girls or age 9 in boys.
body:
#Precocious puberty
Likely _premature thelarche given isolated breast buds / premature adrenarche given pubic hair or odor only / central precocious puberty given progressive puberty.
Onset age _, Tanner breast _ pubic hair _, testes _ mL, growth velocity _, bone age _.

DDx:
>_; most likely given _, _
>Central precocious puberty; considered but unlikely given _, LH _, bone age _
>Peripheral precocious puberty (CAH, tumor, hypothyroidism, exogenous sex steroids); considered but unlikely given _, _
>Lipomastia; considered but unlikely given glandular tissue on supine exam _

- Evaluate puberty signs before 8 yr in girls or 9 yr in boys
- Tanner stage, testicular volume, height and growth velocity on chart
- Supine breast exam to separate glandular tissue from fatty tissue
- Left-hand bone age x-ray
- Early-morning LH, FSH, TSH, free T4; estradiol in girls, total testosterone in boys
- LH >0.3 mIU/mL suggests central precocious puberty
- LH low but high suspicion: GnRH stimulation test via peds endocrinology
- Bone age advanced >2 SD favors true precocious puberty over a benign variant, but predicts poorly alone

If pubic hair, acne, body odor, or virilization:

- Early-morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone and DHEA-S
- 17-OHP >200 ng/dL suggests CAH, ACTH stimulation test

If boy:

- hCG for hCG-secreting germ cell tumor

If estradiol >100 pg/mL or diagnosis unclear:

- Pelvic US for ovarian tumor and uterine or ovarian volume

If central precocious puberty:

- Brain MRI with contrast if girl <6 yr, any boy, or any neurologic signs
- Girls 6-8 yr, normal neuro exam: MRI optional, CNS tumor risk 1% or less
- GnRH agonist decision by peds endocrinology, mainly if bone age predicts short adult height

If benign variant (premature thelarche or adrenarche):

- Recheck growth and Tanner stage every 3-6 mo

- Refer to peds endocrinology: puberty signs <6 yr in girls or <9 yr in boys, or rapid progression
- Also refer: headaches, vision changes, seizures, NF1, prior CNS irradiation, or known neoplasm
- F/u in _ mo

use: Use for the workup of bleeding or suspected miscarriage before 13 weeks, from first visit to diagnosis.
body:
#First-trimester bleeding
Likely _threatened miscarriage given closed os, IUP w/ FHR / pregnancy loss given heavy bleeding, tissue passed / uncertain viability given sac, no FHR yet.
Gestational age _ by _. BP _, HR _. Os _. hCG _. TVUS _. Hgb _. Rh _.

DDx:
>_; most likely given _, _
>Early pregnancy loss; considered but unlikely given _, repeat TVUS if criteria not met
>Ectopic pregnancy; considered but unlikely given _, serial hCG and TVUS until location known
>Cervicitis, vaginitis, or cervical polyp; considered but unlikely given speculum exam _

- Vitals, abdominal exam; emergent eval if unstable or peritoneal signs
- Speculum exam: os, blood amount, tissue at os, cervical source
- TVUS: gestational sac, yolk sac, embryo, CRL, cardiac activity, adnexa, free fluid
- Quantitative hCG _
- CBC for baseline Hgb
- ABO and Rh if unknown
- Progesterone if TVUS inconclusive: <6 ng/mL excludes a viable pregnancy, does not exclude ectopic _
- Heavy bleeding precautions: soaking more than 2 pads an hour for 2 hr in a row
- Handout given

TVUS diagnostic of pregnancy loss:

- CRL 7 mm or more, no cardiac activity
- Mean sac diameter 25 mm or more, no embryo
- No embryo w/ cardiac activity 2 wk or more after a sac without yolk sac
- No embryo w/ cardiac activity 11 days or more after a sac w/ yolk sac

TVUS suspicious, not diagnostic:

- CRL <7 mm, no cardiac activity; mean sac diameter 16-24 mm, no embryo
- No embryo 6 wk or more after LMP; empty amnion; yolk sac >7 mm
- Mean sac diameter minus CRL <5 mm; embryonic heart rate 85 or less
- No embryo w/ cardiac activity 7-13 days after a sac without yolk sac, or 7-10 days after a sac w/ yolk sac
- Repeat TVUS in 7-10 days before diagnosing loss

If IUP w/ cardiac activity, closed os:

- Threatened miscarriage; expectant management, no bed rest
- Repeat TVUS if bleeding continues _

If products of conception seen at os or in vagina:

- Incomplete miscarriage; expectant management completes over 90% within 4 wk, or offer meds or aspiration

If no IUP and prior TVUS showed an IUP:

- Likely complete miscarriage if bleeding history fits passage of tissue
- Repeat hCG in 48 hr; a fall of 50% or more supports completion

If no IUP and none seen before:

- Pregnancy of unknown location; ectopic precautions, serial hCG q48h and TVUS until location known or hCG <5

If pregnancy loss confirmed:

- Discuss expectant, medical, and uterine aspiration options
- Rh negative and 12 wk or more: Rh immune globulin 300 mcg IM within 72 hr
- Rh negative and <12 wk: Rh immune globulin not routinely needed; consider by shared decision _

If heavy bleeding w/ falling Hgb, unstable vitals, or fever w/ uterine tenderness:

- Urgent uterine aspiration, OB/GYN now; IV abx if infection suspected

use: Use for the workup after 2 or more pregnancy losses.
body:
#Recurrent pregnancy loss
Likely recurrent pregnancy loss given _2 first-trimester losses / 3 or more losses / losses after a prior live birth.
Losses _ at _ wk, confirmed by _. Tissue testing done _. Age _. BMI _.

DDx:
>Unexplained recurrent loss; most likely given _, _
>Chromosome problem in pregnancy tissue or parental rearrangement; considered but unlikely given _, _
>Uterine anomaly, polyp, or fibroid; considered but unlikely given _, cavity imaging
>Antiphospholipid syndrome; considered but unlikely given _, antibody testing
>Thyroid disease or diabetes; considered but unlikely given _, TSH and A1c

- Counts: 2 or more losses, consecutive or not, including hCG-confirmed biochemical losses; ectopic and molar excluded
- Chromosome analysis of miscarriage tissue when available, array-based preferred
- Uterine cavity: saline sonohysterogram preferred, or HSG or hysteroscopy _
- Antiphospholipid antibodies: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG and IgM, beta-2 glycoprotein I IgG and IgM
- Repeat positive antiphospholipid tests in 12 wk; skip testing if all losses were aneuploid
- TSH
- A1c if overweight, family history of diabetes, age >40, PMOS, or prior gestational diabetes
- Prolactin only if galactorrhea or anovulation
- Not routine: inherited thrombophilia, thyroid antibodies, immune or NK cell tests, ovarian reserve
- Lifestyle: stop smoking; alcohol 3 drinks/wk or fewer; caffeine under 100 mg/day
- 50-80% have a live birth later w/o specific treatment
- Psychological support offered; supportive care and early visits in next pregnancy _
- REI or OB/GYN referral _

- Parental karyotypes, then genetic counseling

If antiphospholipid syndrome confirmed:

- START aspirin 81 mg PO daily before conception, add prophylactic heparin once pregnant; MFM referral _

If TSH above 4 or lab upper limit:

- START levothyroxine before conception _
- Do not treat thyroid antibodies alone or TSH under 4

If bleeding in a future pregnancy:

- Vaginal progesterone may be offered by shared decision _

body:
#Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia

body:
#Female sexual dysfunction, _HSDD / interest and arousal disorder / orgasmic disorder / pain or GSM
Likely _HSDD given low desire, distress, acquired, generalized / SSRI effect given onset after SSRI, low desire, low arousal / GSM given postmenopausal, dryness, pain with sex.
Duration _, _lifelong / acquired, _generalized / situational, distress _. DSDS _, FSFI _, PHQ-9 _.
Contributing factors _.

>Medication effect; considered but unlikely given _, med review
>Depression or anxiety; considered but unlikely given PHQ-9 _, _
>GSM or genito-pelvic pain; considered but unlikely given exam _, _

- Reviewed contributing factors: SSRIs and other meds, hormonal meds, menopause, depression, relationship, pain, fatigue, postpartum or breastfeeding _
- Sex therapy, CBT or mindfulness-based therapy referral _
- Sensate focus: scheduled non-genital touch, no intercourse at first, then add genital touch
- Communicate with partner during sexual activity, vary positions, plan time for intimacy
- Use distraction techniques such as fantasy or background noise, and pelvic floor contraction and relaxation
- Non-coital touch such as sensual massage, with each partner giving feedback
- Water- or silicone-based lubricant with sex; oil-based products erode latex condoms
- Vaginal moisturizer 2-3x/wk if dryness _
- Pelvic floor PT referral if pain or high-tone pelvic floor _
- Education provided, f/u in _ wk

If GSM:

- Pelvic exam confirms GSM before hormone therapy _
- START estradiol 10 mcg vaginal insert daily x 2 wk, then twice weekly
- START estradiol 0.01% cream 0.5-1 g vaginally daily x 2 wk, then 0.5-1 g 1-3x/wk, as alternative
- START estradiol 2 mg vaginal ring, replace every 90 days, as alternative _
- No progestogen needed with low-dose vaginal estrogen
- START prasterone 6.5 mg vaginal insert nightly if estrogen not preferred _
- START ospemifene 60 mg PO daily with food as oral option; avoid if VTE, stroke or estrogen-dependent cancer

If SSRI-related:

- START bupropion SR 150 mg PO daily x 3 days, then 150 mg PO BID, added to SSRI
- STOP SSRI; START bupropion XL 150 mg PO daily if switching. Sexual dysfunction rate similar to placebo _
- Avoid bupropion if seizure disorder or eating disorder

If acquired generalized HSDD, age <65, no other cause:

- START flibanserin 100 mg PO nightly at bedtime
- Alcohol: wait 2 hr after 1-2 drinks, skip dose after 3 or more, none after dose until next day
- Contraindicated with moderate or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or hepatic impairment
- No driving for 6 hr after dose; STOP if no benefit at 8 wk

If premenopausal HSDD and on-demand option preferred:

- START bremelanotide 1.75 mg SQ to abdomen or thigh 45 min or more before sex PRN
- Max 1 dose/24 hr and 8 doses/mo; nausea common; avoid with oral naltrexone
- Contraindicated with uncontrolled HTN or CVD; STOP if no benefit at 8 wk

If postmenopausal HSDD after full assessment:

- Baseline total testosterone, SHBG, LFTs, fasting lipid panel
- START testosterone 1% gel 5 mg (1/10 male dose) topically daily, off-label _
- Total testosterone at 3-6 wk, keep in premenopausal range; then every 6 mo
- STOP if no benefit at 6 mo; monitor for acne, hirsutism, voice change
- Avoid pellets, injections and compounded testosterone

body:
Physical exam

[VITALS]

- General: well appearing, no acute distress
- Head: normocephalic, atraumatic
- Eyes: conjunctivae clear, pupils equal and reactive, EOM intact
- Ears: TMs clear bilaterally
- Nose: no congestion
- Throat: oropharynx clear, moist mucous membranes
- Neck: supple, no lymphadenopathy or thyromegaly
- CV: regular rate and rhythm, no murmur, rub, or gallop
- Pulses: radial and DP 2+ bilaterally
- Lungs: clear bilaterally, normal work of breathing
- Abdomen: soft, nontender, nondistended, normal bowel sounds, no organomegaly
- Extremities: no edema, no calf tenderness
- MSK: normal ROM, no joint swelling
- Skin: warm, dry, no rash or suspicious lesions
- Neuro: alert and oriented x3, CN II to XII grossly intact, strength 5/5 throughout, sensation intact, normal gait
- Psych: normal mood and affect, normal judgment

use: Use as a physician reference on low-dose, or micro, buprenorphine initiation. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Low-dose buprenorphine initiation (microdosing)

Small buprenorphine doses overlap with the patient's full agonist, so no withdrawal period is needed.

Why go carefully:

- Precipitated withdrawal is very distressing, and patients may avoid buprenorphine or OUD care afterward
- One bad start can turn a patient away from this medication
- If a patient reports a buprenorphine allergy, ask what happened
- Withdrawal: sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness soon after a dose
- Hypersensitivity: rash, hives, itching, angioedema, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis; this is a contraindication
- A prior precipitated withdrawal is a reason to use low-dose initiation, not to avoid buprenorphine

When to consider:

- Regular fentanyl use
- Prior precipitated withdrawal
- Cannot tolerate withdrawal, or pain that needs ongoing full agonist
- Switching from methadone or a high-dose full agonist

How to do it:

- Start 0.2 to 0.5 mg
- Increase gradually over 3 to 8 days to 8 to 16 mg or more
- Continue the full agonist until the target dose, then stop it
- Pause increases if withdrawal appears
- Warn patients that mild withdrawal symptoms are common during the switch
- Communicate clearly and check in often, by phone if needed
- No schedule is proven best. $bupmicro is a 7-day example; patient schedule $pibupmicro

Forms and strengths:

- Bup-nal SL film: 2/0.5, 4/1, 8/2, 12/3 mg
- Bup-nal SL tablet: 2/0.5, 8/2 mg
- Buprenorphine mono SL tablet: 2, 8 mg. Fine if bup-nal unavailable; naloxone is poorly absorbed SL
- Zubsolv bup-nal SL tablet: 0.7, 1.4, 2.9, 5.7, 8.6, 11.4 mg. 1.4 mg equals 2 mg standard SL; 5.7 mg equals 8 mg
- Buccal film (Belbuca): 75, 150, 300, 450, 600, 750, 900 mcg. FDA-approved for pain only
- Transdermal patch (Butrans): 5, 7.5, 10, 15, 20 mcg/hr. FDA-approved for pain only; strategies in .edbuppatch
- IV buprenorphine: hospital only
- XR injection: Sublocade 100 or 300 mg monthly; Brixadi 8 to 32 mg weekly or 64 to 128 mg monthly

Ways to give about 0.5 mg SL:

- One quarter of a 2 mg SL film
- Buccal film 300 mcg
- IV 0.15 mg
- Patch 20 mcg/hr, about 0.5 mg SL spread over 24 hr
- Swallowed 2 mg SL tablet; absorption varies, about 0.5 to 0.8 mg SL
- If quartering films is a pharmacy barrier, most patients tolerate 1 mg (half a 2 mg film) to start

Schedules, in SL film doses:

Rapid 3-day, hospital:

- Day 1: 0.5 mg SL q3h x 8 doses, or q4h x 6
- Day 2: 1 mg SL q3h x 8 doses, or q4h x 6
- Day 3: 8 mg SL TID, or XR injection

5-day:

- Days 1-2: 0.5 mg SL q6h x 8 doses
- Days 3-4: 1 mg SL q6h x 8 doses
- Day 5: 8 mg SL TID, or XR injection

8-day, outpatient or high-dose methadone:

- Day 1: 0.5 mg (1/4 of a 2 mg film) once
- Day 2: 0.5 mg BID
- Day 3: 1 mg (1/2 film) BID
- Day 4: 2 mg BID
- Day 5: 3 mg (1 1/2 films) BID
- Day 6: 4 mg (2 films) BID
- Day 7: 6 mg (3 films) BID
- Day 8: 8 mg SL TID, or XR injection
- Methadone: continue the full dose through day 7, then stop

IV start, 5-day hospital:

- Day 1: IV 0.15 mg q6h x 4 doses
- Day 2: IV 0.3 mg q6h x 4 doses
- Day 3: IV 0.6 mg q6h x 4 doses
- Day 4: Bup-nal 4/1 mg SL q6h x 4 doses
- Day 5: Bup-nal 8/2 mg SL BID
- After that: bup-nal 2/0.5 mg SL PRN cravings or withdrawal; add PRN doses to the next day's scheduled dose

Timing the doses:

- Doses can be held for sleep. Resume when awake
- q3h can stretch to q4h or q6h if staffing or the patient needs it
- Most patients tolerate 1 or 2 missed doses per step
- To go slower: pause buprenorphine 2 to 4 hr, add doses at each step, or lengthen the interval
- Worse pain or withdrawal: give more full agonist first
- Full agonist during titration: do not wean it (CA Bridge), or taper 25 percent/day from IV day 3 (ACLP)
- Severe or precipitated withdrawal: consider switching to high-dose buprenorphine

Evidence, mostly case series and observational:

- Adams 2025, 59 studies, 682 patients: 81 percent transitioned; any withdrawal in 41 percent of attempts, clinically significant in 7 percent
- Spreen 2022, 47 studies, 924 patients: rotation success 96 percent low-dose vs 95.6 percent traditional
- Ahmed 2021, 18 papers, 63 patients: start 0.2 to 0.5 mg, 4 to 8 days, end at 8 to 16 mg
- Grenier 2025, pregnancy, 25 patients: precipitated withdrawal in 8 percent

Original Bernese case, Hammig 2016:

- Day 1: 0.2 mg
- Day 2: 0.4 mg BID
- Then up 0.4 mg/day to 3.4 mg
- Then up 20 to 30 percent/day to 24 mg
- Full agonist stopped on day 29

Sources:

- Cohen SM et al. J Addict Med 2022;16(4):399-406. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34954746/
- Adams KK et al. Addict Sci Clin Pract 2025;20:19. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39980050/
- Ahmed S et al. Am J Addict 2021;30(4):305-315. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33378137/
- Spreen LA et al. Pharmacotherapy 2022;42(5):411-427. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35302671/
- Grenier 2025, pregnancy review. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40673576/
- Hammig R et al. Subst Abuse Rehabil 2016;7:99-105. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27499655/
- Spadaro A et al. Am J Emerg Med 2022;58:22-26. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35623179/
- Suboxone label, hypersensitivity: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=8a5edcf9-828c-4f97-b671-268ab13a8ecd
- CA Bridge, low-dose initiation with opioid continuation, January 2026: https://bridgetotreatment.org/resource/low-dose-buprenorphine-initiation-with-opioid-continuation/
- ACLP How-To Guide, buprenorphine microinduction, 2024: http://clpsychiatry.org/wp-content/uploads/ACLP-How-To-Guide-Buprenorphine-Microinduction-2024.pdf
- FDA labels via DailyMed: Suboxone, Zubsolv, Belbuca, Butrans, Sublocade, Brixadi, generic buprenorphine SL tablets

use: Use as a physician reference on precipitated withdrawal risk and management. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Fentanyl and precipitated withdrawal

Precipitated withdrawal is a rapid worsening of withdrawal right after buprenorphine. Buprenorphine displaces the full agonist but has lower intrinsic activity.

How often:

- 28 EDs, 1,200 patients, standard dosing of 8 mg if COWS 8 or more then 16 mg/day: precipitated withdrawal in 0.76 percent. All 9 cases were fentanyl positive.
- Hospitalized patients, 226 patients: 11.5 percent overall, 16.3 percent with confirmed fentanyl use. Higher risk with urine fentanyl 200 ng/mL or more, aOR 8.37, and BMI 30 or more, aOR 5.12.

Risk factors: chronic fentanyl use, methadone use, concurrent benzodiazepine use.

Prevention:

- Wait for moderate withdrawal, COWS 13 or more, and enough time since last full agonist use
- Or use a low-dose or high-dose strategy

Management:

- Additional buprenorphine has a pharmacologic basis and has worked in case reports
- Symptom-based adjuncts and support
- Most cases are benign, but patients may avoid buprenorphine afterward

Protocol phrase: $bupprecip.

Sources:

- D'Onofrio G et al. JAMA Netw Open 2023;6(3):e236108. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36995717/
- Thakrar AP et al. JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(9):e2435895. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39331392/
- Spadaro A et al. Am J Emerg Med 2022;58:22-26. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35623179/
- Weimer MB et al. ASAM Clinical Considerations, high-potency synthetic opioids. J Addict Med 2023;17(6):632-639. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37934520/

High-dose buprenorphine initiation

body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Buprenorphine dose limits

FDA, December 2024, recommended labeling changes for transmucosal buprenorphine for OUD:

- Neither 16 mg/day nor 24 mg/day should be read as a maximum dose
- Remove the phrase target dose
- Doses above 24 mg/day have not been studied in randomized trials but may be appropriate for some patients

These are recommendations to manufacturers. Some current labels may still carry older wording.

Source:

- FDA: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fda-recommends-changes-labeling-transmucosal-buprenorphine-products-indicated-treat-opioid-use

body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Buprenorphine prescribing requirements

- The X-waiver is gone. The MAT Act removed the Notice of Intent requirement, effective 29DEC2022.
- There are no patient caps.
- Prescribers need a standard DEA registration with schedule III authority and state authority.
- MATE Act: a one-time 8 hours of substance use disorder training, attested at DEA registration or renewal since 27JUN2023.
- Residents: follow local policy for controlled prescriptions and preceptor signature, see .howcontrolled.

Sources:

- SAMHSA, waiver elimination: https://www.samhsa.gov/substance-use/treatment/resources/mat-act
- DEA letter to registrants: https://www.deadiversion.usdoj.gov/pubs/docs/A-23-0020-Dear-Registrant-Letter-Signed.pdf

Buprenorphine around surgery

Multisociety expert panel, 5 societies, 100 percent consensus:

- Buprenorphine should not be routinely stopped before surgery
- Buprenorphine can be started in the perioperative period

Coordinate the pain plan with surgery and anesthesia before the procedure. Local contacts _.

Source:

- Kohan L et al. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2021;46(10):840-859. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34385292/

- Buprenorphine should not be routinely stopped before surgery
- Buprenorphine can be started in the perioperative period

Coordinate the pain plan with surgery and anesthesia before the procedure. Local contacts ***.

section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
use: Use as a physician reference on complex persistent opioid dependence in long-term opioid therapy. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Complex persistent opioid dependence, CPOD

Definition:

- A gray zone between simple physical dependence and opioid use disorder in patients on long-term opioid therapy.
- Recognized as a desire to continue or increase the dose, or inability to stop despite a prescriber's recommendation to stop.
- Symptoms: worsening pain, function, mood, and sleep; escalating opioid need while on therapy; protracted withdrawal with dose reduction.
- Clinically distinct from but biologically similar to OUD, and neither necessary nor sufficient for OUD.
- Suggested features: 100 MME/day or more and/or significant pain dysfunction, aberrancies or misuse, psychiatric burden, or a substance use history.

Why it matters:

- Tapering in 113,618 patients on 50 MME/day or more: overdose 9.3 vs 5.5 per 100 person-years, aIRR 1.68; mental health crisis 7.6 vs 3.3, aIRR 2.28. Each 10 percent faster monthly reduction raised both risks.
- VA cohort of 1.39 million: overdose or suicide death after stopping rose with treatment length, HR 6.77 after more than 400 days of treatment. Risk was highest right after stopping.

Options:

- Continue with risk reduction: naloxone, no benzodiazepines, PDMP, function goals.
- Slow taper with patient agreement: $opitaper, evidence in .edopitaper.
- Rotate to buprenorphine if unable to taper despite worsening pain or function, whether or not OUD criteria are met: $bupcpod. Review of 22 studies, 1,616 participants: very low-quality evidence that rotation maintained or improved analgesia with low risk of precipitated withdrawal; steady dosing better tolerated than tapered dosing.

Sources:

- Manhapra A et al. Subst Abus 2018;39(2):152-161. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28929914/
- Manhapra A et al. J Gen Intern Med 2020;35(Suppl 3):964-971. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33159241/
- Agnoli A et al. JAMA 2021;326(5):411-419. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34342618/
- Oliva EM et al. BMJ 2020;368:m283. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32131996/
- Powell VD et al. JAMA Netw Open 2021;4(9):e2124152. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34495339/
- HHS Guide for Clinicians on Dosage Reduction or Discontinuation of Long-Term Opioid Analgesics, 2019: https://www.hhs.gov/system/files/Dosage_Reduction_Discontinuation.pdf

section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
use: Use as a physician reference on opioid taper rates and safety. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Opioid tapering

Never abrupt:

- HHS: opioids should not be tapered rapidly or discontinued suddenly.
- CDC 2022: unless there is a life-threatening issue, do not stop abruptly or rapidly reduce from higher doses.
- FDA 2019: serious withdrawal, uncontrolled pain, psychological distress, and suicide reported after sudden discontinuation in dependent patients.

Rates:

- After 1 year or more of use: about 10 percent per month or slower, per HHS and CDC.
- After weeks to months of use: 10 percent of the original dose per week or slower. At 30 percent of the original dose, switch to 10 percent of the remaining dose per week.
- HHS: common tapers are 5 to 20 percent every 4 weeks.
- FDA: no more than 10 to 25 percent every 2 to 4 weeks.

Pauses:

- Tapers may be paused and restarted when the patient is ready, and may need to slow at low doses.
- Significant withdrawal may mean pausing or slowing.
- FDA: it may be necessary to return to the previous dose, then taper more gradually once stable.

If tapering fails or OUD emerges, consider buprenorphine: .edcpod.

Sources:

- HHS 2019 guide: https://www.hhs.gov/system/files/Dosage_Reduction_Discontinuation.pdf
- CDC 2022 guideline, Dowell D et al. MMWR Recomm Rep 2022;71(3):1-95. https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/rr/rr7103a1.htm
- FDA 2019 safety announcement: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-identifies-harm-reported-sudden-discontinuation-opioid-pain-medicines-and-requires-label-changes

section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
use: Use as a physician reference on long-term benzodiazepine use, dependence, and when to taper. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Long-term benzodiazepine use

Is there a benzodiazepine version of CPOD?

- No established term. The joint guideline uses physiologic dependence, distinct from sedative use disorder.
- BIND, benzodiazepine-induced neurological dysfunction, is a proposed term for symptoms during use, tapering, and after stopping. The evidence is a self-selected online survey of 1,207 people with no control group.

FDA 2020 boxed warning:

- Covers abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and withdrawal.
- Abrupt discontinuation or rapid reduction can cause life-threatening withdrawal.
- FDA 2016 warning: limit opioid plus benzodiazepine prescribing to patients without adequate alternatives.

Joint clinical practice guideline, 2025:

- Avoid abrupt discontinuation in patients likely to be physically dependent.
- Taper when risks outweigh benefits; reassess at least every 3 months.
- Generally taper in older adults unless there are compelling reasons to continue.
- Offer CBT or CBT-I alongside the taper.
- Rates and pauses: .edbzdtaper.

Older adults:

- Beers 2023: avoid benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults, with exceptions such as seizure disorders, REM sleep behavior disorder, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, and severe generalized anxiety.
- Deprescribing guideline: taper for adults 65 and older regardless of duration; suggested for ages 18 to 64 after more than 4 weeks of use.

Education-led tapering:

- EMPOWER, 303 adults aged 65 to 95: direct-to-patient education. At 6 months, 27 percent discontinued vs 5 percent with usual care, NNT 4.
- D-PRESCRIBE: pharmacist-led education, sedative-hypnotics stopped in 43 vs 9 percent; no hospitalizations among those tapering.

Phrases: $bzd, #bzd, $bzdtaper, $bzdlet, $pibzd, $pibzdtaper, .edbzdtalk.

use: Use as a physician reference on benzodiazepine taper rates and strategies. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Benzodiazepine taper rates

Joint guideline, 2025:

- Reduce 5 to 10 percent of the current dose every 2 to 4 weeks.
- Do not exceed 25 percent every 2 weeks.
- Strong physiologic dependence: 5 to 10 percent every 6 to 8 weeks, or slower.
- Steps of 10 to 25 percent are reserved for lower doses and use under 3 months.
- If withdrawal is troublesome, pause or slow the taper first.
- Offer CBT for anxiety or CBT-I for insomnia during the taper.

Older deprescribing algorithm, 2018: about 25 percent every 2 weeks, then 12.5 percent near the end and planned drug-free days. This is faster than the 2025 guideline.

Optional, Ashton Manual approach: switch a short-acting drug to a long-acting one such as diazepam before tapering. Equivalents: .edbzdequiv.

Withdrawal: anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, and perceptual changes. Seizures are a risk with abrupt or rapid reduction.

Sources:

- Brunner E et al. J Gen Intern Med 2025;40(12):2814-2859. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40526204/
- Pottie K et al. Can Fam Physician 2018;64(5):339-351. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29760253/
- Deprescribing algorithm: https://deprescribing.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/deprescribing_algorithms2019_BZRA_vf-locked.pdf

section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
use: Use as a physician reference for the first conversation with a patient inherited on long-term benzodiazepines. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Talking with inherited benzodiazepine patients

Before the visit: send $bzdlet, check the PDMP, and calculate the diazepam equivalent.

At the visit:

- Start with reassurance: no one will stop the medicine suddenly.
- Ask what the medicine does for them now, and what they worry about if it changes.
- Name the patient's own risks: falls, memory, driving, opioid or alcohol co-use, sleep apnea.
- Explain dependence plainly: the body adapts, and the medicine often stops working as well over time.
- Offer choices rather than a deadline: taper now, taper later, or continue with risk reduction.
- If they agree to taper, start slowly and promise pauses. Give $pibzd and $pibzdtaper.
- Treat the underlying anxiety or insomnia with CBT, CBT-I, or an SSRI or SNRI.
- Reassess at least every 3 months.

EMPOWER: a mailed patient brochure alone led 27 percent of older adults to stop, vs 5 percent with usual care.

Sources:

- Tannenbaum C et al. JAMA Intern Med 2014;174(6):890-898. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24733354/
- Brunner E et al. J Gen Intern Med 2025;40(12):2814-2859. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40526204/

section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
use: Use as a physician reference on the 2023 Beers Criteria for older adults. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Beers Criteria 2023, key avoid items

- First-generation antihistamines: avoid
- Benzodiazepines: avoid, with exceptions such as seizures, REM sleep behavior disorder, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, severe generalized anxiety
- Z-drugs, eszopiclone, zaleplon, zolpidem: avoid
- Strongly anticholinergic antidepressants: amitriptyline, amoxapine, clomipramine, desipramine, doxepin over 6 mg/day, imipramine, nortriptyline, paroxetine: avoid
- Antimuscarinics for incontinence, such as oxybutynin and tolterodine: strongly anticholinergic, oxybutynin has the best evidence for cognitive harm
- Skeletal muscle relaxants: avoid, except baclofen or tizanidine for spasticity
- Chronic NSAIDs: avoid unless alternatives fail and a gastroprotective agent is used; indomethacin and ketorolac: avoid
- Sulfonylureas, all: avoid as first- or second-line or add-on unless substantial barriers; if used, choose short-acting such as glipizide
- Sliding-scale insulin without basal insulin: avoid
- Aspirin for primary prevention: avoid starting, consider deprescribing
- Warfarin as initial therapy for AF or VTE: avoid unless DOACs are contraindicated
- Rivaroxaban for long-term AF or VTE: avoid in favor of safer alternatives
- Dabigatran: use caution over other DOACs
- Digoxin: avoid as first line for AF or HF; if used, avoid over 0.125 mg/day
- Nifedipine immediate release: avoid
- Peripheral alpha-1 blockers as antihypertensives: avoid
- PPIs: avoid scheduled use over 8 weeks unless high risk
- Antipsychotics for dementia behaviors: avoid unless nonpharmacologic options fail or there is a threat of harm
- Systemic estrogen: do not start, consider deprescribing; low-dose vaginal estrogen is acceptable
- Megestrol: avoid
- Metoclopramide: avoid unless for gastroparesis, no more than 12 weeks
- Meperidine: avoid
- Oral mineral oil: avoid
- Desmopressin for nocturia: avoid
- Nitrofurantoin: avoid if CrCl under 30 or for long-term suppression
- Combinations to avoid: opioid plus gabapentinoid, opioid plus benzodiazepine

Alternatives: .edbeersswap. Kidney dosing: .edbeersrenal.

Source:

- AGS 2023 Beers Criteria Update Expert Panel. J Am Geriatr Soc 2023;71(7):2052-2081. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12478568/

section: Physician education: opioids, benzodiazepines, and deprescribing
use: Use as a physician reference for safer alternatives to Beers medications. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Switch this to that, older adults

- Diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, chlorpheniramine for allergy: intranasal steroid, saline, loratadine, fexofenadine, or cetirizine
- Diphenhydramine or doxylamine for sleep: CBT-I; doxepin 6 mg/day or less if a drug is needed
- Benzodiazepine for anxiety: SSRI other than paroxetine, SNRI, buspirone, CBT; taper per .edbzdtaper
- Benzodiazepine or Z-drug for insomnia: CBT-I; taper, do not stop abruptly
- Amitriptyline or other tertiary TCA for depression: SSRI other than paroxetine, SNRI, or bupropion
- TCA for neuropathic pain: SNRI, gabapentin or pregabalin dosed for kidney function, topical lidocaine or capsaicin
- Paroxetine: sertraline or escitalopram
- Cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, carisoprodol: acetaminophen, topical NSAID, heat, PT
- Chronic oral NSAID: acetaminophen, topical diclofenac; if an NSAID is needed, shortest course with a PPI
- Glyburide or glimepiride: metformin, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA, or DPP-4i; if a sulfonylurea is needed, glipizide
- Sliding-scale insulin alone: basal insulin with correction
- Aspirin for primary prevention: deprescribe
- Warfarin, new start: a DOAC such as apixaban, avoiding rivaroxaban
- Rivaroxaban for long-term AF or VTE: a safer DOAC such as apixaban
- Nifedipine immediate release: amlodipine or nifedipine extended release
- Doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin, or clonidine for hypertension: thiazide, ACEi, ARB, or long-acting dihydropyridine CCB
- Digoxin over 0.125 mg/day: lower dose, or a beta blocker for rate control
- Long-term PPI without a high-risk indication: step down to the lowest dose, on-demand use, or famotidine dosed for kidney function
- Oxybutynin or tolterodine for overactive bladder: bladder training, pelvic floor PT; mirabegron or vibegron are not on the Beers list
- Meperidine: another opioid at the lowest effective dose
- Oral mineral oil: polyethylene glycol
- Systemic estrogen for genitourinary symptoms: vaginal estrogen; for hot flashes, SSRI, SNRI, or gabapentin
- Desiccated thyroid: levothyroxine
- Megestrol for appetite: no drug alternative; address causes and nutrition
- Antipsychotic for dementia behaviors: nonpharmacologic approaches first
- Desmopressin for nocturia: evening fluid limits and treat the cause

Sources:

- Hanlon JT et al. J Am Geriatr Soc 2015;63(12):e8-e18. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26447889/
- AGS 2023 Beers Criteria: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12478568/

section: Physician education: pediatric obesity and Tulsa resources
use: Use as a physician reference on how to discuss weight with children and families. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Talking about pediatric obesity

Words:

- Ask permission first: "Is it OK if we talk about weight today?"
- Use neutral words: weight, healthy weight, BMI. Parents rate weight and unhealthy weight as most acceptable.
- Avoid obese, fat, extremely obese, and large. Families rate these most stigmatizing and least motivating.
- Ask which words the family prefers and use them; preferences vary by family.
- Use person-first language: a child with obesity, not an obese child.

Approach:

- Family-centered and non-stigmatizing; name the biologic, social, and structural drivers.
- Motivational interviewing: open questions, reflect, let the family choose 1 or 2 goals.
- Focus on health and habits, not weight loss or appearance.
- Ask about weight-based bullying and teasing at school and home.
- Screen for disordered eating before and during treatment.
- Weight stigma does not motivate change. It worsens binge eating, isolation, care avoidance, inactivity, and weight gain.

Treatment ladder:

- Intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment for age 6 and older, may offer age 2 to 5. Dose: 26 or more hours of family-based treatment over 3 to 12 months.
- Pharmacotherapy offered at age 12 and older.
- Metabolic and bariatric surgery evaluation at age 13 and older with severe obesity, BMI 120 percent of the 95th percentile or higher.
- Labs and BP: #wuobesk. Family handout: $piobesk. Tulsa programs: .edtulsaobes.

Sources:

- Hampl SE et al. AAP Clinical Practice Guideline on obesity. Pediatrics 2023;151(2):e2022060640. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36622115/
- Pont SJ et al. Stigma experienced by children and adolescents with obesity. Pediatrics 2017;140(6):e20173034. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29158228/
- Puhl RM et al. Parental perceptions of weight terminology. Pediatrics 2011;128(4):e786-793. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21949145/
- Puhl RM et al. Patient and family perspectives on terms for obesity. Pediatrics 2022;150(6). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36404759/

Tulsa pediatric weight management

OU Health Oklahoma Children's, Early Lifestyle Intervention Program:

- Ages 2 to 18 with BMI at the 95th percentile or higher
- Requires at least 3 months of prior weight management by a PCP, dietitian, or specialist, and parents able to attend frequent visits
- Team: pediatrician, dietitian, psychologist, sleep medicine; bariatric input from the Schusterman program
- Partners with the Tandy YMCA for free guest passes, reduced memberships, and cooking classes
- First visit about 4 hours
- Physician referral required
- Phone: 918-619-4300, option 2
- Schusterman Center Pediatric Clinic, 4444 E 41st St, Tulsa 74135
- SoonerCare and wait time not stated, call to confirm

Clover Pediatric Wellness and Weight Management:

- Private pediatric and pediatric endocrinology practice, 11911 S Oxford Ave, Suite 200, Tulsa 74137
- Phone: 918-884-6623
- Services and insurance not confirmed, call first

Bariatric surgery: no accredited adolescent program found in Oklahoma. SoonerCare rules allow bariatric surgery from age 15, younger with prior authorization; confirm with OHCA.

YMCA of Greater Tulsa: financial assistance available, no one turned away for inability to pay. https://ymcatulsa.org

use: Use as a quick reference when ordering lorazepam.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Lorazepam dosing, adults:

- Anxiety: 0.5-1 mg PO BID-TID, max 10 mg/day, short term only
- Status epilepticus: 0.1 mg/kg IV, max 4 mg per dose, may repeat once in 5-10 min
- Alcohol withdrawal, symptom triggered: 1-4 mg PO or IV q1h PRN by CIWA-Ar per protocol
- Severe withdrawal or delirium tremens: 1-4 mg IV q5-15 min PRN to light somnolence, ICU if escalating

Cautions:

- Older adults: start 0.25-0.5 mg, high fall and delirium risk
- Avoid with opioids when possible, monitor respiratory status
- Preferred over chlordiazepoxide in liver disease

body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Check destination resistance on the CDC Yellow Book map.

Chloroquine-sensitive areas:

- Chloroquine 500 mg salt PO weekly, start 1-2 weeks before, continue 4 weeks after; may worsen psoriasis; safe in pregnancy
- Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg salt PO weekly, same timing

Chloroquine-resistant areas:

- Atovaquone-proguanil 250/100 mg PO daily with food, start 1-2 days before, continue 7 days after; avoid if CrCl under 30 or pregnant
- Pediatric atovaquone-proguanil, 62.5/25 mg tabs: 5-8 kg 1/2 tab, 9-10 kg 3/4 tab, 11-20 kg 1 tab, 21-30 kg 2 tabs, 31-40 kg 3 tabs, over 40 kg 1 adult tab
- Doxycycline 100 mg PO daily, start 1-2 days before, continue 4 weeks after; photosensitivity, take upright with water; avoid under age 8 and in pregnancy
- Mefloquine 250 mg PO weekly, start at least 2 weeks before, continue 4 weeks after; avoid with psychiatric or seizure history or conduction disease; usable in pregnancy
- Tafenoquine 200 mg PO daily x3 days before, weekly during, one dose after; G6PD testing required first; avoid in pregnancy

use: Use as a reference when prescribing nirmatrelvir-ritonavir.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Start within 5 days of symptom onset in patients at high risk of progression. Run an interaction check first, ritonavir affects many drugs.

Dosing by eGFR, 5-day course:

- eGFR 60 or more: nirmatrelvir 300 mg plus ritonavir 100 mg PO BID
- eGFR 30-59: nirmatrelvir 150 mg plus ritonavir 100 mg PO BID
- eGFR under 30 or dialysis: nirmatrelvir 300 mg plus ritonavir 100 mg PO once on day 1. Then 150 mg plus 100 mg PO once daily on days 2-5. Give after dialysis on dialysis days

Missed dose: take within 8 hours of the usual time, otherwise skip it. Do not double.

- Clinical ASCVD: high intensity, LDL goal under 55 for most
- LDL 190 or more: high intensity, no risk calculation needed
- Diabetes, age 40-75: at least moderate, high if multiple risk factors

- Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg PO daily

use: Use as a refresher on current newborn bilirubin thresholds and phototherapy decisions.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Use the AAP 2022 hour-specific phototherapy and exchange thresholds by gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors, for example in BiliTool.
Fixed thresholds such as 15 to 20 mg/dL in term infants, or exchange when TSB exceeds weight in kg times 10, are outdated.

Neurotoxicity risk factors:

- Gestational age under 38 weeks
- Albumin under 3 g/dL
- Isoimmune hemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, or other hemolysis
- Sepsis
- Significant clinical instability in the past 24 hours

Escalation of care, TSB within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold: TSB every 2 hours, intensive phototherapy, NICU involvement, and IVIG if isoimmune.
Stop phototherapy when TSB falls at least 2 mg/dL below the threshold at initiation.
If phototherapy started before 48 hours, DAT positive, or known or suspected hemolysis: TSB 6 to 12 hours after stopping and the next day. Otherwise check bilirubin the day after stopping. If readmitted after discharge without birth-hospital phototherapy, or treated with home phototherapy, check bilirubin or follow up clinically 1 to 2 days after stopping.

desc: Failure to thrive and pediatric malnutrition reference
use: Use as a refresher on catch-up calories, expected weight gain, and malnutrition severity.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Routine labs and imaging are low yield in failure to thrive. Let history and exam guide testing.
If testing is warranted, start with CBC, CMP, and UA, and consider TSH, celiac serology, and lead level.

Calories:

- Catch-up kcal/kg/day = RDA kcal/kg/day for weight-age x ideal weight for length in kg / actual weight in kg
- Catch-up growth often needs about 1.5 times usual calories until prior percentiles are regained
- Breast milk and standard term formula are about 20 kcal/oz
- Preterm transitional formula is 22 kcal/oz and preterm formula is 24 kcal/oz
- 1 oz is about 30 mL

Expected weight gain:

- 0 to 1 month: 28 to 35 g/day
- 1 to 3 months: 24 to 29 g/day
- 3 to 6 months: about 15 g/day
- 6 to 9 months: 9 to 10 g/day
- 9 to 12 months: 7 to 8 g/day
- 1 to 2 years: 7 to 9 g/day
- 2 to 3 years: 4 to 10 g/day

Malnutrition severity, single data point:

- Mild: weight for length or BMI z score -1 to -1.9
- Moderate: z score -2 to -2.9
- Severe: z score -3 or lower

Malnutrition severity, two or more data points:

- Mild: under 2 years, weight gain under 75 percent of expected; 2 to 20 years, weight loss of 5 percent of usual weight; decline of 1 z score; intake 51 to 75 percent of need
- Moderate: weight gain under 50 percent of expected; weight loss of 7.5 percent; decline of 2 z scores; intake 26 to 50 percent of need
- Severe: weight gain under 25 percent of expected; weight loss of 10 percent; decline of 3 z scores; intake under 26 percent of need

Weight checks: under 1 month old weekly, under 6 months every 2 to 4 weeks, under 12 months every 4 weeks. Check more often until gaining well.

use: Use as a refresher on the accuracy and pitfalls of ROM tests in triage.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

- Sterile speculum: look for pooling in the posterior fornix, with cough or Valsalva
- Nitrazine: blue means pH over 6.5. Sensitive, but false positives are common with blood, semen, bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas, urine, and soap. False negatives occur with intermittent leak or dilute fluid
- Ferning: swab the posterior fornix, not the cervix, and air-dry on a slide for 10 minutes. A fine fern pattern suggests amniotic fluid; cervical mucus gives thick, wide arborization
- PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1 immunoassay, such as AmniSure: high sensitivity and little effect from trace blood or semen. False positives can occur with intact membranes, especially in labor. Use when standard tests are equivocal
- Ultrasound: low amniotic fluid supports but does not confirm ROM
- Avoid digital cervical exams in suspected PPROM unless in active labor or delivery is imminent

use: Use as a refresher on the sacral structural exam before OMT.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Patient prone, examiner standing to one side.

Palpate for tenderness at:

- Sacral base, left, right, and midline
- Mid sacrum, left, right, and midline
- Lower sacrum, left, right, and midline
- Sacrococcygeal junction
- Coccyx tip
- Mid-pole sacroiliac tender point, about 10 cm below and slightly lateral to the PSIS, at the level of the ILA
- Piriformis tender point, midway between the lateral sacral border and the greater trochanter

Sacral base levelness: thumbs on the sacral base just medial to each PSIS, compare anterior and posterior depth.
ILA levelness: thumbs on the posterior surface of each ILA to compare depth, or on the inferior surface to compare superior and inferior position.

use: Use as a refresher on typical steroid and lidocaine volumes by injection site.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

K40 is triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg/mL, M40 is methylprednisolone acetate 40 mg/mL, and L is 1 or 2 percent lidocaine without epinephrine.

- Subacromial bursa: 1 mL K40 plus 4 mL L
- AC joint: 0.25 to 0.5 mL K40 plus 0.5 to 1 mL L
- Olecranon bursa: 0.5 mL K40 plus 1 to 2 mL L
- Lateral epicondyle: 1 mL M40 plus 2 mL L
- Greater trochanteric bursa: 1 mL K40 plus 4 mL L
- Knee: 1 mL K40 plus 2 to 5 mL L
- Ankle: 1 mL M40 plus 1 mL L
- Plantar fascia: 1 mL K40 plus 2 mL L
- Trigger point: lidocaine alone preferred, 1 to 3 mL L

Lateral epicondyle steroid injections give short-term relief but worse outcomes at 6 to 12 months than physical therapy or waiting.
Plantar fascia steroid injections carry a risk of fascia rupture and fat pad atrophy.
Space steroid injections into the same joint at least 3 months apart.
Steroid injections raise blood glucose for several days in patients with diabetes.

use: Use as a refresher on AKI staging, workup, and causes.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

KDIGO definition, any one of:

- Creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours
- Creatinine 1.5 times baseline within 7 days
- Urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours

KDIGO stages:

- Stage 1: creatinine 1.5 to 1.9 times baseline or a rise of 0.3 or more. Or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 to 12 hours
- Stage 2: creatinine 2.0 to 2.9 times baseline, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more
- Stage 3: creatinine 3 times baseline or 4.0 or more, or dialysis. Or urine output under 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours, or anuria for 12 hours

Approach:

- Look first for an obvious cause: hypotension, volume loss, nephrotoxins, contrast, obstruction
- Send UA with microscopy and urine sodium, creatinine, and urea before fluids or diuretics when possible
- Bladder scan, then renal ultrasound if obstruction is possible or the cause is unclear
- Volume depleted: isotonic crystalloid, reassess in 12 to 24 hours
- Volume overloaded: loop diuretic trial, reassess
- Stop NSAIDs and nephrotoxins, hold ACE inhibitor, ARB, and diuretics if hypovolemic, renally dose all drugs
- Nephrology for unclear intrinsic cause, active sediment, stage 3, or dialysis indications; urology for obstruction
- Dialysis indications: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, or volume overload, uremic pericarditis or encephalopathy, dialyzable toxins

Urine indices:

- FENa under 1 percent suggests prerenal, over 2 percent suggests ATN
- FEUrea under 35 percent suggests prerenal and stays reliable after diuretics
- Muddy brown granular casts suggest ATN, red cell casts suggest glomerulonephritis, white cell casts suggest interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis
- Urine eosinophils are inaccurate for interstitial nephritis and are not recommended

Creatinine lags the fall in GFR by 24 to 48 hours.

use: Use as a refresher on reversal agents and doses for bleeding or procedures on anticoagulants.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Order set: _ local.

- Unfractionated heparin: protamine 1 mg IV per 100 units of heparin given in the last 2 to 3 hours, max 50 mg, given slowly
- Enoxaparin within 8 hours: protamine 1 mg IV per 1 mg of enoxaparin, max 50 mg; 0.5 mg per 1 mg if 8 to 12 hours; reversal is partial
- Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV, given as two 2.5 g doses no more than 15 minutes apart
- Apixaban or rivaroxaban: 4-factor PCC 25 to 50 units/kg IV once; andexanet alfa is no longer sold in the US
- Edoxaban: 4-factor PCC 25 to 50 units/kg IV once
- Argatroban or bivalirudin: stop the infusion, short half-life, no specific reversal agent
- Warfarin with major bleeding: vitamin K 10 mg IV once plus 4-factor PCC IV once. Plasma only if PCC is unavailable
- PCC dose: INR 2 to under 4, 25 units/kg, max 2500 units. INR 4 to 6, 35 units/kg, max 3500 units. INR over 6, 50 units/kg, max 5000 units
- Warfarin, INR 4.5 to 10 without bleeding: hold warfarin, vitamin K not routinely needed
- Warfarin, INR over 10 without bleeding: hold warfarin and give vitamin K 2.5 to 5 mg PO once
- Warfarin before a procedure in 24 to 48 hours, INR 2 or higher: vitamin K 2.5 to 5 mg PO or IV once. Recheck INR. INR under 2 may need no reversal
- Vitamin K lowers the INR in 4 to 6 hours IV and 18 to 24 hours PO; add 4-factor PCC if the procedure cannot wait

use: Use as a reference while admitting community-acquired pneumonia; the chart block is separate.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

CAP admission checklist

Severe CAP is 1 major criterion, septic shock needing pressors or mechanical ventilation, or 3 or more minor criteria:

- RR 30 or higher
- PaO2/FiO2 250 or lower
- Multilobar infiltrates
- Confusion
- BUN 20 or higher
- WBC under 4,000
- Platelets under 100,000
- Temperature under 36 C
- Hypotension needing aggressive fluids

Triage: CURB-65 and PSI for site of care.

Chart check: lung disease, baseline O2, prior cultures, antibiotics in the last 90 days, allergies, influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.

Cannot miss: hypoxemic respiratory failure, sepsis, PE, ACS, empyema.

History:

- Symptoms: onset and course, dyspnea, cough, sputum, fever, rigors, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, diarrhea
- Exposures: sick contacts, travel, animals, occupation, TB, recent healthcare or antibiotics, smoking
- MRSA risk: prior MRSA, post-influenza, IV drug use, cavitary disease, positive nasal swab
- Pseudomonas risk: prior isolation, bronchiectasis, severe COPD, immunosuppression, recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics
- Aspiration risk: dementia, altered mental status, alcohol or drug use, dysphagia, poor dentition, bedbound

Exam: work of breathing, O2 need, crackles, decreased breath sounds, egophony, dullness to percussion, rash, edema.

DDx:

- Infectious: viral such as COVID, influenza, RSV; bacterial such as pneumococcus, H influenzae, Moraxella, Legionella, Mycoplasma, MRSA, Pseudomonas; fungal such as PJP, histoplasmosis, aspergillus
- Noninfectious pulmonary: aspiration pneumonitis, atelectasis, PE, organizing pneumonia, ILD, malignancy, drug pneumonitis, alveolar hemorrhage
- Cardiac: heart failure, ACS
- Other: vasculitis, lupus, sarcoidosis, acute chest syndrome

Workup: CXR for all. CT if PE concern, unclear diagnosis, or complications. MRSA nares PCR. Blood and sputum cultures if severe or MRSA or Pseudomonas risk. Urine Legionella and pneumococcal antigens if severe. Procalcitonin and viral panel as adjuncts.

Treatment:

- Ward, no resistant-organism risk: beta-lactam plus macrolide. Ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV daily or ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5 to 3 g IV every 6 hours, plus azithromycin 500 mg IV or PO daily
- Or levofloxacin 750 mg IV or PO daily alone
- Doxycycline 100 mg IV or PO BID in place of azithromycin only if macrolides and fluoroquinolones are both contraindicated
- Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours, or meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours
- MRSA: vancomycin dosed by pharmacy, or linezolid 600 mg IV or PO every 12 hours
- Severe CAP without influenza: hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours
- Duration: nonsevere CAP, 3 to 5 days once clinically stable; severe CAP, at least 5 days; 7 days for MRSA or Pseudomonas
- Drain large or loculated parapneumonic effusions and all empyemas
- Supportive: acetaminophen, incentive spirometry, benzonatate 100 mg PO TID PRN cough
- Discharge when afebrile 48 hours, at baseline O2, and vitals stable

use: Use as a reference when sorting out a dizziness complaint.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Dizziness differential by type

Vertigo, a false sense of motion:

- BPPV: brief and positional, Dix-Hallpike or supine roll test
- Vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis: continuous for days, hearing loss in labyrinthitis
- Meniere disease: episodes lasting hours with hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness
- Vestibular migraine
- Head trauma
- Posterior circulation stroke: acute continuous vertigo with any central sign, HINTS only if trained, otherwise image

Disequilibrium, feeling off balance:

- Peripheral neuropathy, Parkinson disease, cerebellar disease, medications, stroke, vision loss

Presyncope, near fainting:

- Orthostatic hypotension, including from medications
- Arrhythmia, structural heart disease, ACS
- Volume loss, anemia

Lightheadedness, vague:

- Anxiety, depression, hyperventilation, medication effect, hypoglycemia

Central red flags: new headache, neck pain, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, limb weakness or numbness, inability to walk, vascular risk factors.

Routine labs and imaging are low yield without neurologic findings.

ECG, ambulatory monitoring, and carotid imaging only if a cardiac or vascular cause is suspected.

use: Use as a reference when deciding newborn bilirubin follow-up and treatment thresholds.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Newborn hyperbilirubinemia, AAP 2022 approach

Use hour-specific phototherapy and exchange thresholds by gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors, for example in BiliTool. The old risk-zone nomogram and race-based risk are no longer used.

Risk factors for significant hyperbilirubinemia:

- Lower gestational age, risk rises below 40 weeks
- Jaundice in the first 24 hours
- Predischarge TcB or TSB close to the phototherapy threshold
- Hemolysis, known or suspected from a rise of 0.3 mg/dL/hour or more in the first 24 hours or 0.2 mg/dL/hour or more after
- Phototherapy before discharge
- Parent or sibling who needed phototherapy or exchange transfusion
- Family history or ancestry suggesting an inherited red cell disorder, including G6PD deficiency
- Exclusive breastfeeding with suboptimal intake
- Scalp hematoma or significant bruising
- Down syndrome
- Macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother

Neurotoxicity risk factors, which lower the treatment threshold:

- Gestational age under 38 weeks, risk rises as age falls
- Albumin under 3.0 g/dL
- Isoimmune hemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, or other hemolytic condition
- Sepsis
- Significant clinical instability in the previous 24 hours
