use: Use as a reference when working up common OB triage complaints.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

OB triage by complaint

Term labor rule-out:

- Ask about contraction onset, frequency and intensity, and prior cesarean
- Bedside US for presentation
- Active labor begins at 6 cm; admit for active labor, cervical change with regular painful contractions, or ROM
- No cervical change on repeat SVE in 1 to 2 hours: discharge with labor precautions

Leakage of fluid, term or preterm:

- Ask about timing, intercourse in the past 24 hours, bleeding, discharge odor, and contractions
- Differential: ROM, cervical mucus, vaginitis or cervicitis, urinary incontinence, sweat
- Sterile speculum: look for pooling, have the patient cough or Valsalva
- Nitrazine: blue is positive, sensitivity about 90 percent, false positives with blood, semen, soap, or vaginitis
- Fern: swab posterior fornix, dry 10 minutes, a delicate fern pattern is positive
- PAMG-1 test such as AmniSure if equivocal, sensitivity and specificity about 98 percent
- Ultrasound AFI or MVP if still unclear
- GBS culture if 36 weeks or later and status unknown, GC and chlamydia, vaginal panel if vaginitis suspected

Preterm labor rule-out:

- Ask about prior preterm birth, prior cesarean, and steroids this pregnancy
- Sterile speculum first, UA with culture, GC and chlamydia, vaginal panel, GBS culture
- Under 34 weeks with cervix under 3 cm and intact membranes: transvaginal cervical length
- Cervical length under 20 mm: admit for observation, steroids, and plan with OB hospitalist; over 30 mm: preterm labor unlikely; 20 to 30 mm: send fFN if no bleeding, ROM, exam, or intercourse in 24 hours
- Cervix over 3 cm, effacement over 80 percent, ROM, bleeding, or persistent painful contractions: admit
- Preterm labor at 24w0d to 33w6d: betamethasone 12 mg IM q24h for 2 doses, GBS prophylaxis, short tocolysis to complete steroids
- Under 32 weeks and delivery imminent: magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection
- Magnesium regimen _ local: 4 g IV over 15-30 min then 1 g/h, or 6 g IV load then 2 g/h
- 34w0d to 36w6d: consider betamethasone if delivery likely within 7 days, no prior course, and no pregestational diabetes
- 34 weeks or later: SVE after discussion with senior or attending, discuss findings with the OB hospitalist
- 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate was withdrawn in 2023, do not offer it

Elevated BP, rule out preeclampsia:

- Ask about headache, vision changes, RUQ pain, dyspnea, prior HTN or preeclampsia, aspirin use, and MFM care
- Measure BP seated or semi-reclined, arm at heart level, after 10 minutes of rest
- Labs: CBC, CMP, urine protein to creatinine ratio, LDH if HELLP suspected
- Preeclampsia at 37 weeks or later: delivery; earlier, admit and plan with OB hospitalist
- BP q15min; severe range 160/110 or higher lasting 15 minutes needs treatment within 30 to 60 minutes

Decreased fetal movement:

- Differential: fetal sleep, maternal medications or tobacco, oligohydramnios, fetal compromise
- NST up to 40 min, VAS allowed; then AFI or BPP if NST nonreactive or risk factors present
- Repeat NST only if decreased movement recurs
- Admit for oligohydramnios or persistently nonreactive or nonreassuring testing
- If reassuring, discharge with kick count teaching: 10 movements within 2 hours at rest

Antepartum bleeding:

- Differential: abruption, previa, vasa previa, cervicitis, trauma, labor
- Ultrasound for placental location before any digital exam, then speculum exam
- CBC, type and screen, coags, fibrinogen; Kleihauer-Betke and RhIG if Rh negative
- Nonreassuring FHT suggests abruption; admit for previa, abruption, or labor

use: Use as a reference when ordering outpatient rhythm monitoring.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Ambulatory cardiac monitors

- Holter: 24 to 48 hours, up to 7 days. Misses events more than 48 hours apart.
- Extended-wear patch monitor: up to 14 days, continuous, no leads. Good first choice for symptoms every few days to weeks and for AF screening.
- Event monitor, patient-activated or auto-triggered: 2 to 4 weeks.
- Mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry: continuous, up to 30 days, near real-time transmission. Use when a dangerous arrhythmia such as VT, pauses, or AF with RVR is suspected. Costlier.
- Implantable loop recorder: 1 to 3 years.

How to choose:

- Daily symptoms: Holter
- Every few days to weekly: patch monitor
- Weekly to monthly: event monitor, or MCOT if higher suspicion of dangerous arrhythmia
- Rare unexplained syncope or cryptogenic stroke: implantable loop recorder
- High pretest probability of significant arrhythmia or sudden death risk: MCOT or loop recorder rather than Holter

use: Use as a reference when planning anticoagulant holds and restarts around procedures.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Perioperative anticoagulation

Procedure bleeding risk:

- Minimal: dental, cataract, minor skin; continue anticoagulant or skip one DOAC dose
- Low to moderate: most procedures under 45 minutes
- High: major surgery, neuraxial anesthesia, kidney or liver biopsy, procedures over 45 minutes

DOAC hold, no bridging:

- Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban: hold 1 day before low bleed risk and 2 days before high bleed risk procedures
- Dabigatran, CrCl 50 or more: hold 1 day before low and 2 days before high bleed risk; CrCl under 50: hold 2 days before low and 4 days before high bleed risk
- Restart 24 hours after low bleed risk and 48 to 72 hours after high bleed risk procedures once hemostasis is secure

Warfarin:

- Hold 5 days before; check INR the day before only in selected patients
- INR >1.5 1 to 2 days before: routine vitamin K not suggested (CHEST 2022, conditional, very low certainty)

- Bridge only if very high thrombotic risk: mechanical mitral valve, older mechanical aortic valve, stroke or TIA within 3 months, VTE within 3 months, or severe thrombophilia

- Factor Xa inhibitor reversal: 4-factor PCC per _ local protocol; andexanet alfa is no longer sold in the US
- Warfarin reversal: 4-factor PCC per INR and weight plus vitamin K 10 mg IV once

use: Use as a reference when evaluating a seizure or managing status epilepticus.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Seizure and status epilepticus

Provoked seizure causes:

- Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, drug intoxication or withdrawal
- Antiseizure medication nonadherence
- Hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, uremia
- CNS infection, stroke, hemorrhage, mass

Epilepsy risk factors:

- Febrile seizures in infancy, family history of epilepsy
- Prior TBI, stroke, subdural hematoma, anoxic injury, CNS infection, neurodegenerative disease, tumor

Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or recurrent seizures without return to baseline.

- ABCs, monitors, fingerstick glucose, IV access
- Thiamine 100 mg IV before glucose if alcohol use or malnutrition, dextrose 50% 50 mL IV if glucose under 60
- Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV, max 4 mg per dose, may repeat once in 5 minutes
- No IV: midazolam 10 mg IM once if over 40 kg, 5 mg IM if 13 to 40 kg
- Second line, choose one:
- Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV, max 4500 mg
- Valproate 40 mg/kg IV, max 3000 mg
- Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV, max 1500 mg PE
- Refractory: intubate, continuous midazolam or propofol infusion, continuous EEG, neurology and ICU
- Not back to baseline after the expected postictal period: consider nonconvulsive status, get EEG

Seizure mimics:

- Convulsive syncope, rigors, myoclonus, migraine, posturing
- Functional or psychogenic nonepileptic spells: involve neurology, supportive approach, avoid overtesting; can coexist with epilepsy

Medications that lower seizure threshold:

- Tramadol, bupropion, antipsychotics, some SSRIs
- Fluoroquinolones, high-dose penicillins, cefepime, carbapenems
- Abrupt benzodiazepine or barbiturate withdrawal

Workup:

- CMP, magnesium, phosphorus, CBC, tox screen, antiseizure drug levels if on one, pregnancy test
- LP if infection suspected
- CT head without contrast for acute hemorrhage, then MRI brain with and without contrast, seizure protocol
- EEG, continuous for status or to characterize spells

body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Palliative Performance Scale, version 2: ambulation, activity and disease, self-care, intake, consciousness. Approximate median survival is from older palliative cohorts and varies widely by setting.

- 100%: full ambulation, normal activity and work, no disease, full self-care, normal intake, full consciousness
- 90%: full ambulation, normal activity and work, some disease, full self-care, normal intake, full consciousness; no median survival data in the source cohorts
- 80%: full ambulation, normal activity with effort, some disease, full self-care, normal or reduced intake, full consciousness; no median survival data in the source cohorts
- 70%: reduced ambulation, unable to do normal job or work, significant disease, full self-care, normal or reduced intake, full consciousness; about 108 to 145 days
- 60%: reduced ambulation, unable to do hobbies or housework, significant disease, occasional assistance, normal or reduced intake, full or confused; about 29 to 108 days
- 50%: mainly sits or lies, unable to do any work, extensive disease, considerable assistance, normal or reduced intake, full or confused; about 30 to 41 days
- 40%: mainly in bed, unable to do most activity, extensive disease, mainly assistance, normal or reduced intake, full, drowsy, or confused; about 18 to 41 days
- 30%: totally bed bound, unable to do any activity, extensive disease, total care, normal or reduced intake, full, drowsy, or confused; about 8 to 41 days
- 20%: totally bed bound, extensive disease, total care, minimal to sips, full, drowsy, or confused; about 4 to 6 days
- 10%: totally bed bound, extensive disease, total care, mouth care only, drowsy or coma; about 1 to 6 days

Approximate systolic BP reduction by lifestyle change:

- Weight loss: about 1 mmHg per 1 kg lost, initial goal at least 5 percent weight loss
- DASH diet with fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy and less saturated fat: 8-11 mmHg
- Sodium under 1500 mg/day, or at least 1000 mg/day less than baseline: 5-6 mmHg
- Potassium-rich diet, 3500-5000 mg/day unless CKD or on potassium-raising drugs: 4-5 mmHg
- Aerobic activity 90-150 min/week: 5-8 mmHg
- Dynamic resistance training 90-150 min/week: about 4 mmHg
- Alcohol: abstain or reduce, no more than 2 drinks/day for men and 1 for women: about 4 mmHg

use: Use when deciding whether chronic abdominal pain with bowel change meets IBS criteria and which subtype.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Recurrent abdominal pain on average at least 1 day/week in the last 3 months. Onset at least 6 months before diagnosis. Plus 2 or more of:

- Related to defecation
- Associated with a change in stool frequency
- Associated with a change in stool form

Subtype by stool form on days with abnormal stools:

- IBS-C: over 25% Bristol 1-2 and under 25% Bristol 6-7
- IBS-D: over 25% Bristol 6-7 and under 25% Bristol 1-2
- IBS-M: over 25% Bristol 1-2 and over 25% Bristol 6-7
- IBS-U: meets criteria but does not fit a subtype

Alarm features: age 45 or older at onset, weight loss, GI bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, nocturnal symptoms, family history of colon cancer, celiac disease or IBD.

use: Use when building a differential for abdominal pain.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Pain types:

- Somatic: sharp, well localized, reproducible, from skin, muscle or parietal peritoneum
- Neuropathic: burning or pins and needles from nerve injury, for example zoster or radiculopathy
- Visceral: vague, diffuse, from capsular stretch or hollow viscus obstruction

Visceral patterns:

- Obstruction of bowel, ureter or biliary tree: colicky, patient writhes to find comfort, little fever or leukocytosis
- Inflammation such as pancreatitis, cholecystitis, pyelonephritis, diverticulitis: constant pain, mild fever and leukocytosis
- Perforation: patient lies still, peritoneal signs, marked fever and leukocytosis
- Ischemia: pain out of proportion to exam, surgical emergency
- Referred pain from chest, pelvis or spine

By quadrant and first imaging:

- RUQ, ultrasound first: liver, gallbladder, duodenum, lung base, diaphragm
- RLQ, CT first, ultrasound first in children and pregnancy: appendix, colon, kidney and ureter, ovary or testis
- LUQ, CT: spleen, stomach, pancreas tail, lung base, diaphragm
- LLQ, CT: diverticulitis, colon, kidney and ureter, ovary or testis
- Pelvic ultrasound for suspected ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy or adnexal mass

Medical causes: DKA, uremia, hypercalcemia, adrenal insufficiency, porphyria, lead poisoning, hereditary angioedema, acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Consider ACS in upper abdominal pain, and pregnancy testing in anyone who could be pregnant.

use: Use when building a chest pain history and differential.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Key questions:

- Location and radiation
- Brought on by exertion and relieved by rest, and walking distance before stopping
- Pleuritic, positional or reproducible with palpation
- Associated presyncope, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea
- BP in both arms, difference over 20 mmHg
- CAD risk factors: tobacco, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity, family history, cocaine

Response to nitroglycerin does not distinguish cardiac from noncardiac pain.

Differential by layer:

- Skin: zoster, burns, lacerations
- Soft tissue: cellulitis, abscess
- MSK: strain, costochondritis, rib fracture, myositis
- Trachea: tracheitis
- Lung and pleura: PE, pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleuritis, tumor
- Pericardium: pericarditis, tamponade
- Heart: ACS, myocarditis, aortic stenosis, stress cardiomyopathy
- Esophagus: GERD, esophagitis, spasm, rupture
- Aorta: dissection, aneurysm
- Abdomen: biliary disease, pancreatitis, peptic ulcer
- Other: anxiety or panic, sickle cell crisis

Triple rule-out CT:

- ECG-gated cardiac CTA of the coronaries, thoracic aorta, and pulmonary arteries in one scan
- Best fit: low to intermediate ACS risk when PE or dissection is also possible
- Coronary accuracy is high; data for PE and dissection are thinner
- Hospital only, 0630-1700 Mon-Fri, includes calcium score. Underused here, _ local

use: Use when evaluating acute dyspnea, including on night call.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Differential by system:

- Acid-base: metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
- Blood: anemia, carbon monoxide or methemoglobinemia
- Cardiac: heart failure, arrhythmia, ACS, tamponade, valve disease
- Airway and lung: asthma, COPD, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, ILD, alveolar hemorrhage, ARDS, tumor, aspiration, anaphylaxis
- Vascular: pulmonary embolism
- Other: neuromuscular weakness, anxiety

First tests on night call:

- ABG or VBG with co-oximetry for acid-base, CO and methemoglobin
- ECG for ischemia, arrhythmia and pericardial disease
- CXR for parenchymal, pleural and cardiac causes
- Add CBC, BNP, troponin and bedside ultrasound by suspected cause

These do not exclude PE; risk-stratify separately with Wells and D-dimer or CTPA.

use: Use when describing primary and secondary skin lesions.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Primary lesions:

- Macule: flat color change up to 1 cm, not palpable, for example cafe au lait or ash leaf macule
- Patch: flat color change over 1 cm
- Papule: elevated solid lesion up to 1 cm, for example acne, warts, milia
- Plaque: elevated plateau-like solid lesion over 1 cm, for example psoriasis
- Nodule: elevated solid lesion over 1 cm with depth, for example lipoma
- Cyst: papule or nodule containing fluid or semi-fluid material, so fluctuant
- Vesicle: elevated fluid-filled lesion up to 1 cm, for example herpes simplex
- Bulla: elevated fluid-filled lesion over 1 cm, for example bullous impetigo
- Pustule: elevated pus-filled lesion, for example acne or erythema toxicum

Secondary lesions:

- Scale: excess stratum corneum, fine and branny, thick white and adherent as in psoriasis, or fish-scale-like
- Crust: dried serum, blood or pus over damaged epidermis, for example impetigo
- Erosion: partial loss of epidermis, heals without scarring
- Ulcer: full-thickness loss of epidermis into dermis, heals with scarring
- Fissure: linear painful break, often from dry skin
- Atrophy: thin, wrinkled skin with visible vessels, epidermal from topical steroids or dermal depression from injected steroids
- Scar: fibrous replacement after dermal injury, may be hypertrophic or atrophic

use: Use as a physician reference on fertility awareness-based methods, their biomarkers, effectiveness and counseling. Not for the chart.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Fertility awareness-based methods (FABMs)

Perfect use counts pregnancies when the method rules are followed every cycle. Typical use counts all pregnancies, including cycles with rule departures. Figures are first-year pregnancies per 100 women unless stated.

Overall:

- All FABMs, typical use: 2-23 (CDC, from Contraceptive Technology 22nd ed, 2023)
- Perfect-use estimates (Trussell, Contraception 2011): Standard Days 4.8, TwoDay 3.5, ovulation method 3.2, symptothermal 0.4 per 100 woman-years
- Systematic review of 53 studies, none rated high quality (Urrutia, Obstet Gynecol 2018). Rates vary widely within and across methods.
- Study populations differ too much for valid head-to-head comparison between methods (Urrutia 2018)

By method, biomarkers and data:

- Standard Days: calendar only, no unprotected sex on cycle days 8-19, only for cycles 26-32 days
- Standard Days trial, 478 women over 13 cycles: perfect 4.75, typical 11.96 (Arevalo, Contraception 2002)
- TwoDay: cervical secretions. Perfect 3.5, typical 13.7 (Urrutia 2018).
- Billings ovulation method: cervical mucus. Perfect 1.1-3.4, typical 10.5-33.6 in moderate-quality studies (Urrutia 2018).
- Billings, WHO 5-country trial, 725 women: 19.6% stopped for pregnancy over 13 cycles (Fertil Steril 1981)
- WHO trial per 100 woman-years: method failure 2.8, conscious departure from rules 15.4, inaccurate application 3.5
- Creighton Model: cervical mucus, a fully standardized modification of the Billings method
- Creighton, 5 center studies, 1876 couples: method effectiveness 99.5%, use effectiveness 96.8% at 12 mo (Hilgers, J Reprod Med 1998)
- Creighton CEIBA cohort, 296 couples: 13-cycle pregnancy 29.1-35.3% in cycles with intent to avoid (Stanford, PLoS One 2025)
- In CEIBA, 44% of avoid-intent cycles had intercourse on potentially fertile days. Baseline motivation predicted pregnancy more than cycle intent.
- Marquette: urine estrone-3-glucuronide and LH on an electronic hormonal fertility monitor, with or without mucus
- Marquette monitor plus mucus, 195 women: correct use 2.1, typical 14.2 per 12 mo (Fehring, JOGNN 2007)
- Marquette online RCT: total pregnancy 7 per 100 with monitor vs 18.5 with mucus only over 12 mo (Fehring, Contraception 2013)
- Marquette moderate-quality ranges: monitor only perfect 0, typical 2-6.8; monitor plus mucus typical 6-7 (Urrutia 2018)
- Marquette mucus only: perfect 2.7, typical 4-18.5 (Urrutia 2018)
- Marquette postpartum protocol, 198 women: 2 per 100 correct use, 8 per 100 total at 12 mo postpartum (Bouchard, JABFM 2013)
- Symptothermal (Sensiplan): basal body temperature plus cervical secretions
- Sensiplan cohort, 900 women, 17,638 cycles: 1.8 per 100 over 13 cycles typical (Frank-Herrmann, Hum Reprod 2007)
- Same cohort: 0.6 per 100 over 13 cycles with no unprotected intercourse in the fertile window
- Urrutia 2018: Sensiplan perfect 0.4, typical 1.8. Other symptothermal variants typical 11.2-33.0.
- Basal body temperature methods alone: typical 9.0-9.8 (Urrutia 2018)
- BBT rises only after ovulation, so it confirms ovulation and does not predict it in advance

Lactational amenorrhea method (LAM):

- All 3 required: <6 mo postpartum, amenorrhea, fully or nearly fully breastfeeding (CDC US MEC 2024)
- Feeding intervals no more than 4 hr by day and 6 hr at night (CDC US MEC 2024)
- More than 98% protection in the first 6 mo when criteria met (Trussell 2011)
- 4 prospective studies: 6-mo perfect-use pregnancy 0.5%, 0.6%, 1.0%, 1.5% (Trussell 2011)
- Cochrane 2015: 6-mo life-table pregnancy 0.45% and 2.45% in two controlled studies

FDA-cleared contraceptive apps:

- Natural Cycles, De Novo DEN170052, 2018: BBT and cycle data, women 18 and older
- Natural Cycles Pearl Index: perfect use 1, typical use 6.5 (FDA summary, 15,570 women)
- Natural Cycles notes higher pregnancy risk if hormonal contraception used within the prior 60 days
- Clue Birth Control, 510(k) K193330, 2021: period start dates only, ages 18-45
- Clue eligibility: last 12 cycles 20-40 days, shortest to longest within 9 days, 3 or more cycles after hormones or pregnancy
- Clue Pearl Index: perfect use 0.8, typical use 5.2 (718 women, 6616 cycles)
- Uncleared calendar apps predicted the ovulation day with at most 21% accuracy vs urine LH (ASRM 2022)

Counseling points:

- No medical condition worsens with FABMs. A provider with particular training is generally needed for correct use (CDC US MEC 2024).
- Couple motivation matters: online NFP, 358 couples, 12-mo pregnancy 75 per 100 low-motivation vs 8 high-motivation (Fehring 2013)
- Partner buy-in matters: WHO trial pregnancy discontinuation 1.8% vs 54.7% by male partner difficulty with abstinence (Fertil Steril 1987)
- No STI or HIV protection. Condoms reduce STI risk; PrEP is highly effective against HIV when taken as prescribed.
- Folic acid 0.4-0.8 mg daily for anyone planning or able to become pregnant, grade A (USPSTF 2023)

Achieving pregnancy (ASRM Optimizing natural fertility, 2022):

- Fertile window is the 6 days ending on the day of ovulation
- Intercourse every 1-2 days in the window gives the highest pregnancy rates, 2-3x/wk is nearly equivalent
- Pregnancy rates highest with intercourse on the day of peak mucus
- Ovulation can occur up to 2 days after a positive LH test; false positives in about 7% of cycles
- Using a FABM to time intercourse increases the chance of conceiving in a given cycle
- Infertility evaluation at 12 mo if <35, at 6 mo if 35 or older, more immediate if >40
- Test without delay for irregular cycles, cycle length <25 days, intermenstrual bleeding, oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea (ASRM Fertility evaluation of infertile women, 2021)
- This <25-day infertility cutoff differs from the FIGO <24-day cutoff for abnormal bleeding frequency below

Situations needing extra instruction (CDC US MEC 2024, Accept / Caution / Delay, symptom-based then calendar-based):

- Postmenarche and perimenopause: Caution / Caution, irregular cycles complicate use
- Breastfeeding <6 wk postpartum: Delay / Delay
- Breastfeeding 6 wk or more postpartum: Caution / Delay
- Breastfeeding after menses return: Caution / Caution
- Not breastfeeding <4 wk postpartum: Delay / Delay
- Not breastfeeding 4 wk or more postpartum: Accept / Delay
- Breastfeeding: calendar methods once 3 or more postpartum menses and regular cycles
- Breastfeeding: Standard Days once 4 or more postpartum menses and the latest cycle was 26-32 days
- Not breastfeeding: calendar methods once 3 postpartum menses completed
- Postabortion: Caution / Delay
- Irregular vaginal bleeding: Delay / Delay
- Vaginal discharge: Delay / Accept
- Drugs affecting cycle regularity or signs (lithium, TCAs, anxiolytics, some antibiotics and anti-inflammatories): Caution or Delay
- Chronic febrile illness: Caution / Accept. Acute febrile illness: Delay / Accept.
- PCOS: ovulation does not occur every cycle and periods are irregular, so charting is harder (MedlinePlus)

Abnormal cycle findings to evaluate (AAFP 2019, FIGO):

- Cycle frequency <24 or >38 days
- Cycle-length variation >20 days over 12 mo
- Menses >8 days or >80 mL
- No bleeding for 90 days
- Intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding

use: Use as a physician reference on cannabis use disorder, hyperemesis, medical cannabis, and counseling; the chart block is separate.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Cannabis reference

Cannabis use disorder, DSM-5:

- 11 criteria; 2 or more within 12 months for diagnosis.
- Severity: mild 2-3 criteria, moderate 4-5, severe 6 or more.
- About 3 in 10 people who use cannabis have CUD. Risk is higher with youth onset and frequent use.
- Mean delta-9 THC in tested samples rose from 9% in 2008 to 17% in 2017. High-THC products are linked to more severe CUD symptoms.

Screening:

- CUDIT-R: 8 items, score 0-32. 8 or more suggests hazardous use; 12 or more suggests possible CUD.
- Derivation study: sensitivity 91%, specificity 90%.

Counseling and treatment:

- Nonjudgmental, motivational approach.
- MET, CBT, and contingency management each work; the combination gives the best outcomes. Abstinence rates remain modest.
- No FDA-approved medication for CUD or cannabis withdrawal.
- CBD alone does not appear effective for CUD. Nabiximols reduced withdrawal and craving but is not available in the US.
- SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357, free, confidential, 24/7.

Withdrawal:

- After heavy, prolonged use, usually daily or near daily for at least a few months.
- DSM-5 symptoms: irritability, anxiety, sleep difficulty, decreased appetite or weight loss, restlessness, depressed mood, physical symptoms.
- Physical symptoms: abdominal pain, tremor, sweating, fever, chills, headache.
- Onset 24-48 hr after stopping, peak days 2-5.
- Most symptoms resolve within 2-3 wk on average; sleep disturbance may persist longer.

Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome:

- Rome IV: stereotypical episodic vomiting resembling CVS in onset, duration, and frequency.
- Rome IV: presentation after prolonged, excessive cannabis use; relief of episodes with sustained cessation.
- Rome IV timing: criteria met for the last 3 mo, symptom onset 6 mo or more before diagnosis.
- Supportive: pathologic bathing behavior, prolonged hot baths or showers. This is not specific; about half of CVS patients without cannabis use report it.
- AGA 2024 criteria: episodes 3 or more per yr; cannabis use >1 yr before onset, >4 times/wk on average.
- AGA 2024 confirmation: resolution after 6 mo of abstinence, or at least 3 typical cycle lengths.
- ED, very low certainty: suggest haloperidol or droperidol added to usual care such as ondansetron.
- ED, very low certainty: also suggest topical capsaicin added to usual care.
- Haloperidol 0.05 or 0.1 mg/kg IV beat ondansetron 8 mg IV in a 33-patient RCT. Both acute dystonia returns were at 0.1 mg/kg.
- Capsaicin 0.1% cream to the anterior abdomen reduced nausea at 60 min, not 30 min, in a 30-patient pilot RCT.
- Avoid opioids; they worsen nausea and carry addiction risk. Benzodiazepines are not first line.
- Cure is cannabis cessation. Long-term: cessation counseling plus a TCA such as amitriptyline.
- AGA advises against telling patients to stop cold turkey; it may cause withdrawal and tends to fail.

Medical cannabis evidence:

- Conclusive: oral THC for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
- Substantial: some cannabis products for chronic pain in adults.
- Substantial: oral cannabinoids for patient-reported MS spasticity.
- Living review, 2024: high or comparable THC:CBD products short term gave small pain improvement, mostly neuropathic.
- Same products gave moderate to large increases in dizziness, sedation, and nausea.
- Low THC:CBD oral products may not improve pain or function. Evidence is insufficient for whole-plant cannabis.

FDA-approved cannabinoids:

- Dronabinol, Marinol capsules: chemotherapy nausea and vomiting; anorexia with weight loss in AIDS. Syndros solution is no longer marketed.
- Nabilone, Cesamet: chemotherapy nausea and vomiting after failure of conventional antiemetics.
- Cannabidiol, Epidiolex: seizures with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome, or tuberous sclerosis complex, age 1 yr and older.
- Epidiolex start 2.5 mg/kg PO BID. Check ALT, AST, and total bilirubin before starting.

Drug interactions:

- THC and CBD are metabolized by CYP3A4, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19.
- Most reported clinical interactions: warfarin, valproate, tacrolimus, sirolimus.
- Warfarin case reports: INR 3.49-4.92 with cannabis use, back in range after stopping.
- Dronabinol: CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers change exposure.
- Epidiolex raises N-desmethylclobazam about 3-fold; consider a lower clobazam dose if sedation or other effects occur.
- Epidiolex with valproate raises the risk of transaminase elevation.
- Strong CYP3A4 or CYP2C19 inducers lower CBD levels. Alcohol and other CNS depressants add sedation.
- Delta-8 THC inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 in vitro.

Psychosis:

- Substantial evidence links cannabis use with schizophrenia and other psychoses.
- The link is stronger with earlier onset and more frequent use.
- Case-control study: daily use aOR 3.2 for psychotic disorder; daily high-potency use, THC 10% or more, aOR 4.8.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding:

- ACOG 2025: counsel and screen all pregnant and lactating patients; use evidence-based strategies to reduce use.
- Prenatal cannabis exposure is linked to low birth weight. Other substance use links include preterm birth and developmental delay.
- ACOG 2025 advises cessation in pregnancy and lactation. Continued use is not a contraindication to breastfeeding.
- AAP: avoid marijuana in pregnancy and breastfeeding; no amount is proven safe; THC transfers into breast milk.
- CDC: advise breastfeeding patients not to use marijuana or CBD. If use continues, encourage reduction.
- CDC: no smoking cannabis around infants or children.

Pediatric edible ingestions:

- Children under 6 yr: 207 poison center cases in 2017, 3,054 in 2021, a 1,375% rise.
- Of these, 97.7% were at home, 22.7% were admitted, and 70% with known outcome had CNS depression.
- Signs: trouble walking or sitting up, trouble breathing.
- Counsel locked, childproof storage out of sight. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222.

Driving and delta-8:

- Colorado health department: wait at least 6 hr after smoking, at least 8 hr after eating or drinking cannabis, before driving.
- Substantial evidence links recent cannabis use to motor vehicle crashes.
- Delta-8 THC is not FDA evaluated or approved. FDA had 104 adverse event reports, Dec 2020 to Feb 2022.
- Over half of those needed medical care or admission.

Oklahoma medical marijuana license, _ local:

- OMMA issues patient licenses.
- Age 18 and older: signed Adult Patient Physician Recommendation Form.
- Under 18: two physician signatures on the Minor Patient Physician Recommendation Form.
- Adult licenses are valid for 2 yr.

Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Cannabis reference

Cannabis use disorder, DSM-5:

- 11 criteria; 2 or more within 12 months for diagnosis.
- Severity: mild 2-3 criteria, moderate 4-5, severe 6 or more.
- About 3 in 10 people who use cannabis have CUD. Risk is higher with youth onset and frequent use.
- Mean delta-9 THC in tested samples rose from 9% in 2008 to 17% in 2017. High-THC products are linked to more severe CUD symptoms.

Screening:

- CUDIT-R: 8 items, score 0-32. 8 or more suggests hazardous use; 12 or more suggests possible CUD.
- Derivation study: sensitivity 91%, specificity 90%.

Counseling and treatment:

- Nonjudgmental, motivational approach.
- MET, CBT, and contingency management each work; the combination gives the best outcomes. Abstinence rates remain modest.
- No FDA-approved medication for CUD or cannabis withdrawal.
- CBD alone does not appear effective for CUD. Nabiximols reduced withdrawal and craving but is not available in the US.
- SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357, free, confidential, 24/7.

Withdrawal:

- After heavy, prolonged use, usually daily or near daily for at least a few months.
- DSM-5 symptoms: irritability, anxiety, sleep difficulty, decreased appetite or weight loss, restlessness, depressed mood, physical symptoms.
- Physical symptoms: abdominal pain, tremor, sweating, fever, chills, headache.
- Onset 24-48 hr after stopping, peak days 2-5.
- Most symptoms resolve within 2-3 wk on average; sleep disturbance may persist longer.

Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome:

- Rome IV: stereotypical episodic vomiting resembling CVS in onset, duration, and frequency.
- Rome IV: presentation after prolonged, excessive cannabis use; relief of episodes with sustained cessation.
- Rome IV timing: criteria met for the last 3 mo, symptom onset 6 mo or more before diagnosis.
- Supportive: pathologic bathing behavior, prolonged hot baths or showers. This is not specific; about half of CVS patients without cannabis use report it.
- AGA 2024 criteria: episodes 3 or more per yr; cannabis use >1 yr before onset, >4 times/wk on average.
- AGA 2024 confirmation: resolution after 6 mo of abstinence, or at least 3 typical cycle lengths.
- ED, very low certainty: suggest haloperidol or droperidol added to usual care such as ondansetron.
- ED, very low certainty: also suggest topical capsaicin added to usual care.
- Haloperidol 0.05 or 0.1 mg/kg IV beat ondansetron 8 mg IV in a 33-patient RCT. Both acute dystonia returns were at 0.1 mg/kg.
- Capsaicin 0.1% cream to the anterior abdomen reduced nausea at 60 min, not 30 min, in a 30-patient pilot RCT.
- Avoid opioids; they worsen nausea and carry addiction risk. Benzodiazepines are not first line.
- Cure is cannabis cessation. Long-term: cessation counseling plus a TCA such as amitriptyline.
- AGA advises against telling patients to stop cold turkey; it may cause withdrawal and tends to fail.

Medical cannabis evidence:

- Conclusive: oral THC for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
- Substantial: some cannabis products for chronic pain in adults.
- Substantial: oral cannabinoids for patient-reported MS spasticity.
- Living review, 2024: high or comparable THC:CBD products short term gave small pain improvement, mostly neuropathic.
- Same products gave moderate to large increases in dizziness, sedation, and nausea.
- Low THC:CBD oral products may not improve pain or function. Evidence is insufficient for whole-plant cannabis.

FDA-approved cannabinoids:

- Dronabinol, Marinol capsules: chemotherapy nausea and vomiting; anorexia with weight loss in AIDS. Syndros solution is no longer marketed.
- Nabilone, Cesamet: chemotherapy nausea and vomiting after failure of conventional antiemetics.
- Cannabidiol, Epidiolex: seizures with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome, or tuberous sclerosis complex, age 1 yr and older.
- Epidiolex start 2.5 mg/kg PO BID. Check ALT, AST, and total bilirubin before starting.

Drug interactions:

- THC and CBD are metabolized by CYP3A4, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19.
- Most reported clinical interactions: warfarin, valproate, tacrolimus, sirolimus.
- Warfarin case reports: INR 3.49-4.92 with cannabis use, back in range after stopping.
- Dronabinol: CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers change exposure.
- Epidiolex raises N-desmethylclobazam about 3-fold; consider a lower clobazam dose if sedation or other effects occur.
- Epidiolex with valproate raises the risk of transaminase elevation.
- Strong CYP3A4 or CYP2C19 inducers lower CBD levels. Alcohol and other CNS depressants add sedation.
- Delta-8 THC inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 in vitro.

Psychosis:

- Substantial evidence links cannabis use with schizophrenia and other psychoses.
- The link is stronger with earlier onset and more frequent use.
- Case-control study: daily use aOR 3.2 for psychotic disorder; daily high-potency use, THC 10% or more, aOR 4.8.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding:

- ACOG 2025: counsel and screen all pregnant and lactating patients; use evidence-based strategies to reduce use.
- Prenatal cannabis exposure is linked to low birth weight. Other substance use links include preterm birth and developmental delay.
- ACOG 2025 advises cessation in pregnancy and lactation. Continued use is not a contraindication to breastfeeding.
- AAP: avoid marijuana in pregnancy and breastfeeding; no amount is proven safe; THC transfers into breast milk.
- CDC: advise breastfeeding patients not to use marijuana or CBD. If use continues, encourage reduction.
- CDC: no smoking cannabis around infants or children.

Pediatric edible ingestions:

- Children under 6 yr: 207 poison center cases in 2017, 3,054 in 2021, a 1,375% rise.
- Of these, 97.7% were at home, 22.7% were admitted, and 70% with known outcome had CNS depression.
- Signs: trouble walking or sitting up, trouble breathing.
- Counsel locked, childproof storage out of sight. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222.

Driving and delta-8:

- Colorado health department: wait at least 6 hr after smoking, at least 8 hr after eating or drinking cannabis, before driving.
- Substantial evidence links recent cannabis use to motor vehicle crashes.
- Delta-8 THC is not FDA evaluated or approved. FDA had 104 adverse event reports, Dec 2020 to Feb 2022.
- Over half of those needed medical care or admission.

Oklahoma medical marijuana license, *** local:

- OMMA issues patient licenses.
- Age 18 and older: signed Adult Patient Physician Recommendation Form.
- Under 18: two physician signatures on the Minor Patient Physician Recommendation Form.
- Adult licenses are valid for 2 yr.

use: Use as a physician reference on evidence-based supplements, drug-nutrient depletion, harmful supplements, and unproven functional-medicine tests.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Supplements with reasonable evidence:

- Riboflavin, migraine prevention: 400 mg PO daily. Probably effective (AAN/AHS level B). Side effect: discolored yellow urine.
- Magnesium, migraine prevention: 600 mg PO daily (studied as dicitrate). AAN/AHS level B, AAFP possibly effective. Diarrhea common; toxicity risk rises with reduced kidney function.
- Magnesium note: migraine dose exceeds the 350 mg/day supplemental UL, so use under clinician supervision.
- CoQ10, migraine prevention: 100 mg PO TID. Possibly effective (level C). Mild GI upset or insomnia; may interact with warfarin and insulin.
- Butterbur: AAN retired its 2012 complementary therapy guideline over butterbur hepatotoxicity concerns.
- Psyllium, LDL: about 10 g/day lowers LDL about 13 mg/dL (0.33 mmol/L), moderate-quality meta-analysis evidence.
- Psyllium, IBS: soluble fiber such as psyllium for global IBS symptoms, strong recommendation, moderate quality. Wheat bran not helpful.
- Psyllium, chronic constipation: fiber conditional recommendation, low certainty.
- Psyllium caution: take with at least 8 oz fluid, choking risk per OTC label.
- Icosapent ethyl (prescription EPA): 2 g PO BID added to statin. Trial population: TG 135-499 with ASCVD, or diabetes plus risk factors.
- REDUCE-IT: MACE 17.2 vs 22.0 percent, HR 0.75. AF or flutter hospitalization 3.1 vs 2.1 percent.
- OTC fish oil is not equivalent. VITAL, 1 g/day EPA plus DHA, did not reduce composite MACE in primary prevention.
- STRENGTH, 4 g/day EPA plus DHA carboxylic acid: no CV benefit and more AF.
- Omega-3 and AF: meta-analysis HR 1.25 overall, 1.49 at doses over 1 g/day.
- Vitamin D: use for documented deficiency. Routine testing and above-DRI empiric dosing not advised in healthy adults under 75.
- Vitamin D, empiric (Endocrine Society 2024, suggestion): age 75 or older, pregnancy, high-risk prediabetes, age 1-18. Prefer daily over intermittent high doses.
- Vitamin D, USPSTF: screening for deficiency is an I statement (2021). Against 400 IU or less plus calcium 1000 mg or less for fracture prevention (D, 2018).
- Vitamin D, USPSTF Dec 2024 draft, not final as of Nov 2026: against vitamin D, with or without calcium, to prevent falls or fractures (D). Applies to community-dwelling postmenopausal women and men 60 or older.
- Creatine with resistance training, older adults: meta-analysis of 22 RCTs, about 1.4 kg more lean mass and modest strength gains.
- Creatine dosing in trials: 3-5 g PO daily, some with 20 g/day loading for 5-7 days. Trials that checked kidney and liver function found no harm.
- Melatonin, jet lag: 0.5-5 mg PO at destination bedtime for 5 or more time zones, especially eastward. NNT 2.
- Melatonin, delayed sleep-wake phase: strategically timed melatonin, AASM weak recommendation.
- Melatonin, chronic insomnia: AASM suggests against. Caution with epilepsy and warfarin. Product content often differs from the label.

Medication-induced nutrient depletion:

- Metformin and B12: deficiency risk rises with long-term use and can worsen neuropathy. Check B12 periodically.
- PPI and magnesium: hypomagnesemia, usually after more than 1 yr. FDA: consider Mg before long-term PPI and periodically.
- PPI and B12: reduced food-bound B12 absorption with prolonged use. AGA: do not stop a needed PPI for adverse-event fears alone.
- PPI and iron: patients with iron deficiency may respond less well to oral iron.
- Loop and thiazide diuretics: urinary potassium and magnesium loss.
- Diuretic monitoring: BMP plus Mg at baseline, 2-4 wk after start or dose change, then every 3-6 months.

Supplements with harms or interactions:

- Biotin: interferes with biotin-streptavidin immunoassays. Falsely low troponin; FDA reports 1 death after a missed MI.
- Biotin and thyroid tests: falsely low TSH and results mimicking Graves disease. A single 10 mg dose can interfere within 24 hr.
- Biotin action: ask about biotin use. Tell the lab, and suspect biotin when results do not fit the clinical picture.
- St John's wort: weakens OCPs, warfarin, cyclosporine, digoxin, some HIV and cancer drugs, simvastatin, anticonvulsants.
- St John's wort and SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs: risk of serotonin syndrome.
- Kava: rare serious or fatal liver injury. Avoid with other sedatives.
- Red yeast rice: monacolin K is identical to lovastatin. Content varies over 60-fold, and some products contain the nephrotoxin citrinin.
- Red yeast rice risks: same potential muscle, liver, and kidney harm as statins, plus drug interactions.
- High-dose vitamin E: no CV or cancer benefit (USPSTF D). More hemorrhagic stroke, possible prostate cancer risk at 400 IU/day, and higher mortality in meta-analyses.
- Beta-carotene: USPSTF D. Increased lung cancer in smokers, 18 percent in ATBC and RR 1.28 in CARET.

Functional-medicine tests not supported by evidence:

- IgG food sensitivity panels: IgG marks exposure and tolerance, not allergy. CSACI strongly discourages; AAAAI Choosing Wisely says do not order.
- Salivary cortisol for adrenal fatigue: Endocrine Society says adrenal fatigue is not a real diagnosis and its tests are unvalidated.
- Adrenal fatigue risk: unneeded adrenal hormone supplements can suppress the adrenals and risk adrenal crisis.
- Hair mineral analysis: split samples varied over 10-fold between labs. Unreliable for nutrition or toxic exposure.
- Intracellular or broad micronutrient panels: no studies show clinical validity or utility, per payer evidence reviews.

Sources:

- AAFP, Migraine headache prophylaxis, Am Fam Physician 2019;99(1):17-24
- NIH ODS fact sheets: magnesium, riboflavin, vitamin B12, vitamin E, omega-3, biotin
- Jovanovski E et al. Am J Clin Nutr 2018;108:922-932
- ACG IBS guideline 2021; AGA-ACG chronic idiopathic constipation guideline 2023
- Bhatt DL et al. REDUCE-IT, N Engl J Med 2019;380:11-22
- Gencer B et al. Circulation 2021;144:1981-1990
- Endocrine Society vitamin D guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2024;109:1907-1947
- Chilibeck PD et al. Open Access J Sports Med 2017;8:213-226
- Herxheimer A, Cochrane CD001520; AASM circadian guideline 2015; AASM insomnia guideline 2017
- ADA Standards of Care 2026, section 9; FDA PPI magnesium communication 2011; AGA PPI de-prescribing update 2022
- StatPearls, Antihypertensive medications
- FDA biotin safety communication 2017 and update; NCCIH St John's wort, kava, red yeast rice
- USPSTF vitamin supplementation 2022; ATBC N Engl J Med 1994; CARET N Engl J Med 1996
- CSACI IgG position 2012; Endocrine Society adrenal fatigue; Seidel S et al. JAMA 2001;285:67-72

use: Use when reading an echo report's RVSP, PASP, or RA pressure before acting on it.
body:
Physician reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Echo pressure estimates

RVSP or PASP = TR gradient + estimated RA pressure. Both parts are estimates, and the errors add up.

TR gradient:

- Calculated as 4 x (peak TR velocity in m/s) squared, not measured
- Underestimates with a weak or incomplete TR Doppler signal, or with severe TR
- Overestimates in high-output states such as liver disease or sickle cell disease, and with valve or boundary artifacts

RA pressure from the IVC:

- IVC 2.1 cm or less with >50% sniff collapse: 3 mmHg
- IVC >2.1 cm with <50% sniff collapse: 15 mmHg
- Anything in between: 8 mmHg
- IVC not seen: RA pressure cannot be estimated. Many reports plug in 8 mmHg anyway. Check the report.
- Positive-pressure ventilation: IVC size is unreliable. Use a measured CVP if available.

How to read it:

- Poor TR signal plus a poorly seen IVC: the RVSP is a rough guess. Do not diagnose or exclude PH from it.
- Use peak TR velocity, not estimated RVSP. Peak TRV >2.8 m/s may suggest PH.
- TRV alone cannot confirm or exclude PH. Look at RV size and function signs too.
- PH is defined by right heart cath, mPAP >20 mmHg at rest.

Sources: 2022 ESC/ERS PH guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618, https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/43/38/3618/6673929. Rudski et al, ASE right heart guidelines, J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2010;23:685.

use: Use for the facility teaching physician attestation when the attending reviewed the resident note.

use: Use as a reminder of the specific diagnosis wording that coders and CDI need.
body:
Workflow reference, not for the chart. Delete before signing.

Documentation specificity for coding

Write the specific diagnosis instead of the vague term:

- Infection with organ dysfunction: sepsis with the source, such as sepsis due to UTI, never urosepsis
- Altered mental status: acute metabolic or toxic encephalopathy, when supported
- AKI: acute kidney injury, or acute tubular necrosis when supported
- Uncontrolled nausea and vomiting: intractable nausea and vomiting
- Uncontrolled pain: intractable pain, with location
- Course: write resolving instead of improving, resolved instead of better, worsening instead of worse
- Poor outlook: state the prognosis, such as poor prognosis
- New or increased O2 or ventilatory support for hypoxemia: acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, with SpO2 or PaO2 and the support used
- CO2 retention: acute, chronic, or acute on chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, with pH and PaCO2
- Malnutrition: mild, moderate, or severe protein-calorie malnutrition by intake, weight loss, and muscle or fat loss criteria, not albumin
- Weakness: debility or physical deconditioning, or critical illness myopathy or polyneuropathy after ICU stay when supported
- Heart failure: acute, chronic, or acute on chronic, systolic, diastolic, or combined, HFrEF, HFmrEF, or HFpEF with EF
- Troponin rise with an ischemic picture: type 1 or type 2 MI, with the cause
- Troponin rise without an ischemic picture: acute or chronic non-ischemic myocardial injury
